entries.title: 5 secrets pg fast
titles: 5 secrets pg fast
titleKeys: 5 secrets pg fast
paragraphs: If your PostgreSQL database feels slow, the most dangerous mistake is assuming the problem is hardware. Most teams reach for a bigger server, more CPU, or more memory, while the real problem is hiding in plain sight: one missing index, one N+1 loop, one connection storm, one bloated table, or one query nobody has ever explained properly. Here is the tension: users do not care that PostgreSQL is powerful. They only feel the wait. Every extra second means abandoned checkout flows, slower dashboards, angry support tickets, and engineers guessing under pressure. But the good news is that the biggest wins are usually not exotic. They are five practical fixes you can prove with PostgreSQL's own evidence. In the next few minutes, we are going to turn a slow database into a blazing fast one. We will find the hidden sequential scans, collapse 101 round trips into one query, stop wasting time on connection setup, clean up table bloat, and use EXPLAIN ANALYZE as the truth source. Stay with this deck, because secret number one alone can turn an eight-second query into a sub-millisecond lookup.

Secret number one is missing indexes. Without an index, PostgreSQL has no shortcut. It must read every row in the table and check the predicate one row at a time. That is called a sequential scan. On ten million rows, a missing index can turn a simple lookup into an eight-second table scan. With a B-tree index on the filter column, the same lookup can finish in less than a millisecond. Use pg_stat_user_tables to find tables where sequential scans dominate index scans, especially on tables with more than ten thousand live rows. Then use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so production writes keep flowing while the index builds. The rule is direct: columns used frequently in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses on large tables usually deserve an index, but always verify the new plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

Secret number two is the N+1 query problem. This usually hides in application code and ORMs. The application fetches one list of orders, then loops through every order and fetches the user one query at a time. One hundred orders becomes one hundred and one database round trips. Each round trip has network latency, planning overhead, execution time, and result transfer. The database may be fast for each single query, but the user pays for the repeated trips. The fix is to collapse the loop into one query. Use a JOIN in raw SQL, select_related in Django, joinedload in SQLAlchemy, or a WHERE IN batch query when a join is not appropriate. Detect this with pg_stat_statements. High call counts with very low mean execution time often mean the problem is not one slow query. The problem is the same small query called thousands of times.

Secret number three is connection overhead. Every new PostgreSQL connection is not just a socket. PostgreSQL forks or starts a backend process, allocates memory, negotiates authentication, and may negotiate SSL. That overhead can cost five to twenty milliseconds before the first query even starts. At high request rates, opening fresh connections for every request wastes CPU, memory, and latency. Five hundred concurrent connections can consume gigabytes of memory just sitting idle. PgBouncer solves this by pooling a small number of persistent server connections and letting many application clients reuse them. For typical web applications, transaction pooling is the best balance: the server connection returns to the pool after each transaction. Check pg_stat_activity and SHOW max_connections to understand your current connection pressure. If the application opens many short-lived connections, connection pooling is often one of the fastest wins available.

Secret number four is table bloat. PostgreSQL uses MVCC, which means UPDATE and DELETE do not immediately remove old row versions. They leave dead tuples behind until VACUUM cleans them. When dead tuples accumulate, the table grows far larger than the live data. Queries read more pages, indexes become larger, cache efficiency drops, and even indexed queries become slower because there is more heap and index material to touch. Use pg_stat_user_tables to inspect n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, and last_autovacuum. If a high-traffic table has many dead tuples, run VACUUM ANALYZE and tune autovacuum settings more aggressively for that table. Be careful with VACUUM FULL. It can reclaim disk space, but it locks the table. For online space reclamation, prefer routine VACUUM, better autovacuum thresholds, or pg_repack when you need to rebuild without a long table lock.

Secret number five is EXPLAIN ANALYZE, the most powerful PostgreSQL performance tool. EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL expects to use. ANALYZE executes the query and shows what actually happened. Look for three red flags. First, a sequential scan on a large table where the query returns only a few rows. Second, Rows Removed by Filter in the millions, which means PostgreSQL read many rows and discarded most of them. Third, actual rows much greater than estimated rows, which means statistics are stale or misleading. The before and after example is the whole lesson. Before the index, PostgreSQL scans almost ten million rows and takes several seconds. After the index, the plan becomes an index scan and returns the same rows in a fraction of a millisecond. Never call a performance fix complete until EXPLAIN ANALYZE proves it. The plan is your evidence, not your opinion.

Keep this performance cheat sheet close. To diagnose live pain, start with pg_stat_activity and sort active queries by duration. That shows what is slow right now. To find repeated expensive query patterns, use pg_stat_statements. It tells you calls, mean execution time, total execution time, and which query shapes are costing the system the most overall. To find missing indexes, compare seq_scan and idx_scan in pg_stat_user_tables. To fix safely, use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. To clean dead tuples, run VACUUM ANALYZE and tune autovacuum for the tables that churn constantly. For configuration, remember the broad rules: shared_buffers around twenty-five percent of RAM, effective_cache_size around seventy-five percent of RAM, checkpoint_completion_target near point nine, and aggressive autovacuum settings for high-write tables. Measure before and after every change.

Let us recap the five secrets. First, missing indexes turn targeted lookups into full table scans. Find them with system statistics and fix them with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Second, N+1 query patterns make the application call the database again and again when one JOIN would do the work. Third, connection overhead wastes latency and memory unless PgBouncer or another pooler reuses connections. Fourth, table bloat from dead tuples makes every query touch more pages than necessary. VACUUM and autovacuum tuning keep the table healthy. Fifth, EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the X-ray for every slow query. It shows the real plan, real rows, and real time. Apply even two of these five fixes and users will feel the difference. Apply all five and your PostgreSQL system becomes much easier to reason about under pressure.

Your database is now on the path to blazing fast. The secret is not magic and it is not one hidden setting. It is disciplined diagnosis followed by targeted fixes. Index the paths your queries actually use. Collapse N+1 loops into joins. Pool connections instead of creating them repeatedly. Vacuum away dead tuples before bloat becomes the workload. And use EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after every change. examples.title: Try it yourself
examples.code:
SELECT current_user,
       rolsuper       AS is_superuser,
       rolbypassrls   AS skips_row_security,
       rolcreaterole  AS can_make_roles,
       rolcreatedb    AS can_make_databases
  FROM pg_roles
 WHERE rolname = current_user;

examples.title: Example 2
examples.code:
SELECT r.rolname AS grants_shell_execution
  FROM pg_auth_members m
  JOIN pg_roles r ON r.oid = m.roleid
  JOIN pg_roles u ON u.oid = m.member
 WHERE u.rolname = current_user
   AND r.rolname IN ('pg_execute_server_program', 'pg_read_server_files',
                     'pg_write_server_files');

examples.title: Example 4
examples.code: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE orders, order_items TO agent_ro;

examples.title: Example 5
examples.code:
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE app_owner IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO agent_ro;

examples.title: Example 6
examples.code: ALTER ROLE agent_ro SET default_transaction_read_only = on;

takeaways: So what is your agent connected as?

references.claim: COPY FROM PROGRAM runs a shell command as the OS user owning the server process, and is available to superusers and members of pg_execute_server_program
rolsuper in pg_roles identifies a superuser role, which bypasses all permission checks except LOGIN
Superuser bypasses all permission checks, including row level security
pg_authid holds role password hashes and is readable only by superuser
PostgreSQL 15 removed the default CREATE privilege for PUBLIC on the public schema
default_transaction_read_only is USERSET; a session can change it with SET at any time
Reported incident: an agent retained write access after a build phase, deleted production records, then generated synthetic rows
GRANT supports column-level privileges for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and REFERENCES
Table owners bypass row security unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set; roles with BYPASSRLS skip policies entirely
statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and lock_timeout can be set per role with ALTER ROLE SET
application_name is settable in the connection string and is available to log_line_prefix via %a
pg_stat_activity exposes application_name, state, query, wait_event and query_start per backend

entries.title: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL: Complete Production Architecture
titles: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL: Complete Production Architecture
titleKeys: amazon aurora postgresql complete production architecture
paragraphs: Managed doesn't mean unbreakable. But on Aurora, the thing that breaks is compute. Your data sits in a separate storage service that the instance failure never touched. So when the writer dies, what happens next depends on one question. Do you have a replica? With one, Aurora promotes it, usually in under thirty seconds. Without one, Aurora has to build you a new writer, and that takes minutes. Lose a whole availability zone and writes keep going. We'll build all of it, break it, and measure it.

So who owns what? On Aurora the line moved down. AWS now runs the whole storage layer. Six copies, the write quorum, segment repair, continuous backup. All of it, invisible to you. Everything above that is still yours. Your schema, your queries, your parameters, how the app reconnects. And one thing hasn't changed. The rds_superuser role is powerful, but it is not a real superuser, and there is still no shell.

Here's the idea everything else follows from. On Aurora, compute and storage are two different services. The instance has no volume of its own. And the writer doesn't push pages down to a disk. It ships redo log records to the storage service, and storage builds the pages. Now look at the layout. Your cluster volume is cut into ten gibibyte pieces called protection groups. Every one of those pieces is stored six times. Two copies in each of three availability zones. Not six copies of your database. Six copies of every slice.

Six copies buys you a specific guarantee, so let's be precise. A write is acknowledged when four of the six copies have it. A read needs three. Now lose an availability zone. Two copies are gone, four are left, and four of six is still met. Your writes never stop. Lose that zone plus one more copy and you have three. Still readable, still repairable, but no longer writable. That's the honest edge. And repair happens per ten gibibyte segment, from the surviving peers, in parallel.

Notice what you never configured. There is no volume type, no size, no provisioned throughput. The cluster volume grows on its own, in ten gibibyte steps, up to two hundred and fifty six tebibytes. Most articles still say one hundred and twenty eight, and that number is out of date. And unlike RDS, this volume shrinks. Dynamic resize hands space back after you delete data, which is something RDS storage has never done.

Let's create it. And the first difference is the API you call. On RDS you create a DB instance. On Aurora you create a cluster, and then you create instances inside it. Engine, Aurora PostgreSQL. Notice there is no storage size field anywhere on this page. But there is a choice that decides your bill. Aurora Standard charges you per storage request. I O Optimized doesn't, and costs more per hour. We'll come back to that. Your subnet group needs at least two availability zones. Use three where you can. Aurora's storage keeps six copies across three either way.

Networking is the same discipline as any production database. The cluster sits in private subnets, and that subnet group has to span at least two zones. The security group allows five four three two from your application only, never from anywhere. Force TLS with the cluster parameter, and verify the certificate from the client. IAM authentication gives you short lived tokens instead of stored passwords. And public accessibility stays off.

Now prove it. Connect to the cluster endpoint with verify-full, so the certificate is actually checked. Ask the server whether it's in recovery. False means you reached the writer. Ask for the Aurora version, and you get the engine build underneath. One rule before we go on. There is an instance endpoint for every instance, and it must never appear in your application config.

Aurora splits parameters into two groups, and that trips people up. The cluster parameter group holds settings that must agree across the cluster. Logical replication, force SSL. The DB parameter group is per instance. Shared buffers, work memory, max connections. Which gives you something RDS can't do. You can tune a reader differently from the writer. Static parameters still need a reboot to take effect.

Serverless version two changes how you buy compute. Capacity is measured in Aurora capacity units. One unit is roughly two gibibytes of memory plus matching CPU and network. You set a floor and a ceiling, and Aurora resizes in place, in seconds, with no failover. It can go all the way down to zero on recent PostgreSQL versions, and pause. But be honest about the trade. Waking up costs about fifteen seconds, and at steady load this is more expensive than a provisioned instance.

Backup on Aurora works differently, and it's genuinely better. It's continuous, and it happens inside the storage layer. Not a job running on your instance. So there is no backup window, no snapshot pause, and nothing to schedule around. Retention runs one to thirty five days, and you can land on any second inside it. One honest note on cost. You're billed on how much the volume changes. So a write heavy database is expensive to keep for thirty five days.

Point in time recovery is still not an undo button. And on Aurora there's an extra thing to understand. Restore doesn't rewind your cluster. It builds a new one. New volume, new writer, new endpoints. Which means your application is pointed at the old cluster until you move it. Check the earliest restorable time before you promise anyone anything. And you choose the storage billing mode again at restore.

Two things here, and one of them is a warning. First, cloning. Aurora can hand you a full writable copy of a terabyte cluster in minutes, because it copies nothing. The clone shares the same pages, and you only pay for what diverges. That's the best pre-migration tool Aurora has. Now the warning. People come to Aurora expecting Backtrack, that rewind the cluster in seconds feature. Watch what happens when you ask for it. Backtrack is Aurora MySQL only. On PostgreSQL, your undo is point in time recovery into a new cluster.

Now add readers. And this is where the shared volume pays off. An Aurora replica doesn't get a copy of your data. It attaches to the same volume the writer is already using. So adding a reader adds compute, and nothing else. No second copy, no storage bill, no replication stream to fall behind. You can run up to fifteen of them. Every one of them is reading pages the writer just wrote.

Replica lag changes unit, and that's the whole lesson. On RDS you watch lag in seconds. On Aurora you watch it in milliseconds. Typically ten to twenty, and usually well under a hundred. Because nothing is being shipped. The pages are already there. What you're actually measuring is how fast a reader applies and caches them. So the causes are different, and so are the fixes.

Aurora gives you four kinds of endpoint, and each has one job. The cluster endpoint always points at the writer. The reader endpoint spreads connections across your readers. Custom endpoints let you name your own subset of instances. And instance endpoints are for debugging, only. Let's prove the reader is read only. Ask it whether it's in recovery, and it says true. Try to insert, and PostgreSQL refuses, because it's a read only transaction.

One warning about the reader endpoint. It is not a load balancer. It's DNS, and it round robins per new connection. It never rebalances the connections you already have. So a long lived pool resolves once, and can pin every single connection onto one reader. Three readers, and one of them is doing all the work. Custom endpoints isolate reader groups. The real fix is recycling connections, or an RDS Proxy endpoint.

When the writer dies, Aurora promotes a reader. And because the volume already holds every acknowledged commit, promotion isn't data recovery. It's a role change, plus a cache that has to warm up. Which reader wins? You decide, with promotion tiers, zero through fifteen. Lowest number wins. If two readers tie, the larger instance wins. So set them deliberately. Otherwise Aurora will happily promote your smallest analytics reader into production.

Let's simulate a writer failure. One command triggers the failover. Watch the probe. Writes fail for a few seconds, the cluster endpoint moves, and the promoted reader starts taking writes. AWS documents under sixty seconds, and often under thirty when a replica is there to promote. Every acknowledged commit survived, and here's why. The volume was never in doubt. Four of six copies had every one of those commits before the writer died. In flight transactions still aborted. The old writer comes back as a reader.

Now the same test, on a cluster with one instance. No reader, so nothing to promote. Watch how different this is. Aurora has to provision a replacement writer, and that is minutes of downtime, not seconds. AWS documents that replacement as typically under ten minutes. So be clear about what you're buying. Fast failover comes from having a promotable reader, not from Aurora by itself.

sections.heading: Storage Fault
paragraphs: Now let's simulate losing an availability zone, and watch the promise from earlier hold. Two of the six copies are gone. Four remain, four of six is still the write quorum, and look at the probe. Not one failed write. Meanwhile the volume rebuilds the missing segments from surviving peers, ten gibibytes at a time, in parallel. That's why recovery is minutes and not hours. The blast radius of a bad disk is one segment.

Everything so far has been one region. Aurora Global Database extends the same trick across regions. The storage layer replicates, not the engine, so there's no logical replication to break. You get up to ten secondary regions, sixteen readers in each, and lag that's typically under a second. A planned failover is managed and loses nothing. An unplanned promotion is faster, but you accept a small gap. Secondary regions are read only. Write forwarding sends their writes to the primary. And you pay for a second region you hope never to use.

RDS Proxy works with Aurora, and it does two useful things. It pools connections, so thousands of clients become a handful of database sessions. And it gives you read only proxy endpoints that route to your readers. Use it mainly for connection management. But don't dismiss the failover benefit. It bypasses DNS caching and holds application connections through a promotion.

Here's the proxy failure mode nobody warns you about. Multiplexing only works while a session stays clean. The moment a client does something session specific, the proxy pins that connection to one backend, and stops sharing it. Set a parameter, prepare a statement, create a temp table, listen on a channel, take a session advisory lock. All of those pin. Watch pinning climb, and your effective pool collapses. PostgreSQL has no pinning filters to turn this off.

What you watch on Aurora is different, because some of these numbers are money. Volume bytes used is your storage bill. Volume read and write counters are your request bill, if you're on Standard. Aurora replica lag, in milliseconds. Capacity unit utilization, if you went serverless. And the buffer cache hit ratio, which on Aurora is not just latency. A cache miss is a billable read. Shared buffers is now a cost parameter.

sections.heading: Maintenance Zdp
paragraphs: Minor version upgrades try something clever, called zero downtime patching. Aurora waits for a quiet moment, preserves your connections, and swaps the engine underneath them. When it works, nobody notices. But read the words best effort carefully. A long running transaction, open temporary tables, an active logical replication slot. Any of those, and Aurora falls back to an ordinary restart. So you can plan for probably zero downtime. You cannot promise zero.

Major version upgrades are a different problem, and Aurora has a good answer. A blue green deployment clones your cluster, upgrades the copy, and keeps it in sync with logical replication. You test the green cluster properly, with real traffic shapes, for as long as you like. Then you switch over, and AWS documents that as typically under a minute. Your endpoints follow. The old cluster stays around, in case you need it.

Before you decide, here's what Aurora is not. There is no operating system and no shell. rds_superuser is not a superuser. You get the extensions AWS supports, and no others. There is no Backtrack on PostgreSQL, so no rewind. There are no storage knobs at all. No volume type, no throughput setting, no filesystem, so your only lever is doing fewer reads and writes. Max connections is bound by a formula on instance memory. And nothing here protects you from a delete you wrote yourself.

Now the part that decides whether Aurora fits. Compute is the obvious line, and readers multiply it. Storage is per gibibyte of what you use. And then there are requests. On Aurora Standard, every storage read and write is metered, and that line has no ceiling. A plan that flips to a sequential scan now costs you money, every time it runs. I O Optimized removes that risk. You pay about thirty percent more per hour, and no request charges. Once requests pass about a quarter of your Aurora spend, switch. And know the direction. Dropping back to Standard is available any time. Going the other way is once every thirty days.

So here's the checklist. One volume, six copies, three zones. At least one replica, or you don't actually have fast failover. Promotion tiers set on purpose. Endpoints routed properly, with custom endpoints for analytics. Clone before you migrate, and remember there is no rewind. And pick your storage billing mode deliberately. Then three questions decide Aurora against RDS. How available does this need to be. How much read scale do you need. And how predictable does the bill need to be.

entries.title: postgresql dba cheat sheet 5 slow query diagnostics
titles: postgresql dba cheat sheet 5 slow query diagnostics
titleKeys: postgresql dba cheat sheet 5 slow query diagnostics
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:00 Narration This query takes forty-seven seconds. It ran fine last week. Nothing changed - except the data grew. Here is what happened. Week one: report query, two hundred milliseconds. Sequential scan on fifty thousand rows. Fine. Month three: the table hits two million rows.

The planner still picks a sequential scan. No one notices. Month six: five million rows. Nested loop with a thousand iterations. Twelve seconds. Someone files a ticket. Today: ten million rows. Forty-seven seconds. The dashboard times out. Users complain. One index will fix this. Forty-seven seconds down to zero point two.

Two hundred thirty-five times faster. EXPLAIN ANALYZE is not how you find slow queries - it is how you understand WHY they are slow. Stay to the end. I show the full workflow: find it, understand it, fix it. No greeting. The incident timeline on the left is the main visual - walk through each degradation step with increasing urgency.

Three stat cards on the right: 47s (red), 0. 2s (green), 235× (cyan). SVG shows the diagnostic workflow: Find → Understand → Fix, with auto_explain and pg_stat_activity as supporting tools below. Timestamp: 0:30 Narration EXPLAIN versus EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Know the difference. EXPLAIN shows the plan.

It does NOT execute the query. Safe to run on UPDATE and DELETE. Use it to check plan shape. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows reality. Actual rows, actual time, actual buffers. Always add BUFFERS. Without BUFFERS you cannot see I/O. The minimum for real diagnostics: EXPLAIN open parenthesis ANALYZE comma BUFFERS close parenthesis.

Look at the output. Estimated rows fifteen. Actual rows twelve. Close enough - statistics are good. But the execution time: eight hundred forty-seven milliseconds. Sequential scan on the orders table. Rows removed by filter: nine million nine hundred ninety-nine thousand. It read the entire table to find twelve rows.

Shared read one hundred twenty-seven thousand pages. That is disk I/O. Shared hit eight twelve - that was in cache. The read number is the problem. Danger: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query. Wrap UPDATE and DELETE in BEGIN, ROLLBACK. Right: 2×2 grid comparing EXPLAIN vs ANALYZE, BUFFERS explanation card, and two warning callouts.

The key teaching moment: 'Rows Removed by Filter: 9,999,988' - that number should shock. Timestamp: 1:30 Narration Reading an execution plan. Four things to check every time. One: row estimates. Compare the estimated rows with actual rows. If they differ by ten times or more, statistics are stale.

Run ANALYZE on the table. Two: scan type. Sequential scan on a large table with a selective filter is a problem. Missing index. But sequential scan returning most rows is normal - do not blindly add indexes. Three: join type. Nested Loop is great when the outer side is small. Bad when it is large.

Check the loops count. Actual time zero point zero one milliseconds looks fast. But with loops equals one hundred thousand, that is one thousand milliseconds total. Always multiply. Four: buffer I/O. Shared hit means the page was in shared buffers. Fast. Shared read means it was NOT in cache - could be disk.

Temp read and write means sort or hash spill to disk. Increase work_mem per session. Remember: cost units are arbitrary. Compare within a plan, not across queries. And sequential scan is NOT always bad - on small tables or when returning most rows, it is faster than an index scan.

Each has a code snippet example. Right sidebar: four callout boxes covering cost units, Seq Scan defense, loops multiplier, and Bitmap Heap Scan phases. The loops multiplier is the most commonly missed concept. Timestamp: 3:00 Narration pg_stat_statements. This is how you find the worst queries.

Create the extension. Add it to shared_preload_libraries and restart. Now it tracks every query: total execution time, calls, mean time, rows, and buffer hits. The top ten query: SELECT LEFT of query sixty characters, calls, round total_exec_time divided by one thousand as total_sec, round mean_exec_time as avg_ms, rows, shared_blks_hit plus shared_blks_read as total_blks, FROM pg_stat_statements, ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC, LIMIT ten.

Sort by what matters. Total_exec_time for biggest overall cost. Mean_exec_time for slowest per call. Calls for most frequent. Shared_blks_read for most I/O. Prioritize by impact. A query running ten thousand times per hour at fifty milliseconds equals five hundred seconds of total database time.

More impactful than one query at five seconds. Reset periodically with pg_stat_statements_reset. PostgreSQL fourteen and later normalizes query text - WHERE id equals dollar one groups all parameter variants. Right: 'Sort By What Matters' card with four sort strategies, 'Prioritize by Impact' card with the frequency×time math, and two callouts on reset and PG 14+ normalization.

Timestamp: 4:30 Narration pg_stat_activity for what is slow right now. auto_explain to catch slow plans in production logs. pg_stat_activity: SELECT pid, now minus query_start as runtime, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, LEFT of query eighty characters. Filter where state equals active and runtime over five seconds.

The wait_event column tells you WHY it is slow. DataFileRead means the table needs caching or an index. Lock means contention. Client means the application is slow to consume results. auto_explain: add it to shared_preload_libraries. Set log_min_duration to one second. Enable log_analyze, log_buffers, and log_timing.

Now every query over one second gets its full EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan logged automatically. You do not need to reproduce the problem. For per-session debugging without a restart: LOAD auto_explain, then SET auto_explain. log_min_duration equals five hundred milliseconds. The overhead: log_analyze adds timing to every query.

Start with a high threshold and lower gradually. Also set log_min_duration_statement equals one second in postgresql. conf - no extension needed. It logs the SQL text of every slow query. auto_explain (yellow card, right) with postgresql. conf config + per-session LOAD trick. Bottom: log_min_duration_statement callout.

Emphasis on 'you do not need to reproduce the problem. '

Timestamp: 5:30 Narration Five fix patterns that solve ninety percent of slow queries. One: add a missing index. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on orders, customer_id comma order_date. Always CONCURRENTLY in production - no write lock.

sections.heading: Cold Open: Your Primary Just Died
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:00 Narration Your primary just died. And the standby is six hours behind. Thursday, two AM. Last WAL replay confirmed. Standby is in sync. Three AM. A network glitch drops the replication stream. Nobody notices. Three through eight AM - the standby falls six hours behind. No alert. Nine AM. Primary disk fails. Database down. Nine-oh-two. You promote the standby - and six hours of transactions are gone. Six hours of lag equals six hours of data loss. With synchronous mode, data loss drops to zero. With automatic failover, promotion happens in under thirty seconds. In this video, every replication command you need. Streaming, logical, failover, and monitoring. PostgreSQL 14 through 18. Replication lag is invisible until failover makes it catastrophic. Stay to the end - I show the monitoring queries that catch it early. Delivery Notes Open fast. No greeting. The disaster timeline is the visual - walk through each step. Pause after 'six hours of transactions are gone.' The failover SVG on the right shows Primary → Standby → Promote. Lighter slide now - no 'What You Will Learn' card, just tension + the SVG.

sections.heading: Two Types of Replication
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:30 Narration Before we touch any commands, the architecture. Your primary sends data two ways. Streaming replication: raw WAL bytes to the standby. Exact byte-for-byte copy. Same version required. This is your HA and failover path. Logical replication: decoded changes to subscribers. Table-level selection. Cross-version. Subscriber stays writable. This is your migration and analytics path. Streaming: exact copies, near-zero lag, failover capable. But all-or-nothing and version-locked. Logical: table-level control, cross-version PG 14 to 18, writable subscribers. But DDL and sequences are not replicated. Most production setups need both. Streaming for HA, logical for migration. Delivery Notes SVG architecture diagram is the main visual. Trace the two paths. The comparison cards below are the reference. Emphasize 'most production setups need both.'

sections.heading: Streaming Replication Setup
paragraphs: Timestamp: 1:00 Narration Streaming replication. Primary to standby in five commands. On the primary: wal_level equals replica, max_wal_senders ten, max_replication_slots ten, wal_keep_size one gigabyte, hot_standby on. In pg_hba.conf, add a replication line. Create the user and a physical replication slot. On the standby: pg_basebackup with dash R. The dash R flag creates standby.signal and writes primary_conninfo automatically. Then pg_ctl start. The dash R flag does the heavy lifting. No manual configuration needed. Delivery Notes Left column is primary, right is standby. Walk through each parameter. The -R flag callout is the key insight.

sections.heading: Logical Replication: Pub/Sub
paragraphs: Timestamp: 2:30 Narration Logical replication. Publish and subscribe. On the publisher: wal_level to logical. CREATE PUBLICATION - three options. FOR ALL TABLES, FOR TABLE with specific names, or PG 15 plus WHERE clause for row filtering. ALTER PUBLICATION to add or drop tables. On the subscriber: create tables first, schema must match. CREATE SUBSCRIPTION with connection string and publication. In PG 17 plus, add failover equals true for slot synchronization. Check pg_stat_subscription. Pause and resume with DISABLE and ENABLE. Critical: DDL is not replicated. Schema changes must be applied manually on both sides. Delivery Notes Left is publisher, right is subscriber. Emphasize PG 15 WHERE and PG 17 failover. The DDL warning is the key teaching moment.

sections.heading: Failover + Promote
paragraphs: Timestamp: 4:30 Narration Primary is down. Three promotion methods. SQL: SELECT pg_promote true comma sixty. pg_ctl: pg_ctl promote. Trigger file: touch the promote trigger file. After promotion: pg_is_in_recovery returns false. Update other standbys. PG 17 adds pg_createsubscriber to convert physical standby to logical. Seven-step failover checklist. Confirm primary is down. Check lag. Promote. Verify. Update DNS. Redirect standbys. Notify teams. For zero data loss, set synchronous_standby_names. The primary waits for standby WAL write. Promotion is irreversible - the old primary needs pg_rewind or a fresh pg_basebackup to rejoin. Delivery Notes Left column: three methods and post-promotion steps. Right: checklist and sync/async. Emphasize 'promotion is irreversible.'

sections.heading: pg stat replication The DBA Dashboard
paragraphs: Timestamp: 6:00 Narration pg_stat_replication. Run on the primary. Every standby appears. The query: client address, state, sync state, replay lag bytes, replay lag interval. Healthy: streaming, sync, zero lag. Problem: catchup, async, two gigabytes behind, six hours lag. If you see this, investigate immediately. Network, disk I/O, max_wal_senders. Three more queries. pg_replication_slots for slot monitoring. Drop inactive slots - they bloat WAL. pg_stat_subscription for logical replication status. Delivery Notes The monitoring query is the top visual. Healthy vs problem comparison is the teaching moment. Red highlighted problem row is what viewers screenshot.

sections.heading: Demo Part 1: Streaming + Failover
paragraphs: Timestamp: 7:00 Narration Live demo part one. Streaming replication and failover. On the primary: configure wal_level and max_wal_senders. Restart. Create the replication user and slot. Create a test table, insert a hundred thousand rows. Check pg_stat_replication - streaming, zero lag. On the standby: pg_basebackup with dash R. Start it. pg_is_in_recovery returns true. Query the test table - hundred thousand rows. Read replica works. Now failover. pg_promote true comma sixty. Returns true. pg_is_in_recovery returns false - it is the primary now. Insert a row. INSERT zero one. Writes accepted. Delivery Notes Two terminals. Left is PRIMARY node1, right is STANDBY node2. Walk through commands as if typing live. The pg_promote moment is the dramatic peak. Let 'INSERT 0 1' breathe.

sections.heading: Demo Part 2: Logical Pub/Sub
paragraphs: Timestamp: 7:45 Narration Demo part two. Logical replication. On the publisher: set wal_level to logical, restart. Create an orders table with sample data. CREATE PUBLICATION orders_pub FOR TABLE orders. On the subscriber: create the matching table. CREATE SUBSCRIPTION with the connection string and publication name. Initial sync happens automatically - both rows appear. Insert a new row on the publisher - it appears on the subscriber automatically. And the subscriber is writable. You can insert local-only data that does not go back to the publisher. This is the key difference from streaming - logical replication is selective and the subscriber stays independent. Delivery Notes Two terminals. Left is PUBLISHER node1, right is SUBSCRIBER node2 with orange badge. The 'subscriber is writable' moment is the key insight. Walk through initial sync, then live replication, then local write.

sections.heading: 5 Replication Mistakes That Cause Outages
paragraphs: Timestamp: 8:30 Narration Five mistakes that cause outages. One: not monitoring replication lag. Lag grows silently. Alert when replay_lag exceeds one minute. Two: inactive slots bloating WAL. A disconnected standby fills pg_wal until the disk is full. Drop inactive slots. Three: forgetting DDL in logical replication. ALTER TABLE does not replicate. Subscriber breaks. Apply DDL manually. Four: rejoining old primary without pg_rewind. After promotion, the timeline diverges. You cannot just restart it. Five: using async when you need zero data loss. Set synchronous_standby_names for zero RPO. Delivery Notes Five red cards. Walk through with increasing urgency. One and two are most common. This is the slide people share.

sections.heading: Quick Summary + Cheat Sheet
paragraphs: Timestamp: 9:30 Narration Five tools. Streaming with pg_basebackup dash R. Logical with CREATE PUB/SUB. Failover with pg_promote. Monitor with pg_stat_replication. pg_rewind to rejoin old primary. Streaming cheat sheet: pg_basebackup dash R, pg_create_physical_replication_slot, pg_promote, pg_rewind. Logical cheat sheet: CREATE PUBLICATION, CREATE SUBSCRIPTION, pg_stat_replication, pg_stat_subscription, pg_replication_slots. From single point of failure to replicated, monitored, failover-ready. Delivery Notes Five tool cards. Two cheat sheet panels. Gradient progress bar. Keep energy up before the CTA.

sections.heading: Subscribe + Next Episode
paragraphs: Timestamp: 10:00 Narration If you manage PostgreSQL in production, subscribe and press the bell icon. Like if this helped. Save for reference. Next up: Cheat Sheet number three - PostgreSQL Monitoring Commands. pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_user_tables, VACUUM monitoring, and bloat detection. Dr. Ibrar Ahmed. PostgreSQL Deep Dives. See you in the next one. Delivery Notes Premium CTA. 120px bell icon with floating animation. Rainbow gradient bar. SUBSCRIBE button. Like + Save. Cheat Sheet #3 teaser. End on channel name.

titles: postgresql dba cheat sheet 1 backup
titleKeys: postgresql dba cheat sheet 1 backup
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:00 Narration Your database has no backup. Or worse - it has one you have never tested. Let me show you what that looks like. Monday, nine AM. Last successful backup ran. Everything is fine. Tuesday, two AM. The cron job fails silently. Nobody notices. Wednesday through Sunday - five days of backups are missing.

Still no alert. The following Monday, three PM. A junior developer runs DROP TABLE users on production. And the latest backup is seven days old. Two point eight million rows, gone. Seventy-five percent of organizations have never tested a restore. The average cost of database downtime is a hundred and fifty thousand dollars per hour.

And with no backup, your recovery time is zero - because there is nothing to recover from. In the next ten minutes, I am going to teach you every PostgreSQL backup command you need. pg_dump, pg_dumpall, pg_basebackup, pg_restore, and Point-in-Time Recovery. Every command runs on PostgreSQL 14 through 18.

No extensions required. Five seconds. That is how long it took to destroy that database. Stay to the end - I will show you the five mistakes ninety percent of DBAs make. No greeting. No intro. The disaster timeline is the visual - walk through each step with increasing tension. Pause briefly after 'two point eight million rows, gone.

' The 5-second hook at the end is the retention anchor. Timestamp: 0:30 Narration Before we touch any commands, let me show you the big picture. Your application writes to PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL stores data files and WAL - Write-Ahead Log - files. From here you have two paths. Logical backup with pg_dump and pg_dumpall - these extract SQL or custom-format archives.

Physical backup with pg_basebackup - this copies the entire cluster at the file system level. Both should go to off-site storage - S3, NFS, a second data center. And from storage, you restore. The critical step most people skip: verify monthly. Now, three backup methods. Logical: pg_dump for single databases, cross-version compatible, but slow on large databases and no point-in-time recovery.

Physical: pg_basebackup for full cluster copies, fast, great for replication standby, but locked to the same major version. And PITR - Point-in-Time Recovery - combining a base backup with WAL archiving so you can restore to any second. We cover logical and physical in depth today.

Full PITR deep dive comes in Cheat Sheet number two. Trace the flow left to right as you narrate. Pause on 'verify monthly' - that is the key takeaway. The three method cards at the bottom get a quick comparison. Mention the PITR teaser to build series anticipation. Timestamp: 1:00 Narration pg_dump.

The workhorse of logical backup. Seven commands you need to know. First: pg_dump dash Fc. Custom format. Compressed, supports parallel restore. This is your default for production. Second: pg_dump dash Fd dash j four. Directory format with four parallel jobs. Fastest dump for large databases.

Third: single table. Dash t users. When you just need one table back. Fourth: schema only. No data, just structure. Perfect for migrations. Fifth: exclude a table. Dash capital T audit_logs. Skip the massive audit table nobody needs in the backup. Now pg_dumpall. Two commands. pg_dumpall for the entire cluster - all databases, roles, tablespaces.

But it only outputs plain SQL. No compression. No parallel. So in practice, use pg_dumpall dash dash globals-only for roles and tablespaces, then run pg_dump dash Fc on each database individually. Format comparison. Plain SQL is readable but slow to restore. Custom format is compressed and supports selective restore.

Directory format gives you parallel on both dump and restore. Always use Fc or Fd in production. Five to ten times faster restore, half the file size. Point to flags as you say them. The format comparison sidebar is the reference - pause on it. Emphasize: 'Always use Fc or Fd. ' The globals-only callout is the key insight most tutorials miss.

Timestamp: 2:30 Narration pg_basebackup. Physical backup. Copies the entire cluster at the file level. Five commands. Plain format with dash Fp - a direct copy of the data directory. Tar plus gzip with dash Ft dash z - a single portable archive. Replication standby with dash R - automatically configures recovery.

And new in PostgreSQL 17: incremental backup. Instead of copying everything again, only the blocks that changed since the last backup get copied. Then pg_combinebackup merges the incremental with the base. Now pg_restore. Six commands. Basic restore from custom format. Parallel restore with dash j four - this is massive.

Four concurrent connections rebuilding your database. Single table restore - pull just the users table out of a full dump. List contents with dash l - this gives you a table of contents file you can edit, then restore selectively with dash capital L. And cross-server restore with dash dash no-owner and dash dash no-privileges - when you are moving between servers with different role configurations.

The dash j four flag runs parallel connections. On a multi-core server, this cuts restore time dramatically. Walk through each command. Emphasize PG 17 incremental as the new feature. The parallel restore callout is the key production tip. Timestamp: 5:00 Narration Live demo. Real numbers.

We have a production database. Forty-eight gigabytes. Step one - confirm the size. pg_database_size returns forty-eight GB. Step two - dump it. pg_dump dash Fc dash Z six. Custom format, compression level six. This takes a while on forty-eight gigs, but the output is worth it. Step three - verify the dump is readable.

pg_restore dash l reads the archive header and table of contents. Two hundred and forty-seven TOC entries. Step four - check the compressed size. Eight point two gigabytes. Eighty-three percent smaller than the original. Now the restore. Create a fresh empty database. Run pg_restore with dash j four for parallel.

Four concurrent connections rebuilding tables, indexes, constraints. Watch it work. Creating table public. users. Processing data. Creating indexes. Total restore time: four minutes and twelve seconds. Verify row counts. Orders: twelve point eight million. Users: two point eight million.

Everything matches. Forty-eight gigs backed up, compressed to eight point two gigs, restored in four minutes twelve seconds. That is what dash Fc and dash j four give you. Left is BACKUP (red REC badge), right is RESTORE (green REC badge). Walk through each command as if typing live.

Pause on 'verify monthly' - that is the key takeaway. The three method cards at the bottom get a quick comparison. Mention the PITR teaser to build series anticipation.

sections.heading: pg dump + pg dumpall
paragraphs: Timestamp: 1:00 Narration pg_dump. The workhorse of logical backup. Seven commands you need to know. First: pg_dump dash Fc. Custom format. Compressed, supports parallel restore. This is your default for production. Second: pg_dump dash Fd dash j four. Directory format with four parallel jobs. Fastest dump for large databases. Third: single table. Dash t users. When you just need one table back. Fourth: schema only. No data, just structure. Perfect for migrations. Fifth: exclude a table. Dash capital T audit_logs. Skip the massive audit table nobody needs in the backup. Now pg_dumpall. Two commands. pg_dumpall for the entire cluster - all databases, roles, tablespaces. But it only outputs plain SQL. No compression. No parallel. So in practice, use pg_dumpall dash dash globals-only for roles and tablespaces, then run pg_dump dash Fc on each database individually. Format comparison. Plain SQL is readable but slow to restore. Custom format is compressed and supports selective restore. Directory format gives you parallel on both dump and restore. Always use Fc or Fd in production. Five to ten times faster restore, half the file size. Delivery Notes Walk through each command on the left code block. Point to flags as you say them. The format comparison sidebar is the reference - pause on it. Emphasize: 'Always use Fc or Fd.' The globals-only callout is the key insight most tutorials miss.

sections.heading: pg basebackup + pg restore
paragraphs: Timestamp: 2:30 Narration pg_basebackup. Physical backup. Copies the entire cluster at the file level. Five commands. Plain format with dash Fp - a direct copy of the data directory. Tar plus gzip with dash Ft dash z - a single portable archive. Replication standby with dash R - automatically configures recovery. And new in PostgreSQL 17: incremental backup. Instead of copying everything again, only the blocks that changed since the last backup get copied. Then pg_combinebackup merges the incremental with the base. Now pg_restore. Six commands. Basic restore from custom format. Parallel restore with dash j four - this is massive. Four concurrent connections rebuilding your database. Single table restore - pull just the users table out of a full dump. List contents with dash l - this gives you a table of contents file you can edit, then restore selectively with dash capital L. And cross-server restore with dash dash no-owner and dash dash no-privileges - when you are moving between servers with different role configurations. The dash j four flag runs parallel connections. On a multi-core server, this cuts restore time dramatically. Delivery Notes Left column is pg_basebackup, right is pg_restore. Walk through each command. Emphasize PG 17 incremental as the new feature. The parallel restore callout is the key production tip.

sections.heading: Live Demo: Backup 48 GB, Restore in 4 Minutes
paragraphs: Timestamp: 5:00 Narration Live demo. Real numbers. We have a production database. Forty-eight gigabytes. Step one - confirm the size. pg_database_size returns forty-eight GB. Step two - dump it. pg_dump dash Fc dash Z six. Custom format, compression level six. This takes a while on forty-eight gigs, but the output is worth it. Step three - verify the dump is readable. pg_restore dash l reads the archive header and table of contents. Two hundred and forty-seven TOC entries. Step four - check the compressed size. Eight point two gigabytes. Eighty-three percent smaller than the original. Now the restore. Create a fresh empty database. Run pg_restore with dash j four for parallel. Four concurrent connections rebuilding tables, indexes, constraints. Watch it work. Creating table public.users. Processing data. Creating indexes. Total restore time: four minutes and twelve seconds. Verify row counts. Orders: twelve point eight million. Users: two point eight million. Everything matches. Forty-eight gigs backed up, compressed to eight point two gigs, restored in four minutes twelve seconds. That is what dash Fc and dash j four give you. Delivery Notes Two terminals side by side. Left is BACKUP (red REC badge), right is RESTORE (green REC badge). Walk through each command as if typing live. The stats sidebar on the right shows the compression and timing. Let the numbers breathe - 83% smaller and 4:12 are the money stats.

sections.heading: Automate or It Does Not Exist
paragraphs: Timestamp: 7:00 Narration If it is not automated, it does not exist. Here is a complete backup script. Set your variables - timestamp, directory, database name, retention period. Run pg_dump dash Fc. Then immediately verify with pg_restore dash l. If the exit code is not zero, send an alert. This catches corrupted dumps before you need them. Finally, prune old backups with find. Anything older than seven days gets deleted. Cron schedule. Daily pg_dump at two AM. Globals dump at two-thirty AM. Weekly pg_basebackup on Sunday at three AM. Two critical callouts. Always verify - pg_restore dash l confirms the dump header and table of contents are intact. It takes seconds and catches failures early. And at scale, look at pgBackRest or Barman. They handle S3 storage, encryption, differential backups, and automatic verification out of the box. Delivery Notes The bash script is the main visual. Walk through each section. The verification step is the key insight - most backup scripts skip it. The cron schedule is the reference card people will screenshot. Mention pgBackRest as the production-grade option.

sections.heading: 5 Mistakes DBAs Make With Backups
paragraphs: Timestamp: 8:00 Narration Five mistakes I have seen in production. Number one: using plain SQL for large databases. pg_dump mydb greater-than backup.sql - no compression, no parallel restore, five to ten times slower. Use dash Fc or dash Fd. Number two: never testing restores. The dump file exists, but can you actually restore it? On a clean server? In how many minutes? Schedule a monthly restore test. Number three: forgetting roles and globals. pg_dump does not back up roles, passwords, or tablespace definitions. You need pg_dumpall dash dash globals-only separately. Number four: storing backups on the same server. The disk dies, the database and the backup both disappear. Copy to S3, NFS, or a second data center. Off-site is non-negotiable. Number five: no monitoring or alerting. Cron fails silently for three weeks. Nobody notices until DROP TABLE happens. Monitor backup age, file size, and exit codes. Delivery Notes Five numbered cards, red styling. Walk through each with increasing urgency. Numbers two and five are the most common. Pause after 'off-site is non-negotiable.' This is the slide people share on social media.

sections.heading: PITR Overview + The Cheat Sheet
paragraphs: Timestamp: 9:00 Narration Point-in-Time Recovery. This is how you undo that accidental DELETE. Three steps. First, enable WAL archiving in postgresql.conf. Set wal_level to replica, archive_mode to on, and configure an archive command. Second, take a base backup with pg_basebackup. Third, when disaster strikes, restore the base backup, set a recovery target time to one second before the disaster, and promote. Look at the timeline. Base backup, WAL segments accumulating, then the DROP TABLE happens. You restore to the point just before it. The table is back. Critical: WAL archiving must be enabled before the disaster. You cannot retroactively recover WAL that was never archived. Full PITR deep dive in Cheat Sheet number two. And here is your pinnable cheat sheet. Backup commands on the left. Restore commands on the right. Screenshot this. Pin it to your terminal. These are the commands you will use every week. Delivery Notes The PITR section is the left column - walk through the three steps. The timeline SVG shows the restore point visually. The cheat sheet cards on the right are the screenshot reference. Remind viewers to screenshot.

sections.heading: Quick Summary
paragraphs: Timestamp: 9:30 Narration Quick summary. Five tools. pg_dump for single database logical backups. pg_dumpall for roles and globals. pg_basebackup for full physical cluster copies. pg_restore with parallel and selective options. And PITR for any-second recovery. The backup readiness checklist. Automated daily pg_dump dash Fc. Globals dump for roles. Weekly pg_basebackup for disaster recovery. WAL archiving enabled. Backups copied off-server. And verification: pg_restore dash l on every dump, monthly full restore test, backup failure alerts, retention policy defined, and documented RTO and RPO targets. From no backup to automated, tested, and monitored. That is the journey. Delivery Notes Five tool cards at the top - quick summary of each. Two checklist panels below. The gradient progress bar at the bottom shows the journey from red to green. Keep the energy up - this is the wrap-up before the CTA.

No alert. Nine AM. Primary disk fails. Database down. Nine-oh-two. You promote the standby - and six hours of transactions are gone. Six hours of lag equals six hours of data loss. With synchronous mode, data loss drops to zero. With automatic failover, promotion happens in under thirty seconds.

In this video, every replication command you need. Streaming, logical, failover, and monitoring. PostgreSQL 14 through 18. Replication lag is invisible until failover makes it catastrophic. Stay to the end - I show the monitoring queries that catch it early. No greeting. The disaster timeline is the visual - walk through each step.

Pause after 'six hours of transactions are gone. ' The failover SVG on the right shows Primary → Standby → Promote. Lighter slide now - no 'What You Will Learn' card, just tension + the SVG. Timestamp: 0:30 Narration Before we touch any commands, the architecture. Your primary sends data two ways.

Streaming replication: raw WAL bytes to the standby. Exact byte-for-byte copy. Same version required. This is your HA and failover path. Logical replication: decoded changes to subscribers. Table-level selection. Cross-version. Subscriber stays writable. This is your migration and analytics path.

Streaming: exact copies, near-zero lag, failover capable. But all-or-nothing and version-locked. Logical: table-level control, cross-version PG 14 to 18, writable subscribers. But DDL and sequences are not replicated. Most production setups need both. Streaming for HA, logical for migration.

Trace the two paths. The comparison cards below are the reference. Emphasize 'most production setups need both. '

Timestamp: 1:00 Narration Streaming replication. Primary to standby in five commands. On the primary: wal_level equals replica, max_wal_senders ten, max_replication_slots ten, wal_keep_size one gigabyte, hot_standby on.

In pg_hba. conf, add a replication line. Create the user and a physical replication slot. On the standby: pg_basebackup with dash R. The dash R flag creates standby. signal and writes primary_conninfo automatically. Then pg_ctl start. The dash R flag does the heavy lifting. No manual configuration needed.

Walk through each parameter. The -R flag callout is the key insight. Timestamp: 2:30 Narration Logical replication. Publish and subscribe. On the publisher: wal_level to logical. CREATE PUBLICATION - three options. FOR ALL TABLES, FOR TABLE with specific names, or PG 15 plus WHERE clause for row filtering.

ALTER PUBLICATION to add or drop tables. On the subscriber: create tables first, schema must match. CREATE SUBSCRIPTION with connection string and publication. In PG 17 plus, add failover equals true for slot synchronization. Check pg_stat_subscription. Pause and resume with DISABLE and ENABLE.

Critical: DDL is not replicated. Schema changes must be applied manually on both sides. Emphasize PG 15 WHERE and PG 17 failover. The DDL warning is the key teaching moment. Timestamp: 4:30 Narration Primary is down. Three promotion methods. SQL: SELECT pg_promote true comma sixty.

pg_ctl: pg_ctl promote. Trigger file: touch the promote trigger file. After promotion: pg_is_in_recovery returns false. Update other standbys. PG 17 adds pg_createsubscriber to convert physical standby to logical. Seven-step failover checklist. Confirm primary is down. Check lag. Promote.

Verify. Update DNS. Redirect standbys. Notify teams. For zero data loss, set synchronous_standby_names. The primary waits for standby WAL write. Promotion is irreversible - the old primary needs pg_rewind or a fresh pg_basebackup to rejoin. Right: checklist and sync/async. Emphasize 'promotion is irreversible.

'

Timestamp: 6:00 Narration pg_stat_replication. Run on the primary. Every standby appears. The query: client address, state, sync state, replay lag bytes, replay lag interval. Healthy: streaming, sync, zero lag. Problem: catchup, async, two gigabytes behind, six hours lag. If you see this, investigate immediately.

Network, disk I/O, max_wal_senders. Three more queries. pg_replication_slots for slot monitoring. Drop inactive slots - they bloat WAL. pg_stat_subscription for logical replication status. Healthy vs problem comparison is the teaching moment. Red highlighted problem row is what viewers screenshot.

Timestamp: 7:00 Narration Live demo part one. Streaming replication and failover. On the primary: configure wal_level and max_wal_senders. Restart. Create the replication user and slot. Create a test table, insert a hundred thousand rows. Check pg_stat_replication - streaming, zero lag.

On the standby: pg_basebackup with dash R. Start it. pg_is_in_recovery returns true. Query the test table - hundred thousand rows. Read replica works. Now failover. pg_promote true comma sixty. Returns true. pg_is_in_recovery returns false - it is the primary now. Insert a row. INSERT zero one.

Writes accepted. Left is PRIMARY node1, right is STANDBY node2. Walk through commands as if typing live. The pg_promote moment is the dramatic peak. Let 'INSERT 0 1' breathe. Timestamp: 7:45 Narration Demo part two. Logical replication. On the publisher: set wal_level to logical, restart.

Create an orders table with sample data. CREATE PUBLICATION orders_pub FOR TABLE orders. On the subscriber: create the matching table. CREATE SUBSCRIPTION with the connection string and publication name. Initial sync happens automatically - both rows appear. Insert a new row on the publisher - it appears on the subscriber automatically.

And the subscriber is writable. You can insert local-only data that does not go back to the publisher. This is the key difference from streaming - logical replication is selective and the subscriber stays independent. Left is PUBLISHER node1, right is SUBSCRIBER node2 with orange badge.
