entries.title: postgresql dba cheat sheet 3 wal checkpoints
titles: postgresql dba cheat sheet 3 wal checkpoints
titleKeys: postgresql dba cheat sheet 3 wal checkpoints
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:00 Narration Your checkpoints are killing performance. Here is what happened. Default PostgreSQL: max_wal_size equals one gigabyte. Nobody changed it. A batch job runs overnight. Two gigabytes of WAL generated. max_wal_size exceeded. Forced checkpoint. All dirty pages flushed to disk at once.

I/O stall. Queries spike to ten times normal latency. Users see timeouts. One gigabyte is the default. Production needs four to sixteen gigabytes. And checkpoint_completion_target at zero point nine spreads the writes over ninety percent of the interval. Every INSERT and UPDATE goes to WAL first, data files second.

Misconfigure checkpoints and your database freezes under load. Stay to the end - I show you exactly how to diagnose and fix this. No greeting. Walk through the I/O spike timeline on the left - default, load, forced checkpoint, stall. Pause after 'ten times normal latency. ' The SVG on the right shows Transaction → WAL → Checkpoint → Data Files, with crash recovery path below.

Timestamp: 0:30 Narration Every change hits WAL before it touches data files. That is the durability guarantee. The write path: your transaction writes to shared_buffers - dirty pages in memory. At the same time, the change goes to wal_buffers. On COMMIT, PostgreSQL calls fsync to flush wal_buffers to pg_wal on disk.

That is the moment the transaction is durable. Later, a checkpoint flushes dirty pages from shared_buffers to the actual data files. If the server crashes, PostgreSQL replays WAL from the last checkpoint to bring data files up to date. Key concepts. LSN: Log Sequence Number. A byte offset into WAL, always increasing.

full_page_writes: after each checkpoint, the first change to a page writes the FULL eight kilobyte page to WAL. Torn page safety. More checkpoints means more full page images means more WAL. wal_level: minimal, replica, or logical. More detail means more WAL volume. And fsync: never disable it.

The performance gain is not worth silent data corruption. Trace the write path: shared_buffers → wal_buffers → pg_wal → checkpoint → data files. The crash recovery arrow goes from pg_wal back to data files. Three callout boxes on the right reinforce the key points. Emphasize 'never disable fsync.

'

Timestamp: 1:30 Narration Two types of checkpoints. Timed: fires every checkpoint_timeout. Default five minutes. Writes are spread over ninety percent of the interval thanks to completion_target. Smooth, predictable I/O. Forced: max_wal_size exceeded. PostgreSQL urgently flushes ALL dirty pages.

I/O storm. This is what causes the performance problems. The configuration. checkpoint_timeout: set to fifteen minutes for production. max_wal_size: four gigabytes minimum. Sixteen for write-heavy. min_wal_size: one gigabyte so WAL files are recycled, not removed. checkpoint_completion_target: zero point nine.

Spread writes over ninety percent of the interval. log_checkpoints: on. Always. See write time, sync time, distance, and whether it was timed or forced. wal_compression: zstd on PG 15 plus. Compresses full-page images. Reduces WAL volume forty to sixty percent. Rule of thumb: if you see 'checkpoints are occurring too frequently' in the logs, increase max_wal_size.

Right: timed vs forced comparison cards, production starting points (OLTP, write-heavy, batch), and the rule of thumb callout. This is the slide people screenshot for reference. Timestamp: 3:00 Narration WAL configuration. Every parameter explained. wal_level. Minimal: crash recovery only.

Replica: adds streaming replication and PITR. Logical: adds logical decoding. Default is replica. Never set minimal in production - you lose replication and point-in-time recovery. wal_buffers. Default auto-tunes to one thirty-second of shared_buffers. Usually fine. Increase to sixty-four megabytes for write-heavy workloads.

synchronous_commit. Five levels. Off: do not wait for WAL fsync. About six hundred milliseconds of data loss risk on crash. Local: wait for local WAL only. Remote_write: standby received but not fsynced. On: standby WAL disk. Remote_apply: standby applied. The strictest. You can set synchronous_commit per transaction.

SET LOCAL synchronous_commit equals off. Perfect for analytics tables where you accept the small data loss window. Archive settings. archive_mode on. archive_command copies completed WAL segments. archive_timeout forces archival if a segment is not full. PG 15 adds archive_library for built-in archiving.

Right: sync_commit level comparison table, wal_level comparison, per-transaction tip callout, and the 'never minimal in prod' warning. Dense slide - move steadily through each parameter. Timestamp: 4:30 Narration Your monitoring dashboard. Three views. pg_stat_wal: wal_records, wal_bytes, wal_buffers_full, wal_write, wal_sync.

This tells you how much WAL your workload generates. pg_stat_checkpointer. PG 17 plus. num_timed: scheduled checkpoints. num_requested: forced. num_done in PG 18: completed. write_time and sync_time in milliseconds. buffers_written. The goal: num_requested equals zero. All checkpoints should be timed.

If the ratio of requested to total is above ten percent, your max_wal_size is too small. pg_stat_bgwriter. buffers_clean: how many the background writer handled. maxwritten_clean: how often it hit its limit and stopped. If maxwritten_clean is greater than zero, increase bgwriter_lru_maxpages.

Quick health check: SELECT num_requested, num_timed FROM pg_stat_checkpointer. Calculate the forced percentage. If it is above ten percent, increase max_wal_size. Bottom grid: pg_stat_checkpointer on the left, pg_stat_bgwriter on the right. Each has a callout. The health check formula at the bottom is the one-liner viewers will use immediately.

Timestamp: 5:30 Narration WAL archiving. The safety net. Enable archive_mode, set archive_command to copy segments to your archive directory. Set archive_timeout to five minutes so partially-filled segments get archived too. PG 15 adds archive_library for built-in archiving - no shell command needed.

Point-in-time recovery. Stop the server. Restore the base backup. Set restore_command to copy from your archive. Set recovery_target_time to one second before the disaster. Set recovery_target_action to promote. Create recovery. signal. Start the server. PostgreSQL replays WAL from the base backup through every archived segment up to your target time.

sections.heading: Cold Open: Your Checkpoints Are Killing Performance
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:00 Narration Your checkpoints are killing performance. Here is what happened. Default PostgreSQL: max_wal_size equals one gigabyte. Nobody changed it. A batch job runs overnight. Two gigabytes of WAL generated. max_wal_size exceeded. Forced checkpoint. All dirty pages flushed to disk at once. I/O stall. Queries spike to ten times normal latency. Users see timeouts. One gigabyte is the default. Production needs four to sixteen gigabytes. And checkpoint_completion_target at zero point nine spreads the writes over ninety percent of the interval. Every INSERT and UPDATE goes to WAL first, data files second. Misconfigure checkpoints and your database freezes under load. Stay to the end - I show you exactly how to diagnose and fix this. Delivery Notes Open fast. No greeting. Walk through the I/O spike timeline on the left - default, load, forced checkpoint, stall. Pause after 'ten times normal latency.' The SVG on the right shows Transaction → WAL → Checkpoint → Data Files, with crash recovery path below.

sections.heading: How WAL Works The Write Path
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:30 Narration Every change hits WAL before it touches data files. That is the durability guarantee. The write path: your transaction writes to shared_buffers - dirty pages in memory. At the same time, the change goes to wal_buffers. On COMMIT, PostgreSQL calls fsync to flush wal_buffers to pg_wal on disk. That is the moment the transaction is durable. Later, a checkpoint flushes dirty pages from shared_buffers to the actual data files. If the server crashes, PostgreSQL replays WAL from the last checkpoint to bring data files up to date. Key concepts. LSN: Log Sequence Number. A byte offset into WAL, always increasing. full_page_writes: after each checkpoint, the first change to a page writes the FULL eight kilobyte page to WAL. Torn page safety. More checkpoints means more full page images means more WAL. wal_level: minimal, replica, or logical. More detail means more WAL volume. And fsync: never disable it. The performance gain is not worth silent data corruption. Delivery Notes The SVG is the main visual. Trace the write path: shared_buffers → wal_buffers → pg_wal → checkpoint → data files. The crash recovery arrow goes from pg_wal back to data files. Three callout boxes on the right reinforce the key points. Emphasize 'never disable fsync.'

sections.heading: Checkpoints: Timed vs Forced
paragraphs: Timestamp: 1:30 Narration Two types of checkpoints. Timed: fires every checkpoint_timeout. Default five minutes. Writes are spread over ninety percent of the interval thanks to completion_target. Smooth, predictable I/O. Forced: max_wal_size exceeded. PostgreSQL urgently flushes ALL dirty pages. I/O storm. This is what causes the performance problems. The configuration. checkpoint_timeout: set to fifteen minutes for production. max_wal_size: four gigabytes minimum. Sixteen for write-heavy. min_wal_size: one gigabyte so WAL files are recycled, not removed. checkpoint_completion_target: zero point nine. Spread writes over ninety percent of the interval. log_checkpoints: on. Always. See write time, sync time, distance, and whether it was timed or forced. wal_compression: zstd on PG 15 plus. Compresses full-page images. Reduces WAL volume forty to sixty percent. Rule of thumb: if you see 'checkpoints are occurring too frequently' in the logs, increase max_wal_size. Delivery Notes Left column: the config block with comments. Right: timed vs forced comparison cards, production starting points (OLTP, write-heavy, batch), and the rule of thumb callout. This is the slide people screenshot for reference.

sections.heading: WAL Configuration: Every Parameter
paragraphs: Timestamp: 3:00 Narration WAL configuration. Every parameter explained. wal_level. Minimal: crash recovery only. Replica: adds streaming replication and PITR. Logical: adds logical decoding. Default is replica. Never set minimal in production - you lose replication and point-in-time recovery. wal_buffers. Default auto-tunes to one thirty-second of shared_buffers. Usually fine. Increase to sixty-four megabytes for write-heavy workloads. synchronous_commit. Five levels. Off: do not wait for WAL fsync. About six hundred milliseconds of data loss risk on crash. Local: wait for local WAL only. Remote_write: standby received but not fsynced. On: standby WAL disk. Remote_apply: standby applied. The strictest. You can set synchronous_commit per transaction. SET LOCAL synchronous_commit equals off. Perfect for analytics tables where you accept the small data loss window. Archive settings. archive_mode on. archive_command copies completed WAL segments. archive_timeout forces archival if a segment is not full. PG 15 adds archive_library for built-in archiving. Delivery Notes Left: full config block. Right: sync_commit level comparison table, wal_level comparison, per-transaction tip callout, and the 'never minimal in prod' warning. Dense slide - move steadily through each parameter.

sections.heading: Monitoring WAL & Checkpoints
paragraphs: Timestamp: 4:30 Narration Your monitoring dashboard. Three views. pg_stat_wal: wal_records, wal_bytes, wal_buffers_full, wal_write, wal_sync. This tells you how much WAL your workload generates. pg_stat_checkpointer. PG 17 plus. num_timed: scheduled checkpoints. num_requested: forced. num_done in PG 18: completed. write_time and sync_time in milliseconds. buffers_written. The goal: num_requested equals zero. All checkpoints should be timed. If the ratio of requested to total is above ten percent, your max_wal_size is too small. pg_stat_bgwriter. buffers_clean: how many the background writer handled. maxwritten_clean: how often it hit its limit and stopped. If maxwritten_clean is greater than zero, increase bgwriter_lru_maxpages. Quick health check: SELECT num_requested, num_timed FROM pg_stat_checkpointer. Calculate the forced percentage. If it is above ten percent, increase max_wal_size. Delivery Notes Top: pg_stat_wal query. Bottom grid: pg_stat_checkpointer on the left, pg_stat_bgwriter on the right. Each has a callout. The health check formula at the bottom is the one-liner viewers will use immediately.

sections.heading: WAL Archiving & Point in Time Recovery
paragraphs: Timestamp: 5:30 Narration WAL archiving. The safety net. Enable archive_mode, set archive_command to copy segments to your archive directory. Set archive_timeout to five minutes so partially-filled segments get archived too. PG 15 adds archive_library for built-in archiving - no shell command needed. Point-in-time recovery. Stop the server. Restore the base backup. Set restore_command to copy from your archive. Set recovery_target_time to one second before the disaster. Set recovery_target_action to promote. Create recovery.signal. Start the server. PostgreSQL replays WAL from the base backup through every archived segment up to your target time. The PITR timeline SVG: base backup on Monday, WAL segments accumulating, DROP TABLE happens Thursday three PM, you restore to fourteen fifty-nine fifty-nine. Table recovered. Critical warning: WAL archiving must be enabled BEFORE the disaster. You cannot retroactively archive WAL that was never saved. Delivery Notes Left: archive config + PITR restore steps. Right: PITR timeline SVG showing base backup → WAL segments → disaster → restore point. The warning callout is the key teaching moment. Pause before the warning.

sections.heading: Demo Part 1: Diagnose & Tune Checkpoints
paragraphs: Timestamp: 6:30 Narration Live demo part one. Diagnose and tune checkpoints. Left terminal: diagnose. Query pg_settings for all WAL and checkpoint parameters. Then the key query: pg_stat_checkpointer. num_timed eight forty-seven. num_requested three twelve. Calculate the forced percentage: twenty-six point nine percent. Over a quarter of your checkpoints are forced. That is your I/O problem. Check WAL generation: forty-two gigabytes since last reset. Right terminal: fix. ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_size eight gigabytes. checkpoint_timeout fifteen minutes. wal_compression zstd. log_checkpoints on. pg_reload_conf - no restart needed for these. Reset stats with pg_stat_reset_shared checkpointer. Wait for some traffic, then check again. num_timed forty-seven, num_requested zero. Zero percent forced. Problem solved. Delivery Notes Two terminals side by side. Left: DIAGNOSE with red 'before' badge. Right: FIX with green 'after' badge. The 26.9% forced number is the dramatic reveal. The 0.0% at the end is the payoff. Let it breathe.

sections.heading: Demo Part 2: WAL Size, Logs & pg waldump
paragraphs: Timestamp: 7:15 Narration Demo part two. Measuring WAL and reading logs. Left terminal: WAL on disk. du dash sh pg_wal. Two point four gigabytes. Count segments: one fifty-six files at sixteen megabytes each. pg_current_wal_lsn shows your current position. pg_stat_wal gives you total WAL generated, record count, and full page image count. Right terminal: checkpoint logs. With log_checkpoints on, you see exactly what happened. Wrote twelve thousand eight hundred forty-seven buffers. Write time twelve seconds, sync time ninety-three milliseconds. Distance one point eight gigabytes. This is how you validate your tuning. Then pg_waldump with dash dash stats. Breaks down WAL by record type: Heap sixty-one percent, Btree twenty-four percent, XACT ten percent, Standby four percent. This tells you WHERE your WAL comes from. Delivery Notes Two terminals. Left: WAL measurement commands with cyan 'measure' badge. Right: log output + pg_waldump with orange 'inspect' badge. The checkpoint log output is what viewers will compare against their own logs. The waldump breakdown is the advanced insight.

sections.heading: 5 WAL Mistakes That Tank Performance
paragraphs: Timestamp: 8:00 Narration Five mistakes that tank performance. One: leaving max_wal_size at one gigabyte. The default is too small for any production workload. Forced checkpoints cause I/O spikes. Set four to sixteen gigabytes. Two: not enabling log_checkpoints. Without it you are blind to checkpoint timing, write and sync duration, and WAL distance. Enable it. Always. It costs nothing. Three: disabling fsync for performance. fsync equals off means WAL is not durable. A crash can silently corrupt your entire database. Never disable in production. Tune synchronous_commit instead. Four: pg_wal on the same disk as data. WAL writes are sequential. Data writes are random. Mixing them causes I/O contention. Symlink pg_wal to a dedicated fast disk or NVMe. Five: not enabling wal_compression. Full-page images after checkpoints generate massive WAL. wal_compression equals zstd on PG 15 plus reduces WAL volume forty to sixty percent with minimal CPU overhead. Delivery Notes Five red cards, numbered. Walk through with increasing urgency. One and two are the most common. Three is the most dangerous. Four and five are the optimizations. This is the slide people share.

sections.heading: Quick Summary + WAL Cheat Sheet
paragraphs: Timestamp: 9:00 Narration Five topics covered. WAL: the write-ahead log. Checkpoints: flushing dirty pages. pg_stat_wal: monitoring generation. Archiving: point-in-time recovery. Tuning: no more I/O storms. Configuration cheat sheet: wal_level replica, max_wal_size four to sixteen gigabytes, min_wal_size one gigabyte, checkpoint_timeout fifteen minutes, completion_target zero point nine, wal_compression zstd, log_checkpoints on, archive_mode on. Monitoring queries: pg_stat_checkpointer for forced ratio, pg_stat_wal for generation, pg_current_wal_lsn for position, du dash sh pg_wal for disk usage. From I/O storms and forced checkpoints to smooth, timed, compressed WAL. Delivery Notes Five tool cards at top. Two-column cheat sheet: config left, monitoring right. Gradient progress bar at bottom - red to green. Keep energy up before the CTA.

sections.heading: Subscribe + Next Episode
paragraphs: Timestamp: 10:00 Narration If you manage PostgreSQL in production, subscribe and press the bell icon. Like if this helped. Save for reference. Next up: Cheat Sheet number four - PostgreSQL Index Tuning. B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, partial indexes, and EXPLAIN plus index selection. Dr. Ibrar Ahmed. PostgreSQL Deep Dives. See you in the next one. Delivery Notes Premium CTA. 120px bell icon with floating animation. Rainbow gradient bar. SUBSCRIBE button. Like + Save. Cheat Sheet #4 Index Tuning teaser. titleKeys: postgresql dba cheat sheet 4 vacuum bloat
paragraphs: Timestamp: 0:00 Narration Your table is eighty percent dead rows. And it is getting bigger, not smaller. Every UPDATE creates a new copy. Five hundred megabytes on disk. Only one hundred megabytes of live data. The rest is dead tuples. Five times bigger than it needs to be. A query that should take three seconds takes forty-seven.

How does this happen? Every UPDATE in PostgreSQL creates a new row version. The old version stays until VACUUM marks the space for reuse. But VACUUM does NOT shrink the file. To actually reclaim disk space, you need pg_repack. This table grew four hundred megabytes in a week without a single INSERT.

Stay - I show you why, and how to fix it in production without downtime. No greeting. The bloat visualization SVG on the left shows dead/live page blocks - mostly red. The bloat bar below: 80% DEAD, 20% live. Right side: 3 stat cards (5x bigger, 47s query, 3s after fix) + clean SVG showing UPDATE → Dead Tuple → VACUUM → pg_repack.

No 'What You Will Learn' card. Timestamp: 0:30 Narration Why does bloat happen? PostgreSQL MVCC. Multi-Version Concurrency Control. Every UPDATE is an INSERT new plus mark old dead. Step one: original row, transaction ID one hundred, row version one. Step two: UPDATE changes the email.

PostgreSQL inserts a NEW row with transaction ID one-oh-one. The old row is marked dead but stays in the page. Step three: another UPDATE. A third row version. Now two dead tuples. The page fills with dead rows. New inserts go to new pages. The table grows. VACUUM marks dead space for reuse by future inserts.

But it does NOT remove the empty pages. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table but takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock - blocks everything. pg_repack rewrites without locking. The key insight: VACUUM prevents growth but does not reverse it. Right side: comparison table (VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL vs pg_repack) and the critical callout about VACUUM preventing growth.

Timestamp: 1:30 Narration How to detect bloat. Three queries. First: pg_stat_user_tables. Select n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, calculate dead percentage, and check last_autovacuum. Sort by dead tuples descending. This gives you the quick overview. Second: pgstattuple. This is the precision tool.

It scans every page and gives you exact dead_tuple_percent, free_percent, and table_len. The cost: it reads the entire table. Run on small tables or during low traffic. Third: pg_relation_size versus pg_total_relation_size. The first is the table only. The second includes indexes and TOAST.

If relation size is three times the actual data, you have bloat. Quick interpretation. Dead percent over twenty: needs attention. Over fifty: critical. last_autovacuum null: autovacuum never ran - check if it is disabled. Right: quick interpretation guide with red/green thresholds and the pgstattuple result table.

This is the detection toolkit slide. Timestamp: 3:00 Narration Three tools. Different trade-offs. VACUUM. No lock on reads or writes. Marks dead space for reuse. Does NOT shrink the file. Fast. Run it frequently. Autovacuum does this automatically. VACUUM FULL. Rewrites the entire table.

Returns space to the OS. But takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Blocks ALL reads and writes. On a five hundred megabyte table, this can take minutes. Use only during maintenance windows. pg_repack. Best of both worlds. Rewrites the table without locking. Creates a new copy, applies changes via triggers, then swaps.

Needs free disk space equal to the table size. Install the extension first: CREATE EXTENSION pg_repack. VACUUM ANALYZE is the daily driver. Run after bulk operations. Updates statistics for the planner. VACUUM FREEZE prevents transaction ID wraparound - the silent emergency that can freeze your entire database.

Each with lock type, speed, and shrink behavior. Below: VACUUM ANALYZE and VACUUM FREEZE sections. Emphasize 'ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocks ALL reads and writes. '

Timestamp: 5:00 Narration Autovacuum tuning. The defaults are conservative. The formula: threshold plus scale_factor times number of rows.

Default threshold is fifty. Scale factor is zero point two - twenty percent. So on a ten million row table, autovacuum triggers after two million dead rows. That is too many. For hot tables: set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to zero point zero one. Set autovacuum_vacuum_threshold to one thousand.

Now it triggers after one hundred and one thousand dead rows. Per-table override: ALTER TABLE orders SET storage parameters. Global tuning: autovacuum_max_workers three to five. autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit four hundred to eight hundred. autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay two milliseconds.

These let autovacuum run faster. The naptime is the sleep between database scans. Default one minute. Decrease to ten or twenty seconds for busy databases. Monitor with pg_stat_user_tables: last_autovacuum, autovacuum_count, n_dead_tup. Right: global settings + monitoring callout.

The formula is the key insight - viewers need to understand WHY defaults are too conservative for large tables. Timestamp: 6:30 Narration Index bloat. The silent killer. VACUUM cleans table bloat. But it does NOT clean index bloat. B-tree indexes grow when rows are inserted and deleted.

Deleted index entries leave empty leaf pages. The index gets bigger but the useful data stays the same. How to detect: pgstatindex. It gives you leaf_fragmentation, avg_leaf_density, and empty_pages. If leaf density is below sixty percent, the index is bloated. How to fix: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

Available since PG 12. Builds a new index alongside the old one. No read lock. Also pg_repack with the dash i flag to repack a specific index. Plain REINDEX without CONCURRENTLY locks writes - avoid in production. Right: pgstatindex query + fix options (REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, pg_repack -i).

The density threshold callout is what viewers will screenshot. Timestamp: 7:00 Narration Live demo part one. Detect and VACUUM. Left terminal: detection. Check table size - five hundred megabytes. Check dead tuples: one million fifty-one thousand dead out of three million total. Thirty-five percent dead.

paragraphs: Timestamp: 7:00 Narration Live demo part one. Detect and VACUUM. Left terminal: detection. Check table size - five hundred megabytes. Check dead tuples: one million fifty-one thousand dead out of three million total. Thirty-five percent dead. Then pgstattuple for exact numbers: thirty-four point eight two percent dead, three point one two percent free. Right terminal: run VACUUM VERBOSE. Removed one million fifty-one thousand dead row versions. Sixty-four thousand pages: zero removed, all remain. Check size after VACUUM - still five hundred megabytes. VACUUM does NOT shrink the file. Dead tuples are gone - n_dead_tup is zero. But the space is only marked for reuse, not returned to the OS. To actually shrink: pg_repack. Next slide. Delivery Notes Two terminals side by side. Left: DETECT with red 'before' badge. Right: VACUUM with orange 'run' badge. The key dramatic moment: '500 MB - SAME! VACUUM does not shrink.' Let that land before moving to Part 2.

sections.heading: Demo Part 2: pg repack Shrink the Table
paragraphs: Timestamp: 7:45 Narration Demo part two. pg_repack. Run it: pg_repack dash d prod dash t orders. Repacking table public dot orders. Check size: one hundred five megabytes. Seventy-nine percent smaller. Verify with pgstattuple: dead percent zero, free percent one point two three. Clean. While we are at it, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on the primary key. Done. The sidebar tells the story. Before: five hundred megabytes, thirty-five percent dead. After: one hundred five megabytes, seventy-nine percent smaller. Query time: zero point zero three milliseconds. And zero downtime. Reads and writes continued during the entire repack. pg_repack creates a new copy, applies changes via triggers, then swaps atomically. Delivery Notes Left: pg_repack terminal with green 'fix' badge. Right: before/after stats sidebar with big numbers. The 500 MB → 105 MB reveal is the payoff from Part 1. Let the numbers breathe.

sections.heading: 5 Bloat Mistakes That Fill Your Disk

ALTER TABLE SET autovacuum_enabled false seems harmless. It is a ticking bomb. Dead tuples accumulate silently. Three: default autovacuum on ten million plus row tables. Twenty percent scale factor means two million dead rows before VACUUM triggers. Set scale_factor to zero point zero one per table. Four: bulk UPDATE without VACUUM after. Updating one million rows creates one million dead tuples instantly. Run manual VACUUM ANALYZE after bulk operations. Five: ignoring index bloat. VACUUM cleans table bloat but NOT index bloat. B-tree indexes grow silently. Use pgstatindex to check, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY to fix. Delivery Notes Five red numbered cards. Walk through with increasing urgency. entries.title: eight steps to bullet proof database disaster recovery
titles: eight steps to bullet proof database disaster recovery
titleKeys: eight steps to bullet proof database disaster recovery
paragraphs: [225 seconds] This slide is about Cover. The goal is to set the goal for a production postgres recovery practice. For a production postgres system, the important signals are recovery discipline, evidence preservation, verified backups, archived write ahead log, and final validation. I want the audience to hear this as an operating standard, not as a list of tools. Every item on the slide should answer a practical incident question: what happened, what state is safe, what evidence do we trust, and what action is allowed next. In real recovery work, the dangerous moment is usually not the first error message. The dangerous moment is the first irreversible action. That is why this section emphasizes sequence. entries.title: postgresql documentary deck
titles: postgresql documentary deck
titleKeys: postgresql documentary deck
paragraphs: Cold-open incident dashboard. Red production alert, latency spike, deadlock, rollback, WAL, and the central question: what survives when the database fails?

Imagine it is two forty seven in the morning. The application is slow. The dashboard is red. Open transactions are climbing. A checkout request is stuck behind a lock. Someone says the word deadlock, and suddenly the room gets quiet.

This is where databases stop being a feature list and become a survival system. The question is no longer which database has the best logo, the trendiest cloud service, or the loudest marketing campaign. The question is simple: if the database fails, what survives?

Are committed transactions still true? Are failed transactions cleanly erased? Can the system replay its log and come back without mystery data loss? This video is about why PostgreSQL became the answer engineers trust when being wrong is expensive.
Problem map with correctness, concurrency, and recovery cards. Static PostgreSQL production log stays visible during render.

Most databases are fine on normal days. Normal days are easy. The real test is the bad day. Partial writes. Concurrent updates. Application bugs. Disk stalls. Replicas behind. A CTO asking whether the numbers on screen can still be trusted.

That is the real issue. Correctness under pressure. A committed transaction must be real. A failed one must disappear. Readers and writers need predictable behavior when traffic is ugly. And after a crash, recovery must land on a known consistent state.

PostgreSQL earned trust because it kept these promises again and again. Not in demos. In incident rooms. In logs. In recoveries where the system came back, the rollback was clean, and the team could move on.
Roadmap slide. Five chapters: origin, trust mechanics, extension moat, cloud default, AI relevance.

Here is the roadmap. First, we go back to Berkeley and the research culture that shaped PostgreSQL before it was popular. Then we look at the trust mechanics: ACID, MVCC, write ahead logging, crash recovery, and clean rollback.
After that, we look at the extension moat. PostGIS for geospatial. TimescaleDB for time series. Citus for distribution. pgaudit for compliance. Foreign data wrappers. And eventually pgvector.

Then we follow the cloud era, where every major platform chose PostgreSQL as a flagship relational service. Finally, we look at the AI era, where pgvector turned PostgreSQL from a boring relational database into a serious platform for RAG applications. The point is not that PostgreSQL won overnight. The point is that every era gave it one more reason to matter.

LEFT: Live MVCC simulation panel with 'Running' green dot. Two transaction boxes: T1 (xid=105) with BEGIN, SELECT orders, SELECT users, COMMIT. T2 (xid=106) with BEGIN, UPDATE orders, COMMIT -> v2. Row version chain shows v1 crossed out, v2 green. RIGHT: ACID card with blue border, MVCC card with green border, then REAL WAL crash recovery log embedded, 2026 timestamps, showing system interrupted -> starting PITR -> redo at LSN -> consistent recovery state reached -> ready to accept connections -> recovery complete 0 data lost.
Trust in a database is not built in a product launch. It is built across thousands of production incidents.

The first decision was ACID correctness. Not as a marketing claim. As a design constraint. When PostgreSQL says a transaction committed, it committed. When it says it failed, nothing half-persisted. This was not universal in the 2000s.

The second was MVCC. Multi-Version Concurrency Control. Readers and writers do not block each other. Transaction T1 reads the orders table while Transaction T2 updates it. They see different snapshots. Both consistent. Zero locks. This is why PostgreSQL performance stays predictable under mixed workloads.

The third was Write-Ahead Logging. Every change goes to the WAL before it touches data files. The log on screen is a real PostgreSQL 18 recovery sequence with actual LSN numbers. Power was cut. The server restarted. WAL replayed. Recovery complete. Zero data lost.
These three decisions were made because correctness was the design principle, not because they were easy.
SLIDE 05. Extension Ecosystem: One Engine, Every Workload

LEFT: Orbital extension ecosystem map. PostgreSQL core in glowing center (130px, glow animation). Seven extensions orbit at two radii: PostGIS, TimescaleDB, pgvector, Citus, pg_stat, pgaudit. Each has themed color icon. RIGHT: 42px Playfair headline. Four extension feature cards with icons.

titles: postgres explain
titleKeys: postgres explain
paragraphs: [Delivery] Urgent. No greeting. Straight into the pain. Forty-seven seconds. One query. Ninety-eight percent CPU. Twelve blocked sessions. Stop guessing. Read the plan. [Pacing] Hold 2 seconds on metrics.

[Delivery] Confident. Guiding. In this video, you will learn to read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan and fix a real slow query. Six steps: query, plan, estimate, join, buffers, fix. We will not guess. We will prove.

[Delivery] Calm. Let the query breathe. Here is the query. It joins orders with order items, filters by status and date range, groups, sorts, and limits to a hundred rows. Nothing exotic. Five million rows in orders. Fifteen million in order items. Execution time: forty-seven seconds.

[Delivery] Slow and deliberate. Pause between each flag. Let us run EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS. Four red flags. Flag one: bad estimate. Expected two hundred. Got twenty-eight thousand four hundred and fifty. Flag two: wrong join. Nested Loop with twenty-eight thousand inner loops. Flag three: buffer reads. Eighty-nine thousand two hundred shared reads. Flag four: disk sort. External merge. Fourteen megabytes on disk. Four red flags. One root cause. Now we prove it.

Estimated two hundred. Actual twenty-eight thousand. A hundred and forty-two times underestimate. The planner chose Nested Loop for two hundred rows. For twenty-eight thousand, catastrophic. Root cause: stale statistics. Last ANALYZE was four months ago.
Nested Loop ran the inner scan twenty-eight thousand times. Roughly a hundred seventy thousand random lookups. This is where forty-seven seconds come from.

Shared hit: twelve thousand. Fast. Shared read: eighty-nine thousand two hundred. Not found in shared buffers. May come from OS cache or physical disk. Eighty-eight percent missed the PostgreSQL cache.
Over a hundred eighty thousand rows sorted. Default work_mem is four megabytes. External merge. Fourteen megabytes on disk.
[Delivery] Transition. Calm. Four problems. Bad estimate. Wrong join. Buffer reads. Sort spill. Now we know what failed. Next we learn how to read every plan like this.

EXPLAIN shows the estimated plan. Does not execute. Safe on anything. EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS executes and measures reality. Actual rows, actual time, buffer hits and reads. Important: ANALYZE executes the query. Wrap UPDATE and DELETE in BEGIN and ROLLBACK.
Plans read bottom-up. Most indented nodes are leaf scans. Move up. Each parent combines data. Top node delivers. Leaves scan. Branches join and sort. The root delivers.
Cost is arbitrary. Compare within the same query. Rows is the estimate. Width is bytes per row. Loops: multiply actual time by loops for the real total.
The single most important comparison. Ten times or more difference means the planner made a bad decision. This is the line most people skip, and it often explains the whole outage.

[Delivery] Expert content. Slower pace. PostgreSQL assumes columns are independent. If status and created_at are correlated, normal stats estimate poorly. CREATE STATISTICS with dependencies and ndistinct. Then ANALYZE. The planner understands the correlation.

entries.title: PostgreSQL 18 High Availability — The Complete Framework, Built Layer by Layer
titles: PostgreSQL 18 High Availability — The Complete Framework, Built Layer by Layer
titleKeys: postgresql 18 high availability the complete framework built layer by layer
paragraphs: Let's build a PostgreSQL cluster that survives things going wrong, and let's build it one honest step at a time. This is where everyone starts: one application, one PostgreSQL eighteen server called db one. A write arrives, it is recorded in the write-ahead log, and the commit comes back. It works perfectly. And that is exactly the trap, because the postgres processes, the kernel, the disk, and the address your clients dial all live inside a single failure domain.

So let's break it. db one is gone. Sockets reset, transactions in flight are lost, and libpq comes back with connection refused. And notice there is nothing to fall back to: no second address, no second copy. Right now your recovery time is however long a human takes to wake up and repair the machine, and your recovery point is whatever happens to be in your last backup.

Fix number one: stop keeping a single copy. db two is cloned with pg basebackup and then follows db one continuously. On the primary, a WAL sender pushes write-ahead log records over port five four three two. On the standby, a WAL receiver writes them to disk and the startup process replays them, one record at a time. And because hot standby is on, db two will answer read-only queries while it is still catching up.

Two details decide whether this actually protects you. First, a physical replication slot. It forces db one to hold on to WAL until db two confirms it, so a slow standby can never quietly fall off the end of the log. But an uncapped slot will fill the WAL directory, so bound it with max slot wal keep size, and accept that the slot gets invalidated instead of your disk filling. Second, this is asynchronous, so pg stat replication always shows a gap. Watch the flush lag, because that number, in bytes, is your real recovery point objective.

Now the interesting part. Kill db one again. This time the data survived; it is sitting right there on db two. So send it an insert. Cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. A standby that is still in recovery refuses writes by design, every single time. The copy is alive. The writable service is not. And nothing on this board has permission to change that.

Someone has to make the call. The promote command ends recovery, db two finishes replaying what it has, and it becomes writable. And at that moment PostgreSQL increments the timeline from one to two and writes a history file to record the fork. Which creates a second problem. When db one comes back, it is still on the old timeline and it has diverged, so it needs pg rewind before it can follow. This does work. But the clock running during the outage is a human clock, and humans sleep.

So let's replace the human. Patroni is one agent per node, and it owns its PostgreSQL completely. It bootstraps replicas, renders the postgres configuration, watches health, and issues promote and demote itself. It also publishes a REST API on port eight thousand eight, where a GET to slash primary returns two hundred on the leader, and only on the leader. Patroni now decides how to act. But here is the thing: it must never decide alone.

Why not? Because three agents, each convinced that it should be primary, is precisely how you corrupt a database. So we give them an outside referee. etcd: three members running Raft over one replicated log, where every write needs a majority, two out of three. Lose a member and decisions keep flowing. And be very clear about what lives in here. Member state, dynamic configuration, and one leader key. No tables. No WAL. Not one byte of your data.

Leadership is not a flag; it is a lease. The primary writes its own name into the leader key with a thirty-second time to live, then comes back every ten seconds to refresh it. Patroni insists that the lease time to live is at least loop wait plus two times retry timeout, so one slow etcd round trip can never expire a perfectly healthy leader. One key, one holder, enforced by compare and swap.

And that lease does double duty, because it is also a fence. If a node cannot refresh the key, it has to assume somebody else is about to take over, so Patroni demotes it to read-only before that can happen. Add the hardware watchdog and the kernel resets the entire box if Patroni itself hangs. Set the safety margin to minus one and the watchdog fires at half the lease time, which is the tightest timing Patroni offers. Configured properly and actually tested, this is what makes split-brain very unlikely.

Let's watch it work. db two dies. Nobody refreshes the lease, so within thirty seconds the leader key simply vanishes. Every healthy candidate compares its replay position, and the winner claims the key with a create-if-absent write. Only one can win, and only the winner promotes. Now watch what does not happen. Nobody's open connection is moved. Your clients see a reset socket, and they have to reconnect and retry. Remember that.

Two nodes buy you exactly one failover, and then you are back where we started. So db three joins as a second standby, and now the cluster can lose a node and still hold an election with a candidate to spare. But only, and this matters, if the failure domains are genuinely independent. Separate hosts, separate storage, ideally separate availability zones, with the etcd members spread out the same way. Three replicas on one hypervisor is one replica wearing a costume.

More candidates means Patroni has to choose, and it does not choose blindly. It compares each standby's received position against the leader's and disqualifies anything lagging further behind than maximum lag on failover, sixteen megabytes here. Look at db two: a hundred and twenty-five megabytes behind. Rejected. db three is two megabytes behind, and db three is promoted. Raise that limit and you fail over more often. Lower it and you sometimes refuse to. One knob, two objectives.

And if losing even two megabytes is unacceptable, you switch Patroni into quorum synchronous mode. You set synchronous node count to one, and Patroni takes over the synchronous standby list for you. That is a list you should never write by hand. Now every commit waits for at least one standby to flush the record to disk, so a normal single-node failure loses no acknowledged transaction. And you pay for that on every commit, forever, in latency. Choose it deliberately.

The database layer is solved. Your clients still have no idea where the primary is. Enter HAProxy, and notice what it health-checks. Not PostgreSQL. Patroni. An HTTP check against slash primary on port eight thousand eight, every three seconds, three consecutive failures to mark a backend down. Port five thousand carries writes to the one node that answers two hundred. Port five thousand one spreads reads across the standbys. And on marked down shutdown sessions drops stale sessions the instant a role moves.

One more component in front of each database. PgBouncer, on port six four three two, in transaction pooling mode. In this single-user, single-database example, five hundred client connections share a pool of up to thirty-two PostgreSQL server connections, so PostgreSQL is never asked to fork thousands of backends just to leave them idle. Note that the default pool size is per user and database pair, so every extra pair gets its own pool. The trade-off is real: no session-level state, and protocol-level prepared statements need max prepared statements enabled. And be clear about the job. PgBouncer pools connections. It has no idea what a primary is.

Now look closely, because we have just recreated the original problem one layer up. One HAProxy is one single point of failure. So lb two runs the identical configuration with the identical checks. Neither router holds an opinion of its own. Both read the role from Patroni and independently converge on the same answer, although their check phases can differ by a few seconds. Which leaves exactly one thing missing: a single address that survives losing either router.

Keepalived provides it. Both routers speak VRRP with virtual router id fifty-one. lb one advertises the higher priority, so lb one owns the floating address, ten, twenty, zero, thirty. A tracking script watches the local HAProxy and drops that priority the moment it dies. And notice the boundary. Keepalived moves an IP address between machines. It has no opinion whatsoever about which database is primary. Two different jobs, two different components.

Step back, because this is the whole system, and every layer owns exactly one decision. PostgreSQL stores the data and ships the WAL. Patroni operates PostgreSQL. etcd decides who is allowed to lead. HAProxy discovers where the leader is right now. PgBouncer rations connections. Keepalived keeps the address still. Zero single points of failure, and that comes from the separation of duties, not from any one product on this board.

Claims are cheap, so let's run the drills. Drill one: kill the primary. Patroni notices inside one loop wait, ten seconds. The lease is gone by thirty. Promotion itself takes about two. HAProxy marks the new backend up after two good checks. Add that up and on this configuration you should expect roughly twenty to forty seconds, an estimate derived from the timers, not a measurement. Run the drill yourself and record your own number. And every transaction that was open has been rolled back, which is exactly why your application's retry logic is part of this architecture and not an afterthought.
