One setting changes immediately, another needs reload, and a third waits for restart. Authentication and TLS add sharper risks: clients may stop connecting, or encrypt traffic without verifying server identity. You will inspect active values, parameter contexts, pending-restart state, parsed access rules, and connection trust. Then you can choose the least disruptive action without confusing an edited file, encrypted transport, and verified running behavior.

SHOW tells us what the server is using now; pg_settings tells us how those values became active and how they may change. The key evidence is context. shared_buffers and max_connections are postmaster settings, so changing them requires restart. work_mem has user context and can change per session. pending_restart is false for all three displayed rows. If a file says something different, the live setting remains the operational truth while you investigate its source.

ALTER SYSTEM writes a request to postgresql.auto.conf; it doesn’t guarantee that request is active. Here, max_connections is requested as 110 and pg_reload_conf returns true, yet pg_settings still shows 100 with postmaster context and pending_restart true. That means the reload succeeded but this setting needs a restart. Contrast work_mem: setting it to 32 megabytes applies immediately to the session, with user context and no restart pending. Always distinguish a successfully reread configuration from an effective value, or you may finish a change window with the old behavior still running.

For this ALTER SYSTEM change, reload is the correct action, so choice B is the operational answer. One accuracy note matters: pg_settings reports log_min_duration_statement with superuser context, not sighup. ALTER SYSTEM writes a cluster default, and pg_reload_conf() makes that request available without restart. Verify the resulting value, source, true context, and pending_restart state instead of relying on the label alone.

pg_hba_file_rules parses the authentication file into rows we can inspect, which is safer than assuming the text means what we intended. This lab shows scram-sha-256 for local, host, and replication rules, and password_encryption also reports scram-sha-256. That protects stored password verifiers, but it doesn’t encrypt network traffic. SSL is off in this packaged Docker example, and native defaults may differ. In production, remote password authentication should add verified TLS. Also review rule order carefully: PostgreSQL uses the first matching HBA rule, so one broad line can override safer rules below it.

sections.heading: TLS: encrypted is not the same as verified
paragraphs: Encryption can still carry credentials to the wrong server if the client never verifies identity. SHOW ssl and the pg_stat_ssl row prove that this session uses TLS, including its protocol and cipher. They don't prove that the client trusted the intended hostname. hostssl selects TLS connections, but client policy decides identity verification. sslmode=require encrypts transport, while verify-full checks both the trusted certificate chain and requested hostname. Where certificate infrastructure exists, make verify-full the normal production client policy.

PgBouncer separates client capacity from PostgreSQL backend capacity. In transaction pooling mode, max_client_conn allows up to 500 clients here, while the default and reserve pool sizes bound server connections. The live pool example makes that concrete: eight active clients are sharing five server connections, with three active and two idle. PostgreSQL still enforces max_connections at 100 across its backends. Don’t treat a larger client limit as more database concurrency. Pooling reduces connection overhead and queues demand; it doesn’t remove the server’s process and workload limits.

Configuration changes are safer when you know how they become effective and how clients authenticate afterward. Compare the reloadable setting with max_connections, inspect SCRAM and hostssl, then state which production clients should require verified TLS identity. Work through the change decision and explain the proof for each action.

Tenant isolation is decided early, when the first columns and constraints are named. If ownership must later be reconstructed through fragile joins, security and reporting inherit that ambiguity. Here the commerce schema becomes an enforceable contract through tenant identity, deliberate roles, constraints that reject invalid rows, and safely validated changes. A verified bootstrap gives every later write, policy, and recovery exercise the same meaning.

Treat this model as the commerce system’s spine. Customers, products, orders, line items, and inventory carry explicit account ownership, while scoped business keys keep identities meaningful within the correct tenant. Separate owner, application, analyst, and backup roles make privileges deliberate. A controlled search_path keeps object resolution predictable. Primary keys, foreign keys, and CHECK constraints are not decorative overhead; they reject invalid state at the database boundary for every client.

Before loading the model, make sure labdb exists and that this session is connected to it. The generated CREATE DATABASE command runs only when the catalog has no labdb entry, so a clean native setup may create it while a prepared container simply continues. After connecting, check the server version and current_database(). The important result is labdb. Accidentally bootstrapping into postgres is easy and confusing because the SQL may succeed, but every later session will look in the intended database and find nothing.

Now include the canonical bootstrap script and set the search path to app, public. This one script creates the roles, schemas, tables, indexes, grants, constraints, and deterministic seed data that later examples expect. Don’t focus on every status line; look for the bootstrap completion marker, then interpret the counts. Three tenants establish the multitenant shape, fifty thousand products support realistic indexing work, and twelve thousand forty orders give later query plans useful scale. If those numbers differ, resolve that now before comparing downstream results.

Why repeat tenant_id on every business table instead of reconstructing ownership through joins? Put the key on the row being protected or grouped. Row-level security becomes easier to audit, reporting gets a stable dimension, and a missed join can't quietly cross tenant boundaries. Isolation starts in the schema, long before a policy is written.

Let’s verify structure and seed meaning, not just script completion. The schema listing should include app, audit, public, and staging, and app’s table listing should show the six core tables owned by app_owner. Then use a known business row as a checksum: SKU-100 is Wireless Keyboard Pro at 19.99. Finally, the shipped-order count is 2,408. These checks cover namespaces, ownership, table presence, a specific product, and aggregate data shape. Together they catch partial bootstraps that a single success message could miss.

Application checks are useful, but they aren't the final authority. Imports, maintenance scripts, background workers, and every future application must obey the same database constraints. The temporary tables combine identity, keys, required values, tenant-scoped uniqueness, a price rule, and a parent reference. The valid row enters. The negative price is rejected with demo_product_price_check named in the error. The rule remains active when application code changes. That rejection proves PostgreSQL protects state at the shared database boundary, regardless of which writer submitted the row.

A logically simple migration can wait behind another session or block a deployment queue. The short lock timeout bounds waiting for the metadata lock. NOT VALID avoids scanning old rows during the add, but it doesn't make the DDL lock-free, and new rows must already satisfy the rule. Validation is the longer scan with a lighter lock profile. The final convalidated value of true is the proof. Rehearse this sequence against production-like table size and concurrency before scheduling the real change.

Everything that follows depends on a consistent multitenant foundation. Create and enter labdb, run the canonical setup, then prove the roles and seed shape. Show one named constraint rejection and one safely validated rule as well. Keep the catalog proof. Investigate any mismatch before continuing.

The checkout request returned success, but did it insert, update, or match nothing useful? A follow-up query adds ambiguity and can introduce a race. Make the write explain itself instead. PostgreSQL can return final values, expose conflict outcomes, and identify the branch selected for matched or unmatched data. You will choose the simplest form for each decision and leave the statement holding the evidence the application actually needs.

Choose the write form from the decision the statement must make. RETURNING is the proof channel for rows changed by INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. ON CONFLICT is the narrow choice when one uniqueness collision has one alternative action. MERGE fits when matched state leads to several business branches. COPY addresses volume rather than branching, and staging gives bulk input a validation boundary. Use MERGE only when its additional decision structure is genuinely required.

This insert runs inside a transaction so we can demonstrate it and roll it back cleanly. RETURNING product_id, sku, and price gives the newly written values as part of the same statement; there is no race-prone follow-up SELECT. The sample identity is 50001, although prior sequence use can legitimately produce a different product_id. What matters is that SKU-NEW-1 returns with price 19.99. In application code, this is the natural way to obtain generated identifiers and confirm the database’s final values.

Here the conflict target is the tenant-scoped key, tenant_id plus sku. If SKU-100 already exists for that tenant, EXCLUDED supplies the proposed name and price to the update branch; otherwise PostgreSQL inserts a new row. RETURNING then shows product_id 100, SKU-100, Widget v2, and 21.99 in this seeded example. Notice that the tenant belongs in the conflict key. A global SKU constraint would incorrectly make one tenant’s catalog collide with another tenant’s catalog. The rollback keeps the seed unchanged.

Choose the strongest immediate confirmation after an INSERT. Pause briefly: is it the command tag, another SELECT, or a clause on the write itself? The best answer here is RETURNING product_id, sku. It returns the application-facing identifier and business key from the statement that performed the write, avoiding a second lookup and making it clear which row PostgreSQL produced.

MERGE compares the source row with inventory using both tenant_id and sku. A match adds the incoming quantity; no match inserts a new inventory row. In this run, merge_action() reports UPDATE and the resulting quantity is 55, so we know exactly which branch fired and what state it produced. This is more expressive than treating every collision as the same update. Use MERGE when business behavior depends on matched state, and include all ownership keys in the match condition so one tenant can never modify another tenant’s row.

For bulk input, land the CSV in a temporary staging table first. That separates parsing and inspection from changes to the core products table. The staged rows are then inserted with the tenant identifier and active status; ON CONFLICT avoids duplicates, while RETURNING shows the two SKUs that actually landed. COPY reports two input rows and the insert reports two writes in this example. In production, this pattern gives you a clean place to validate prices, normalize text, and reject malformed records before they reach business tables.

A write path should reveal what PostgreSQL actually changed, especially when duplicate keys or matched state alter the branch taken. Exercise INSERT with RETURNING, a tenant-scoped UPSERT, and MERGE inventory while observing their returned rows. Pause and try all three, then explain when ON CONFLICT or MERGE better expresses the decision.

A report can be valid SQL, execute quickly, and still be wrong. NULL may turn a predicate into unknown, while pagination may repeat or skip rows as data changes. Neither problem must raise an error. Treat filtering and ordering as correctness rules: use NULL-aware comparisons, define a deterministic sequence, and continue from a stable key boundary. The resulting queries remain explainable on page one and dependable as both tables and concurrency grow.

SQL uses three-valued logic: comparisons can be true, false, or unknown. That’s why equals NULL never finds NULLs; use IS NULL. For equality or inequality that treats NULL as a comparable state, use IS DISTINCT FROM or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM. Also watch NOT IN: one NULL in its list can make every comparison unknown and return no rows. For pagination, prefer a stable keyset boundary over a deep OFFSET. OFFSET still scans past earlier rows and can shift when new records arrive.

This basic SELECT establishes good habits before queries become complicated. It projects only the tenant identifier, name, and a date-cast creation value, then orders by name so presentation is deterministic for this dataset. The timing line is informational, not a performance conclusion from one tiny query. More importantly, decide what one output row represents and preserve that grain as joins and filters are added. Beginners often assume result order is stable without ORDER BY; PostgreSQL makes no such guarantee, even when repeated executions happen to look identical.

You need a definite answer to “are these different?” even when either side may be NULL. Which operator fits? IS DISTINCT FROM. Unlike != or <>, it treats NULL as comparable for this purpose: two NULLs aren't distinct, while NULL and a non-NULL value are. Use it when the business rule can't tolerate SQL's unknown result.

Reports can look believable while NULL logic or unstable paging silently loses rows. Compare a NULL-safe predicate with the misleading alternatives, then build a keyset boundary using timestamp and order ID together. Put the video on hold, test both cases, and inspect the plan to see how the next page is reached.

Finance expected one customer row and received five valid-looking copies. The extra money usually enters when a join silently changes the result grain. Keep that question in view while building richer SQL through presence tests, per-parent selection, structured multi-step work, and analytic calculations. The goal is not clever syntax. It is knowing what one row represents at every stage and proving that totals survive each transformation.

sections.heading: Exists / Not Exists
paragraphs: This query asks for customers who have at least one shipped order and no cancelled orders. EXISTS and NOT EXISTS answer those presence questions without returning the matching order rows, so each customer remains one customer. A join could produce several copies when a customer has several shipped orders, and a later aggregate might accidentally count those copies. The misconception is that DISTINCT always fixes such reports; it can hide symptoms while leaving the wrong grain underneath. Start with the business grain, then choose operators that preserve it.

LATERAL lets the subquery refer to the current tenant row. For each tenant, PostgreSQL finds orders for that tenant, sorts by total descending with order_id as a deterministic tie-breaker, and keeps two. The outer result therefore contains at most two orders per tenant-six rows across the three seeded tenants. A LIMIT placed after one large join would keep two rows globally, not two per group. Windows and DISTINCT ON can solve related top-per-group problems, but LATERAL makes this per-parent lookup especially explicit.

Suppose the request is the top two orders for every tenant. Which family of tools preserves those detail rows? Pause, then choose. LATERAL, DISTINCT ON, or a window function can express per-group selection, depending on the exact requirement. GROUP BY alone cannot return arbitrary top detail rows; it collapses each group. The key idea is correlated or ranked set logic, with a deterministic tie-breaker in the ordering.

The top example is a recursive CTE. Its anchor selects root categories at depth one, and the recursive term joins children to the rows already found, increasing depth on each step. The bottom example chains a bounded archival operation: select 128 cancelled order IDs, delete and return those orders, insert their values into orders_archive, then count the inserted rows. Because it runs inside a transaction and returns 128, we can inspect the complete movement before deciding whether to commit. Here we roll back, preserving the lab.

First, aggregate at tenant grain: total orders, shipped orders through FILTER, revenue, and a revenue rank computed over those tenant aggregates. FILTER is valuable because several conditional measures can share one grouping without separate subqueries. Next, GROUPING SETS asks for counts by status, counts by tenant, and the grand total in one statement. The blank grouping columns represent subtotal levels, not necessarily stored NULL values. In a production report, use GROUPING() when you must distinguish generated totals from real NULLs unambiguously.

Finance queries need a defensible row grain, or joins can inflate totals without raising an error. Use existence tests to preserve customer grain, limit each tenant’s detail rows with LATERAL, and compare conditional aggregates carefully. Pause and build the report, checking where cardinality could change before trusting any total.

Treat database logic like testimony: creation is a claim, while behavior is the evidence. A function must return the expected value. A trigger must leave the promised audit row, and a procedure must prove its state change. A view must preserve its declared grain. You will also control name resolution and privileges, so reusable logic earns trust through observable results, deliberate ownership, and safe object lookup.

This SQL function calculates an order total and declares itself STABLE, which tells PostgreSQL it will not modify data and should see a consistent statement-level view. Focus on the call result: order one returns 23.98. That value is the useful signal because it confirms both execution and the expected aggregation. The pinned search_path matters just as much; it makes unqualified order_items resolve predictably instead of depending on the caller's session. Use the declaration to communicate behavior, then use a known input to verify the behavior.

The trigger records a price change only when the new value is distinct from the old one. After updating SKU-100, read the latest audit row and compare the old and new prices. That pair confirms the trigger fired for the intended row and captured meaningful history. An unsafe search path can make a valid trigger resolve a similarly named object in the wrong schema. Pin object resolution, exercise one controlled update, and inspect the audit table immediately.

One setting should travel with a function so object names resolve the same way for every caller. Which one? search_path. Themes affect presentation, while max_connections and wal_level belong to the cluster. Without a deliberate path, an unexpected schema can redirect an unqualified table or routine name. Set the path explicitly, and schema-qualify sensitive objects too.

A reporting view packages daily revenue at one stable grain: tenant and calendar day. Do not dwell on every clause; inspect the output shape. Each row must represent one day for the selected tenant, with revenue aggregated once at that level. Duplicate days usually mean an accidental extra dimension or join fan-out. The sample dates and amounts can vary with seed time, but the one-row-per-day shape should not. A view simplifies consumption only when its grain remains explicit and testable.

A procedure is invoked with CALL because its job is procedural side effects rather than returning a scalar expression. Here the useful signal appears afterward: SKU-PROC-100 has quantity 51, one higher than before. Reading that row confirms the state transition rather than merely confirming that CALL completed. Notice the explicit failure path too: when no SKU matches, NOT FOUND raises an exception. Silent zero-row updates are dangerous in inventory workflows. Pair each side effect with a postcondition you can query, and make impossible inputs fail loudly.

Database logic earns trust when its resolution, side effects, and output are all visible. Test a function with a pinned search path, make one controlled price change, and inspect the resulting audit history and reporting grain. Take a break from watching to run the chain, then explain why each observation supports the next.

Checkout is frozen, CPU is quiet, and the longest-running session may not be the culprit. Separate snapshots, which decide row visibility, from locks, which coordinate conflicting writers. Trace the waiting backend to its holder, then ask which timeout could have bounded the risk earlier. Identify visibility, wait type, blocker, and prevention policy before committing, rolling back, retrying, canceling, or terminating.

Keep two mechanisms separate. Snapshots govern visibility, so a reader may continue seeing an older committed version. Row locks govern conflicting writes, so a second writer may wait even though ordinary readers continue. The most useful signal during an incident is a lock wait tied to a blocking session; it tells you this is coordination, not computation. Deadlocks are cycles and PostgreSQL breaks one by aborting a participant, while advisory locks are application-defined coordination. Name the mechanism first, because each one calls for a different response.

Under Read Committed, Session A first sees quantity 50. Session B changes it to 40 and commits, and A's next statement sees 40 even inside the same transaction. The changed second result shows that PostgreSQL takes a fresh snapshot for each statement at this isolation level. That behavior is correct, not a dirty read, because A sees only B's committed version. If business logic assumes two separate SELECT statements observe the same world, Read Committed does not provide that promise; either lock the row or choose a stronger isolation strategy.

Repeatable Read changes one crucial observation. Session A sees quantity 50, Session B commits 40, and A still sees 50 until its transaction ends. The unchanged second read is the signal that A is using one transaction snapshot. This is valuable when several statements must reason from a stable view, but it does not mean writers cannot proceed, nor does it eliminate every serialization anomaly. Interpret the repeated value as snapshot stability, then remember that a new transaction is required before A can observe B's committed change.

A session is hanging. Where do you look first: historical query totals, index definitions, backups, or current activity plus blocking locks? Pause and choose. Start with pg_stat_activity and the blocking relationship. A waiting backend whose blocker PID points to another live transaction reveals today's lock holder. Find the waiter and holder before deciding whether to commit, cancel, or terminate anything.

Session A locks the inventory row and reduces its quantity to 49. Session B requests the same row and waits on a transaction ID until A commits. That wait event tells us the database is preserving write order, not simply hanging. A common incident pattern is an abandoned transaction left open in a console while checkout queues behind it. Inspect the blocker PID first, then end or shorten the holding transaction according to policy.

There are two different recovery scopes on this slide. A savepoint lets the transaction undo the constraint-violating decrement while preserving the earlier safe change. A serialization failure, by contrast, invalidates the concurrent transaction attempt and asks the application to retry it. The error class separates invalid data from unsafe transaction ordering. Retry serialization failures as a complete transaction with backoff; do not blindly retry invalid business data.

Finding a blocker is reactive; a timeout declares the safety boundary before the incident. Session A holds the inventory row. Session B sets local lock, statement, idle, and transaction budgets, then waits on the same row and fails with a lock timeout. Keep the transaction budget longer than the specific limits. Cancel one query; terminate only when the entire session must end. Set policies per role, application, or transaction after workload analysis.

A blocked checkout is easier to handle when you identify coordination instead of guessing at slowness. Reproduce one row-lock wait, trace the waiting backend to its holder, and release cleanly. Then name a workload-tested timeout boundary and explain whether shorter transactions or selective skipping fits this workload.

CREATE INDEX may be the least informative success message in a tuning change. The object can still be ignored, invalid, or costly to deploy. Useful indexing begins with the operator, predicate, ordering, and expected selectivity. It includes a write-aware build and catalog validity check, then ends with a measured plan. Read scan choices, buffers, and heap fetches to decide whether the complete index lifecycle created a cheaper path.

Choose an index family from the operator the query uses. B-tree supports equality, ranges, and ordered retrieval; GIN suits composite values such as JSONB, arrays, and text-search tokens; BRIN summarizes naturally correlated ranges in large tables. Operator compatibility matters because an index can store a column yet still be unusable for the predicate. INCLUDE columns solve a different problem: they can cover projected values without changing search order. Begin with the predicate, then decide whether covering reduces heap visits.

The index begins with tenant_id and then orders placed_at descending, matching a tenant equality filter followed by a time range and descending sort. In the plan, focus on Index Scan using orders_tenant_placed_idx. It shows that PostgreSQL can navigate directly to the tenant's recent rows instead of sorting a broad scan. The buffer count will vary, so compare it with a baseline on the same data and cache state rather than treating one number as a universal threshold.

A partial index stores only pending and picking orders, so it stays smaller and concentrates on the active workload. The query predicate must logically imply the index predicate; here status equals pending, so the plan can use orders_open_idx. A common deployment mistake is testing a simplified literal while the application sends a parameterized, broader condition the planner cannot prove compatible. Compare the real application predicate, not a convenient demo query, and confirm the selected scan in its plan.

sections.heading: Indexes: decision check
paragraphs: How do you determine whether an index helped: schema inspection, creation output, opinion, or measured plans before and after? Take a breath and choose. The best choice is EXPLAIN with ANALYZE and BUFFERS on the same representative query. The scan node reveals index use; buffers and elapsed time show work. Compare like with like, accounting for cache warmth.

This index searches by tenant and SKU while carrying name and price as included payload. The plan reports an Index Only Scan, but the most informative signal is Heap Fetches: zero. It means the visibility map allowed PostgreSQL to answer this lookup from the index without checking the heap. INCLUDE alone cannot guarantee that result; recently modified pages may not be marked all-visible until vacuum catches up. Interpret heap fetches alongside the scan type, and remember that covering indexes trade faster reads for extra index size and write maintenance.

The deployment goal is to avoid blocking inserts, updates, and deletes while the index is built. Session A runs CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Session B reads pg_stat_progress_create_index while that build is still running, then checks indisready and indisvalid after completion. Concurrent creation cannot run inside a transaction block, and failed builds can leave invalid indexes. Clean up deliberately and confirm the intended query plan. Catalog state plus the plan are the final proof.

An index is useful only when it reduces work for the real query, not when creation succeeds. Capture the plan and buffers, choose a write-aware build, and check indisvalid. Record the final validity state. Repeat the identical query, keeping cache variation separate from genuine access-path improvement.

PostgreSQL plans for the rows it expects, not the rows execution will eventually reveal. If the estimate is ten and reality is ten million, each later choice can be reasonable yet disastrous. Join order, memory, and parallelism all inherit the error. The fastest route to the cause is often the first node where estimates and actuals separate. Find that divergence and repair the statistical model before rewriting otherwise sound SQL.

Read a measured plan as a flow of rows and work, not as decorative indentation. Start near the nodes producing data and compare estimates with actuals. Then inspect join strategy, worker activity, buffers, and any temporary I/O. The first large estimate error is often the most useful signal because every parent node inherits that mistaken cardinality. A hash or nested loop is not inherently good or bad; it becomes inappropriate when its input size differs sharply from what the planner expected. Diagnose the model before blaming the algorithm.

This plan serves the latest 50 tenant orders through the tenant-and-time index. Focus on the shared buffer count, 18 in the example. Buffers translate the query into pages PostgreSQL had to touch, giving you a steadier measure of work than milliseconds alone. The Index Scan also satisfies the ordering, so the plan avoids a separate sort before the limit. Your timings will vary with hardware and cache warmth; compare buffer counts and plan shape against the same query under similar conditions to judge whether a change truly reduced work.

At the scan feeding the aggregate, estimated and actual rows are almost identical, so cardinality statistics are accurate for this tenant filter. The upper HashAggregate also completes in one batch, with no sign of a spill. A sequential scan is not automatically a defect when a substantial share of the table is needed. First ask whether row estimates are trustworthy; then evaluate whether the chosen scan and aggregate are reasonable for that volume.

Which detail deserves first attention: planning time, formatting, node color, or a huge gap between estimated and actual rows? Hold the answer for a beat. Chase the row gap. If a nested loop expects one row but receives hundreds of thousands, its join choice rests on bad cardinality. Find the earliest divergence, then investigate stale statistics, correlated columns, or hard-to-estimate expressions.

Ordinary column statistics often assume tenant and status behave independently. If particular tenants have very different status distributions, that assumption produces weak combined estimates. Dependency statistics teach PostgreSQL about the relationship, and the catalog row with stxkind containing d confirms that dependency statistics were defined. That catalog entry is only the setup signal; the practical test is the next measured plan after ANALYZE. Compare estimated and actual rows for the combined predicate. Keep the statistics object only if it improves the cardinality model used by real queries.

The leading-wildcard search begins with a Parallel Seq Scan and broad buffer work. After adding a trigram GIN index on lower(notes), the plan changes to a Bitmap Index Scan feeding a Bitmap Heap Scan, with far fewer pages touched. That reduction matters more than one timing sample because hardware and cache state vary. A normal B-tree does not solve this search pattern. Match the operator class to the search behavior, then compare plan shape and buffers again.

When a plan changes after bulk loading, the first bad cardinality estimate often explains every expensive choice above it. Find where estimated and actual rows first diverge, refresh statistics on the affected table, and compare the same plan again. Stop and investigate your result, noting whether the estimate and downstream work improve.

A large table may contain far less live data without losing a record. MVCC leaves obsolete versions until vacuum makes space reusable, while damaged pages or structures create a different integrity risk. Read tuple estimates, relation size, freeze age, vacuum progress, checksum state, and scoped amcheck results. Those signals separate routine cleanup, urgent wraparound action, and corruption investigation without pretending that maintenance or a clean check replaces recovery.

Maintenance is a connected loop. Updates and deletes leave dead tuple versions, and vacuum makes their space reusable. Freezing prevents old transaction IDs from approaching wraparound. Vacuum also updates the visibility map, which can make index-only scans avoid heap visits. Planner statistics are refreshed by ANALYZE, including automatic analyze when its threshold is reached. Ordinary VACUUM usually does not shrink the file, so measure dead tuples, freeze age, and physical waste before choosing a rewrite.

Start with the table statistics, not the disk size. For app.orders, pg_stat_user_tables reports about 12,040 live tuples and 4,820 dead tuples, with no recent vacuum in this example. Those values are estimates, but they clearly show cleanup pressure. Also inspect age of the current database's datfrozenxid; that is a separate signal for transaction ID freeze risk. In production, rising dead tuples may explain slower checkout queries, while rising XID age can eventually threaten all writers.

VACUUM with VERBOSE and ANALYZE does two useful jobs here: it reclaims reusable space from dead row versions and refreshes planner statistics. The verbose output reports 4,820 dead item identifiers removed across 210 pages, with 12,040 nonremovable row versions remaining. Afterward, pg_stat_user_tables should show n_dead_tup near zero and a real last_vacuum timestamp. Do not expect the operating-system file to shrink; ordinary VACUUM normally returns space to PostgreSQL for reuse, which is exactly what a busy orders table needs.

What creates most dead tuples in an MVCC table? Updates and deletes. PostgreSQL keeps older row versions so concurrent transactions retain a consistent view, and VACUUM later makes obsolete versions reusable. Inserts alone aren't the usual source. Track n_dead_tup for cleanup demand and transaction-ID age for freeze pressure; those measurements describe separate maintenance risks.

A size baseline separates facts from a vague claim of bloat. For app.orders, the example is about 184 megabytes total: roughly 128 megabytes of heap and 56 megabytes of indexes. pg_total_relation_size, pg_relation_size, and pg_indexes_size expose those components. If pgstattuple is available, pgstattuple_approx adds estimated free-space and dead-tuple percentages. This matters because a large table is not automatically bloated; a heavily used table can be legitimately large. Compare live data, dead space, and growth over time before scheduling a disruptive rewrite.

PostgreSQL 18 can queue eligible reads, execute them through its asynchronous I/O subsystem, and let us observe the configuration. Here, io_method is worker, io_workers is three, and io_max_concurrency is 64 at postmaster scope; effective_io_concurrency and maintenance_io_concurrency are 16 for this session. Sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, VACUUM, and other eligible operations may benefit. The important interpretation is that AIO changes how eligible I/O is performed. It neither invents a new SQL operation nor appears as a special EXPLAIN node.

Transaction ID wraparound is a maintenance failure with a severe consequence: PostgreSQL can eventually refuse new transaction IDs, stopping writes to protect data visibility. Compare age(datfrozenxid) across databases and watch the trend against configured freeze limits. Then inspect the oldest relations and find long-running transactions that pin the horizon. Vacuum or freeze the affected relations safely, remove the blocker when justified, and verify that age falls. This should be a monitored trend, not one universal panic number discovered during an outage.

This output proves that the PostgreSQL 18 asynchronous-I/O subsystem is configured and exposes its live work. worker is the selected method; io_workers and io_max_concurrency bound how requests can be serviced. pg_aios answers a different question: which handles are active at this instant? The displayed SUBMITTED readv row is one snapshot. Zero rows would also be valid when no eligible I/O is in flight, so use broader I/O and query statistics for trends.

Recognize AIO-eligible work from ordinary plan shapes and buffer activity; PostgreSQL does not add an AIO plan node. The first query demonstrates a sequential scan with shared reads. The temporary index and local planner settings expose a bitmap heap path for comparison, and the rollback removes that demonstration index. VACUUM is also eligible work. AIO may improve page fetching for these operations, but it cannot repair a poor predicate or change SQL meaning.

Checksums detect certain damaged data pages; they don't repair them. A newly initialized PostgreSQL 18 cluster enables checksums by default, while an upgraded or deliberately configured cluster may differ, so SHOW data_checksums is the first fact. Failures surface through server statistics, and the offline pg_checksums run broadens the inspection on a stopped cluster. Neither result covers every file or replaces backups. If corruption appears, isolate the system, preserve evidence, and recover through a known-good path.

Checksums verify physical data-page bytes. pg_amcheck asks a different question: are supported relations and B-tree structures internally consistent? The command-line tool scans broadly, while bt_index_check targets one known lab index. A clean run strengthens an integrity drill, but it doesn't replace recovery testing. Any finding needs investigation before repair. Reduce risky writes if necessary and preserve evidence. Determine whether damage is limited to an index or reaches table data, then connect the response to a verified backup and PITR path.

Rising checkout latency may reflect reusable dead space or urgent freeze pressure, and those need different responses. Measure dead tuples and transaction ID age, then observe vacuum progress. Add the cluster checksum state and a scoped amcheck receipt. Diagnose the orders table and state which maintenance or integrity risk the evidence supports.

Users type ‘wireles keybord,’ support searches for part of a SKU, and shoppers filter a structured attribute. Those are different questions, even if the interface shows one search box. A generic wildcard may scan the catalog as traffic grows. You will map each intent to an operator PostgreSQL understands, choose a compatible index, and verify candidate lookup and ranking. Better search starts by modeling meaning, not by indexing every text field.

sections.heading: JSONB containment
paragraphs: JSONB containment asks whether attrs contains a structure such as size equal to L. A GIN index using jsonb_path_ops is specialized for that @> query shape and is usually smaller and more focused than the default operator class when containment is the main need. The tenant predicate still matters for isolation and selectivity. In a production product catalog, this lets shoppers filter structured attributes without flattening every possible field into columns. Do not confuse containment with arbitrary text search: the data shape and operator determine the useful index.

Full-text search models language rather than raw substrings. plainto_tsquery turns “wireless keyboard” into a query, the @@ operator matches it against search_vector, and ts_rank orders stronger matches first. In this data, Wireless Keyboard Pro should outrank weaker results. A GIN index on the tsvector supports candidate lookup, while rank determines presentation. The common misconception is that full-text search is just a faster ILIKE. It also normalizes words and supports relevance, so verify both the access path and the ordering users actually see.

The predicate uses JSONB containment: attrs must contain the object whose size is L. Which index is designed for that operator? Choice B pairs GIN with jsonb_path_ops, matching the displayed @> query. B-tree and BRIN support different access patterns, while a hash index on name is unrelated. The decision comes from the operator and operator class, not from whichever index type is most familiar.

SKU lookup often needs typo tolerance, which is where pg_trgm fits. After enabling the extension, a GIN index with gin_trgm_ops can support trigram similarity operations on sku. The percent operator selects sufficiently similar values, and similarity provides a score for ordering. An exact SKU-442 scores 1, while a near value such as SKU-4420 can still rank highly. A normal B-tree does not generally help a leading-wildcard ILIKE. In support tooling, trigrams can turn a mistyped identifier into a useful candidate list without scanning the full catalog.

Catalog search scales when each user intent is paired with the right operator and index. Test JSONB containment, ranked full-text search, and trigram similarity, focusing on meaningful results and the chosen access paths. Take a few minutes to try them, then explain which search behavior each method serves better than wildcard matching.

Suppose one application query forgets tenant_id. Should that mistake become a breach? It will if isolation exists only in application code. Row Level Security adds a database-enforced boundary, but policy text alone is insufficient. Owners may bypass it, pooled sessions may retain context, and privileged tests may hide defects. You will test isolation through the real application identity, using trusted tenant context, least privilege, and policies that govern both reads and writes.

Use separate roles for ownership, login, and application access so no connection receives privileges it does not need. In an RLS policy, USING controls which existing rows are visible or targetable, while WITH CHECK controls which new or changed rows may be written. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY makes table owners obey policies too. Tenant identity should come through a trusted, membership-checking function such as app.set_tenant_context and app.current_tenant_id, not a client-writable setting. In a connection pool, make that context transaction-local so one customer's identity cannot leak into the next request.

On app.orders, enable Row Level Security, force it, and define tenant_isolation for app_user. Both USING and WITH CHECK compare tenant_id with app.current_tenant_id(), protecting reads as well as inserts and updates. The pg_policies row is the metadata receipt: it names the table, policy, role, command scope, and both expressions. Table owners normally bypass RLS unless it is forced, while superusers and BYPASSRLS roles remain privileged paths that need separate controls.

Test tenant context through the identities used by the application. First, app_login cannot set the raw tenant parameter, and the trusted setter rejects an unauthorized tenant. Then two authorized memberships produce different scoped counts: about 4,120 orders for tenant one and 3,880 for tenant two. Reset the role between checks, commit, and reset session authorization. The setter must verify membership and use transaction-local state, or a pooled connection can carry one customer's context into the next request.

Who should execute the isolation test: a superuser, the owner, or the application role with trusted tenant context? Hold your choice. Use SET ROLE app_user with tenant context, because that reproduces real request authorization. Testing only as postgres proves little: superusers bypass RLS. Also test writes through WITH CHECK and a cross-tenant attempt, so one successful same-tenant read does not create false confidence.

PostgreSQL 18 provides an OAuth authentication framework, but not a built-in validator that makes trust automatic. A separately supplied validator is configured through oauth_validator_libraries. The hostssl rule names the exact issuer, scopes, validator, and user map; pg_ident then maps a validated identity, such as clinician@example.com, to a least-privilege database role. Reject authentication if TLS, signature, issuer, audience, expiry, scope, validator result, or role mapping fails. An issuer that merely looks similar is not acceptable: exact trust configuration is the security boundary.

Follow the trust chain rather than treating the bearer token as a password substitute. libpq receives the server challenge with issuer and required scope, then uses oauth_client_id to obtain a token. TLS protects that token in transit. PostgreSQL passes it to the configured validator, which checks signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and scopes. Only then does the user map authorize a database role. This is an architectural flow, not an executed identity-provider lab. In production, every link-issuer, client, token, TLS, validator, scope, and mapping-must agree.

A policy can exist and still provide only the appearance of isolation. This probe temporarily turns FORCE off inside a transaction, then uses the non-superuser table owner app_owner. That role sees all 12,040 orders because owners bypass RLS by default. Restoring FORCE and checking relforcerowsecurity brings the catalog back to the course state before ROLLBACK. Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles remain privileged paths, so production reviews must inspect role attributes and ownership as well as policy text.

Tenant isolation should survive an application mistake, so test the database boundary through the application identity. Enable and force row security, use the trusted tenant-context function, and attempt both allowed and cross-tenant access. Run those checks, then name any privileged role that can still bypass the policy.

Deleting a month of history row by row can generate WAL, leave dead tuples, and consume a maintenance window. Detaching a correctly bounded partition removes the same period structurally. That advantage exists only when boundaries match retention and query predicates. You will prove pruning, move old periods deliberately, and apply the same discipline to foreign tables by checking whether filters run remotely or unnecessary rows cross the network.

Partitioning divides one logical table into physical children. RANGE is a natural fit for time retention; LIST and HASH address different distribution needs. ATTACH and DETACH let operations move a child into or out of the parent, making retention a structural action rather than a delete storm. Foreign Data Wrappers solve a different problem: accessing remote data. With postgres_fdw, inspect pushdown so eligible filters and joins execute remotely. A frequent misconception is that either feature automatically makes queries faster. Benefit depends on pruning, retention, network cost, and query shape.

orders_p is partitioned by RANGE on placed_at. Because PostgreSQL requires every unique or primary-key constraint on a partitioned table to include all partition key columns, the primary key contains both order_id and placed_at. Quarterly children cover 2026 Q1 and Q2, while a DEFAULT child catches rows outside those bounds. After inserting 500 source rows, grouping by tableoid reveals their physical destination-Q2 and default in this example. That check catches boundary mistakes early; a default partition can otherwise hide missing future partitions until it grows unexpectedly.

A date-bounded count for the Q2 interval should show only orders_p_2026_q2 beneath the aggregate. That plan is the meaningful proof of partition pruning; merely having child tables proves nothing about a particular query. Detaching the Q1 child removes it from the logical parent without deleting its rows, and attaching it again with identical FROM and TO bounds restores it. In production, use this pattern to archive a closed period, but validate bounds and constraints first so attachment does not require an expensive scan or reject overlapping data.

For time-based retention, which operation avoids a large row-by-row delete? Consider the options, then reveal: detach the old partition, followed by archive or drop according to policy. DELETE can generate heavy WAL and leave vacuum work; VACUUM FULL is a blocking rewrite, not a nightly retention mechanism; and truncating products targets the wrong data entirely. Detach is powerful because the partition boundary already identifies the period being removed.

Begin postgres_fdw setup at the remote warehouse. warehouse_db needs the app schema and a products table whose columns-product_id, sku, and qty_on_hand-match the local foreign-table definition exactly. The example warehouse contains 50,000 rows. Confirming that count establishes that the remote source is populated before local troubleshooting begins. Schema drift is a practical production risk: mismatched types or column order can produce errors or misleading behavior. Agree on the remote contract before creating the local server, user mapping, or foreign table.

On the local database, enable postgres_fdw, create a staging schema, and define warehouse_remote with the remote host, port, and warehouse_db name. A user mapping connects the current local role to warehouse_reader. Inspect the server metadata to confirm the wrapper and options. Lab credentials may be simple, but production secrets do not belong in SQL scripts, migration logs, or slides. Prefer protected mechanisms such as .pgpass or .pg_service.conf, apply least privilege to warehouse_reader, and remember that the mapping controls authentication while remote permissions still control accessible data.

Partition only when pruning, retention, or operational isolation provides a measurable gain. A table that fits comfortably in memory may become more complex without becoming faster. One deliberate failure illustrates an important rule: a primary key on a partitioned table is unsupported when it omits placed_at, the partition key. Include that key in the constraint. For FDW changes, compare EXPLAIN output and row counts to verify remote filtering and correct results. In production, a query that silently pulls 50,000 warehouse rows across the network can be correct yet operationally disastrous.

Partitioning pays off when query and retention boundaries align with the physical layout. Create time ranges around placed_at, confirm a bounded query prunes unrelated children, and rehearse detaching and reattaching one period. Complete the drill, then explain why structural retention avoids a large row-by-row delete.

Two requests have waited thirty seconds. One is blocked by an abandoned transaction; the other is waiting for its client. Equal duration does not imply equal action. Start with session state and named waits, follow blockers, and connect statement and I/O evidence. When the query has already finished, correlate the historical log through PID and application name. This preserves clues that an immediate restart would erase.

Start incident triage in pg_stat_activity because it shows what each client backend is doing now. State tells you whether work is active or idle; wait_event_type and wait_event explain why it cannot advance. Here, the active UPDATE waiting on a transaction ID points toward row-version contention, while ClientRead on an idle session means PostgreSQL is waiting for the application. In production, that distinction prevents blaming the database for an open connection and directs you toward blockers when transactions are actually stalled.

Once a lock wait appears, pg_blocking_pids connects the victim to the session holding it. Read blocked PID, blocking PID, wait event, and query together; killing the blocked session alone usually treats the symptom. The lower view answers a different operational question: is VACUUM stuck or progressing? A phase such as scanning heap plus increasing heap_blks_scanned indicates forward movement. During a maintenance window, sample these counters repeatedly before intervening, because a long operation can be healthy even when it looks quiet.

sections.heading: Monitoring: decision check
paragraphs: An API request is stuck and the incident channel wants action now. What's the strongest first branch? Ask which wait_event the backend reports. That answer separates locks, client waits, I/O, and other causes, narrowing the next query without changing the system. Dashboard styling and hardware trivia can wait; name the current wait first.

Use these views to connect accumulated workload cost with its source. pg_stat_io separates page activity by backend type, object, and context, so the displayed rows distinguish client work, vacuum activity, and checkpointer writes. pg_stat_statements then ranks normalized SQL by total execution time and calls. A high total may mean one expensive statement or a cheap statement executed constantly. Correlate both views, form a hypothesis, and compare the counters again after a controlled change.

Live views can't describe a query after it has finished or its backend has gone. A useful log prefix preserves the timestamp, PID, user, database, application name, and transaction ID. SET application_name labels a service or workload, such as checkout-api; it is not a unique request ID. PID and that service label connect history to pg_stat_activity, while request tracing needs its own correlation strategy. Structured jsonlog can simplify downstream parsing. Before detailed logging, test overhead, retention, volume, and sensitive-data exposure.

Good incident response narrows the cause before changing the system. Start with active sessions and named waits, follow a blocker, and connect the finding to statement and I/O cost. Correlate one PID and application name with its log line, choose a low-risk action, and state the signal you would check afterward.

A backup is a promise; a restored row is proof. A green job badge cannot establish that the right files, dependencies, continuous WAL, and recovery target remain reachable. Connect logical, full, incremental, and synthetic-full paths to their limits. Then restore in isolation and validate business data at the selected point. That practice turns recovery objectives from policy language into a result another operator can reproduce.

Think of recovery as a chain, not a single file. A logical dump supports selective, portable restoration through pg_restore. A physical base backup captures the cluster-level starting point. Archived WAL supplies every change needed after that point, and a recovery target tells PostgreSQL where to stop by name, time, or transaction ID. The final row check matters because successful file creation does not prove usable data. In production, your recovery objective determines which links must exist before an incident.

Choose the method from the recovery requirement. pg_dump is logical and portable, and it supports selected databases or objects as well as migration into compatible newer PostgreSQL versions. pg_basebackup is physical and, with continuous WAL archiving, supports cluster-level point-in-time recovery. Neither successful command completes the proof. Monitor archived WAL, schedule isolated restores, and validate application data so a silent archive gap or unusable dump is found before an incident.

The custom-format dump is useful because pg_restore can inspect it, select objects, and support parallel restoration. The archive listing confirms that expected tables such as app.orders and app.products are present, but presence is not correctness. Restore into a separate database, avoid importing ownership when the destination roles differ, and compare a stable business count with the source. Here, twelve thousand forty orders closes the loop. In production, preserve comparable counts or checksums with the change record so restoration has an objective result.

Check archive health before taking the base backup. archive_mode must be on, archive_command must write to the intended durable location, archived_count should advance, and failed_count should remain zero. A real last_archived_wal confirms recent movement rather than configuration alone. Then take and verify the compressed base backup under the PostgreSQL operating-system account. If a temporary replication slot was created for the backup, remove it afterward; an abandoned slot can retain WAL until the primary disk fills.

Incremental backup reduces transferred data, not dependency risk. With WAL summarization enabled, the previous backup manifest identifies changed blocks. Keep every manifest with its chain. An incremental directory can't be restored directly, and every required predecessor must remain available until pg_combinebackup creates a synthetic full. Losing the original full or a required incremental breaks that recovery chain. A successful combine is only an intermediate receipt. Verify the synthetic full, start it in isolation, and validate a business row before treating the result as recoverable.

Suppose an operator must recover to the moment before an accidental update. Is a pg_dump sufficient, or does the path need a restorable physical starting point plus continuous WAL and a target? A verified base backup works; so does a correctly combined and tested synthetic full. Recovery replays archived WAL and stops at the selected name, time, or transaction ID. A logical dump restores its captured state but cannot replay that continuous history.

The restore point belongs after the base backup because recovery can only replay forward from that backup’s checkpoint. First capture the original order count, create the named point before_bad_delete, and switch WAL so the segment containing that marker reaches the archive promptly. Then perform the deliberate delete and observe the lower count. In a real change window, this sequence gives responders an unambiguous pre-change target; a restore point created before the available base backup would be unreachable from that backup.

Verification covers two independent assets. pg_verifybackup checks the base-backup manifest and files; it does not prove that every WAL segment needed for recovery is available. Separately confirm the live PGDATA path, the archive directory, and that the WAL name reported by pg_stat_archiver exists as a real file. That still does not prove complete archive continuity. In production, verify both the starting image and the continuous history before declaring the restore drill ready.

An archive can look healthy until recovery requests the one segment that is missing. Here failed_count is still zero, yet the last_archived_wal file is gone from the archive directory. External deletion can create that gap. A rising failed_count also demands investigation even if later archives succeed. Repair archive_command, recover missing segments from another surviving copy when possible, and test against an isolated restore. Production alerting should detect failures and archive-age stalls before an emergency exposes them.

Recovery begins in an isolated, allowlisted directory. The helper first verifies the base backup and resolves both restore and primary paths. It then rejects path overlap, unsafe ownership, and tablespace hazards. Finally, it confirms expected cluster contents such as PG_VERSION, base, global, pg_wal, and configuration. These guards matter because a correct extraction command aimed at PGDATA would be destructive. Treat the extraction receipt as a mandatory checkpoint before configuring recovery.

Configure the restored cluster, not the primary. Assign a separate port, point restore_command at the WAL archive, select before_bad_delete as recovery_target_name, and create recovery.signal. Starting under the postgres operating-system account lets PostgreSQL replay until that named marker, then promote as configured. The new timeline is important: after promotion, this server has diverged from the old primary. Before sending production traffic, fence the former primary or rewind it; two writable histories create split brain and conflicting data.

This failure is intentionally ordinary: pg_restore cannot connect because the destination database does not exist. Either create the database first and restore into it, or use an archive and options that create the database explicitly. Custom format also leaves room for parallel restore when scale demands it. The broader lesson is to rehearse dependency order-roles, database, schema, then data-and record source-side validation values. A clean command exit without comparable application data is not a complete production restore result.

Validate the recovered service at three layers. pg_is_in_recovery returning false confirms promotion completed. The checkpoint timeline ID shows recovery created a new history rather than silently reconnecting to the source timeline. Finally, the order count of twelve thousand forty demonstrates that rows deleted after the named restore point are present again. That business-level result is stronger than backup size or startup success. After recording it, stop the temporary cluster and remove its isolated tree so no forgotten writable PostgreSQL instance remains on the host.

A backup becomes credible only when it returns meaningful data after a mistake. Restore the logical archive separately, combine and verify an incremental chain when used, then connect a base backup with archived WAL to a named recovery point. Rehearse in isolation and validate recovered rows without touching the primary.

A standby can answer pings and still be unsafe to promote. It may lag, retain WAL, or become a second writable history if the old primary isn't fenced. Readiness includes commit-protection policy, moving WAL positions, controlled promotion, and safe rejoin on the new timeline. Measure replay distance, prove a deliberate write, return the old primary as a standby, and follow logical changes before traffic depends on them.

A standby responds to ping and its tables are visible, but can it safely take traffic after failover? Compare the sender’s sent LSN with the standby’s replay LSN to measure WAL already sent but not yet replayed. That is more useful than reachability alone. For total primary-to-replay backlog, compare the primary’s current WAL location with replay_lsn as well, then judge the result against an explicit recovery objective.

pg_stat_replication shows the primary’s view of each physical standby. Streaming state confirms an active WAL sender connection, sync_state describes commit coordination, and the difference between sent_lsn and replay_lsn shows WAL already sent but not yet replayed. It does not include WAL the primary has generated but not sent. Cross-check the primary’s current WAL location, sender state, receiver activity, slot retention, and replay position before trusting the standby for failover or read freshness.

Promotion is a role change, not proof that applications can write. Run pg_ctl promote on the standby, confirm pg_is_in_recovery is false, and verify that the timeline ID advanced. Then insert into a dedicated health-check table and require a returned identifier. This separates control-plane success from data-plane readiness without touching arbitrary business rows. In production, fence the old primary before routing writes; otherwise both servers may accept divergent transactions, turning failover into a split-brain recovery problem.

RPO and commit latency are one policy decision. Asynchronous replication protects availability but can lose recent WAL at failover. Priority or quorum synchronous rules reduce that exposure by waiting for required standbys, which can add latency or affect availability when they disappear. synchronous_commit chooses remote write, flush, or replay acknowledgment. pg_stat_replication shows sync state and WAL positions. After promotion, fence the former primary before touching its timeline. Then use a rehearsed pg_rewind path, or take a fresh base backup if rewind can't proceed. Failover isn't complete until the old primary safely returns as a verified standby.

The sent-to-replay calculation measures WAL already transmitted but not yet replayed. Treat it as one signal, not a complete verdict. Compare the primary’s current WAL location with replay_lsn to include unsent WAL, watch the gap over time, and read sync_state against the configured commit policy. Check slot retention too. A single zero remains only a momentary lab receipt.

This publication exposes only inserts for orders whose status is pending or shipped. The row filter limits which changes qualify, while the publish option excludes updates and deletes entirely. Verify both dimensions with \dRp+: the publication should show inserts enabled, updates and deletes disabled, and the filter attached to app.orders. In production, confirm that this behavior matches downstream expectations; a consumer will not receive later status updates under an insert-only policy. Also monitor the logical slot, because inactivity retains WAL on the publisher.

sections.heading: Subscriber + publisher slot
paragraphs: Logical replication has two sides that must agree. On the subscriber, pg_stat_subscription shows the worker and received positions, indicating whether changes are arriving. On the publisher, the matching slot should be active, with restart_lsn and confirmed_flush_lsn advancing as the subscriber consumes WAL. Credentials belong in the passfile rather than exposed command text. During production monitoring, alert on inactive slots and growing retained WAL; a disconnected subscriber is not merely stale-it can eventually exhaust the publisher’s storage.

Failover readiness depends on replication progress and a safe role transition, not reachability. Show sync_state and replay backlog, fence the former primary, and explain its verified rejoin path. Confirm the logical slot is moving, then state which lag, commit-latency, or retained-WAL trend should trigger attention.

A PostgreSQL 18 upgrade begins with the old cluster, not the feature list. Inventory, compatibility, extensions, backups, transfer mode, cutover, and rollback must survive rehearsal. pg_upgrade --check is one gate; actual migration, statistics, query plans, and an application write provide acceptance evidence. Only then should uuidv7, temporal constraints, or planner improvements be judged against real workload needs.

This overview separates upgrade safety from feature exploration. pg_upgrade --check finds compatibility problems without modifying either cluster, but it is neither a backup nor a rollback plan. After the upgrade path is rehearsed, test each feature against a concrete need. UUIDv7 may improve key locality. Skip scan may serve a later-column predicate, and OLD/NEW output may strengthen write evidence. Successful demonstrations still do not make the cutover production-ready.

The useful observation here is not merely that uuidv7 generates valid UUIDs. Ordering the rows by the identifier should also order them by creation time, and uuid_extract_timestamp lets us compare the embedded timestamp with the separately recorded insertion time. That temporal ordering generally gives B-tree inserts better locality than fully random UUIDs, which can reduce page churn in write-heavy systems. It does not replace a business timestamp, guarantee gapless order, or remove the need to test real workload behavior.

Skip scan matters when a query constrains a later index column but omits the leading one. With an index on status and sku, PostgreSQL can probe relevant portions for each status value instead of abandoning the index entirely. In this controlled demo, disabling sequential scans makes the behavior easier to observe; it is not a production tuning recommendation. Look for Index Searches greater than one. There is no separate skip-scan plan node, and timings on a tiny temporary table are not capacity evidence.

A later-column predicate uses the composite B-tree, but the plan does not contain a node named skip scan. Which detail proves the behavior? Choice B: Index Searches greater than one. That count shows PostgreSQL made multiple probes across possible leading-column values. Read the search count together with the index condition; the ordinary Index Scan or Index Only Scan node name is not sufficient evidence by itself.

PostgreSQL 18 lets this update report its own transition. OLD.price preserves 19.99, while NEW.price reports 20.99 after the five-percent change. NEW.price_ex_tax is then computed from the updated row and returns 17.49. All three values come from the write statement, avoiding a follow-up query that would lose the original value. This is useful for audit and API output, subject to the expressions, constraints, and triggers applied to the update.

These temporal constraints move subscription validity rules into PostgreSQL, where every writer must obey them. The parent key combines account_id with valid_during and uses WITHOUT OVERLAPS, preventing two validity ranges for the same account from colliding. The PERIOD foreign key on usage asks a different question: is the usage range completely covered by one or more matching parent ranges? That distinction matters. Overlap prevention and coverage are complementary guarantees, and relying only on application checks leaves race conditions between concurrent transactions.

Do not label every multicolumn Index Scan as skip scan. The node name alone cannot prove it. For a predicate on a later index column, inspect Index Searches; multiple searches are the relevant PostgreSQL 18 evidence. Demonstrate the behavior on a disposable, analyzed table. Forcing a production plan or removing a real constraint merely to obtain a screenshot creates risk and does not establish that the optimization helps the workload.

The first result demonstrates temporal coverage across adjacent parent rows. Account forty-two has one validity range ending exactly where the next begins, so usage spanning mid-June to mid-July remains continuously covered and the PERIOD foreign key accepts it. The next insert tests a separate invariant: a June-to-August subscription overlaps existing validity and WITHOUT OVERLAPS rejects it through the generated key constraint. This is important for billing and entitlements, where a tiny gap or accidental overlap can produce incorrect access or double charging.

Run pg_upgrade --check as the PostgreSQL installation user after reviewing the compatibility checklist. A clean result confirms that the old and new clusters satisfy the checks pg_upgrade can perform, and check mode does not modify their data directories. Treat that message as permission to continue rehearsing, not permission to cut over blindly. PostgreSQL 18 preserves many core planner statistics, but not every extended, extension-provided, or cumulative statistic. Validate extensions, drivers, backups, rollback, and representative plans, then ANALYZE where testing shows it is needed.

A major upgrade starts with compatibility and rollback planning, not the transfer command. Inventory databases, roles, extensions, preload libraries, tablespaces, checksums, locale, encoding, and matching versioned binaries. Then initialize the PostgreSQL 18 target and run the check with the same mode you intend to execute. Copy mode is the portable lab choice here. Clone and copy-file-range depend on platform and filesystem behavior. Link and swap change the old cluster's rollback boundary much more sharply. Even when pg_upgrade completes, file migration alone is not application acceptance.

Cutover is an evidence checklist, not a celebration. Inspect generated scripts, verify extensions and preload libraries, then refresh missing and representative statistics. PostgreSQL 18 preserves most optimizer statistics through pg_upgrade, but not every form or runtime history, so plan checks still matter. Re-test roles, RLS through the application identity, data counts, checksums, logs, backup, and replication. One restored query plan and one successful application write prove more than service status. Monitor errors and latency after switching traffic. Keep rollback intact until acceptance criteria and the rollback window are complete.

PostgreSQL 18 features matter after the upgrade has passed application acceptance. Record one restored plan, one successful write, and the rollback window. Then compare UUIDv7 ordering, observe multiple index searches for a later-column predicate, and inspect OLD and NEW from one update. Keep feature proof separate from upgrade proof.

Imagine handing this cluster to the next DBA during an incident. Can they reproduce the isolation test, explain the checkout plan, restore deleted rows, and judge replication readiness from your evidence? This capstone combines separate skills into an operational handoff. Pair each claim with a command, observed result, and interpretation. A system is ready when another careful operator can verify what it protects and recover it under pressure.

Use this mission board as an execution order, not a reading list. Establish the database and roles before testing FORCE RLS, then capture the checkout plan before moving to backup and restore. Continue with point-in-time recovery, streaming lag, logical replication, and the upgrade compatibility check. For each drill, save the command, result, and interpretation. A green-looking cluster is not enough; another DBA should be able to review what was tested.

Before trusting an application row count, verify the security definition itself. pg_policies should show tenant_isolation assigned to app_user, with both the visibility condition and write check tied to current_tenant_id(). Then pg_class must report both row security and forced row security enabled for app.orders. The second flag is easy to miss: without FORCE RLS, the table owner can bypass policies. Production isolation therefore needs both catalog-state inspection and a behavioral test from the actual application identity.

Suppose the walkthrough is complete and every command looked plausible. Can you call the capstone successful? Pause on the choices. The defensible answer is the one tied to matching results from the missions, because attendance and clean-looking output do not establish recovery, isolation, or replication behavior. Operational confidence comes from connecting each claim to the relevant observed result and preserving enough context for someone else to review it.

This is the behavioral half of the RLS test. Session authorization becomes app_login, the tenant context is set to the displayed tenant UUID, and the restricted app_user role runs the query. The example count, four thousand one hundred twenty, is meaningful only because it matches that tenant's seeded rows; it is not a universal target. If the role sees the entire table, investigate policy scope, session context, and FORCE RLS immediately. Superuser testing would hide the very bypass this drill is designed to catch.

The capstone is a handoff test: another DBA should be able to reproduce your confidence from observed results. Connect tenant isolation to the real application identity, recovery to restored data, and continuity to replication and upgrade rehearsal. Pause and run the drill as a peer review, recording both successful observations and corrected failures.

You now have a PostgreSQL 18 operating routine. Explain slow queries with measured plans, restore backups, watch replication slots and WAL storage, and test row security through the application role. Keep those drills recurring, because recovery and isolation evidence goes stale. Continue with one practical habit each week, and share the PostgreSQL problem you want explored next. Thanks for learning with me, and keep testing every change safely.

takeaways: Reliable Postgres work starts with knowing what the server actually did, not what we hoped it did.
Encryption can still carry credentials to the wrong server if the client never verifies identity.
This query asks for customers who have at least one shipped order and no cancelled orders.
How do you determine whether an index helped: schema inspection, creation output, opinion, or measured plans before and after?
JSONB containment asks whether attrs contains a structure such as size equal to L.

entries.title: building multi master workflows with postgresql logical replication
titles: building multi master workflows with postgresql logical replication
titleKeys: building multi master workflows with postgresql logical replication
paragraphs: [2 minutes] Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining this advanced technical session at Postgres Conference in San Jose. My name is Ibrar Ahmed, and today we are going to build a practical mental model for multi-master workflows using postgres logical replication. We will start with the foundation: how physical replication streams the write ahead log, why that model is excellent for high availability, and where it stops helping when applications need writes in more than one place. From there we will move into logical replication, publications, subscriptions, replication slots, identity strategy, conflict management, operational guardrails, automatic DDL replication, ZODAN, and pgEdge Spock. The point of this talk is not theory for its own sake. The point is to connect the diagrams, the SQL, and the production failure modes so that when you design an active-active system, you know exactly which problems you are accepting and which controls must be in place before go-live. Let me set expectations for the level of detail. This is an advanced session, so we will not stay at the marketing diagram level. We will look at the ordinary mechanics first: where a change is written, how postgres remembers it, how another node consumes it, and what metadata is needed when more than one node can write. That foundation matters because multi-master systems usually fail in the gaps between concepts. A team may understand that replication exists, but miss that sequence values collide. They may understand that conflicts exist, but not decide which side wins before the incident. They may understand that a cluster spans regions, but not account for clock skew or a partitioned network. So as we go slide by slide, listen for the operational question behind each architecture choice: what would I monitor, what would I automate, and what rule would my team follow under pressure? That is the lens that turns this from a diagram into an operating model. One more framing point before we begin: multi-master is not a replacement for fundamentals. You still need backups, restore drills, schema review, and clear ownership of operational decisions. Active-active write capability raises the ceiling, but it also raises the cost of vague thinking. Throughout the session, treat every slide as an architecture review question you can ask in your own environment.
