It happens when partitions cause nodes to continue accepting writes while they can no longer agree on cluster membership or ordering. The deck shows four defenses. Quorum means a node must have enough peer agreement before accepting certain writes. A witness can act as a tie-breaker without storing application data. Fencing prevents an isolated node from continuing to serve writes when it should step aside. Application routing keeps traffic aligned with the current ownership and health model. These defenses work best together. If a network partition happens, you want the system to degrade in a controlled way, not create two confident versions of reality. The goal is not just uptime; the goal is safe uptime. Split-brain prevention is about deciding who is allowed to write when the cluster cannot fully communicate. Quorum gives nodes a rule: continue only when enough members or witnesses agree. A witness provides a tie-breaker without storing application data. Fencing cuts off the isolated side so it cannot accept writes that the rest of the cluster will later reject. Application routing reinforces the same decision at the traffic layer. The dangerous situation is not a node going down; it is two sides believing they are both authoritative. Once both sides accept independent writes during a partition, recovery becomes a business reconciliation exercise, not just a database restart. That is why fencing mechanisms must be tested. Power control, load balancer withdrawal, security group changes, or read-only demotion are only useful if they work under the conditions that caused the partition. After a partition, the hardest question is not whether services restart. It is whether the cluster can prove which writes were accepted and which node was authoritative. That proof depends on logs, fencing records, witness decisions, and application routing history. Build those breadcrumbs into the system before you need a post-incident explanation. Additional speaker note: Split-brain prevention is the place where architecture and operations meet. Fencing, routing, quorum, health checks, and human override rules need to work together. The goal is not simply to restore service quickly; the goal is to avoid creating two valid-looking histories that later require emergency reconciliation. Technical correction for this slide: two data nodes do not create a safe majority by themselves. A witness or quorum device acts as a tie-breaker, and fencing prevents an isolated old writer from continuing to accept traffic after the cluster has moved on.

sections.heading: Interactive: Monitoring
paragraphs: [5 minutes including live demo] A multi-master cluster that is not observable will eventually surprise you. This monitoring slide focuses on the signals that tell you whether replication is healthy. Replication lag tells you how far subscribers are behind. Slot health tells you whether retained write ahead log is accumulating and threatening disk capacity. Conflict frequency tells you whether the application is creating more concurrent write contention than expected. Round-trip time tells you whether the network is widening the conflict window. These are not vanity metrics. They are the operational dashboard for active-active correctness. The important habit is to alert before the user-visible symptom. If retained bytes are growing, if lag crosses thresholds, or if conflicts spike, you want the team investigating while the system is still recoverable. Monitoring should map directly to the failure modes we have discussed. Replication lag maps to stale reads and widening conflict windows. Slot health maps to write ahead log retention and disk exhaustion risk. Conflict frequency maps to whether ownership and routing are working. Alert thresholds map to the moment when an operator must act before impact spreads. Good dashboards are not crowded; they are opinionated. Show the signal, show the threshold, show the owner, and link the runbook. Also capture trends. A single lag spike may be harmless; lag increasing every afternoon is capacity planning. A single inactive slot may be maintenance; retained bytes growing for hours is a storage incident. Observability is not just looking at the cluster. It is turning cluster behavior into timely human action. Alert quality matters. A page that says replication is broken is less useful than one that says slot retained bytes crossed threshold on node B, likely because subscriber C has been inactive for twenty minutes. Good alerts point to the runbook and include the first diagnostic query. The goal is to shorten time from signal to correct action.

sections.heading: Testing in Four Phases
paragraphs: [3.5 minutes] Testing needs to happen in phases, and the slide lays them out clearly. Phase one is pre-deployment validation: write ahead log level set to logical, enough replication slots and senders, commit timestamp tracking if your resolution rule requires it, replica identity configured, and clock drift verified. Phase two is functional testing: prove inserts, updates, deletes, schema expectations, and conflict paths behave as designed. Phase three is performance testing: run realistic write volume, measure end-to-end visibility across nodes, and watch CPU, I/O, and replication lag under load. Phase four is chaos testing: kill nodes, partition the network, exhaust disk in a controlled environment, and rehearse recovery. This is how you turn a multi-master design from a diagram into an operational system you trust. The four testing phases are how you earn confidence. Pre-deploy checks catch static mistakes: missing replica identity, insufficient slots, wrong write ahead log level, unsynchronized clocks. Functional tests prove the basic flows: insert on A appears on B, conflict is triggered intentionally, the configured rule resolves it, DDL behaves as expected. Performance tests answer whether the system holds under real write volume. You need end-to-end visibility time, apply throughput, CPU, disk I/O, and slot retention under load. Chaos tests answer whether your runbooks work when things break: kill apply workers, partition regions, fill disks, promote nodes, and verify fencing. The point is not to be dramatic. The point is to discover failure behavior in a lab before customers discover it in production. Testing should also record timings. How long did the partition detection take? How long until fencing completed? How long to catch up after reconnect? How long before dashboards turned green? Those measurements become your real recovery time and recovery point assumptions. If they differ from the architecture slide, believe the drill, not the slide.

sections.heading: Practical Operating Model
paragraphs: [3.5 minutes] This operating model slide ties the database back to the rest of the stack. At the top, the application layer should use idempotent writes, understand ownership where possible, and avoid creating unnecessary conflicts. The write router should direct requests to the right node based on tenant, region, or ownership rules. The database layer is the active-active mesh, but it should be treated as infrastructure as code: same extensions, same parameters, same schema discipline across nodes. Observability sits alongside the whole stack because you need to see lag, slots, conflicts, and node health continuously. Finally, change management matters. Schema changes, node additions, failovers, and upgrades should be rehearsed and automated. Multi-master is not a single feature you turn on; it is an operating model that combines application behavior, database rules, and production discipline. The operating model is where architecture becomes routine. The application layer should use idempotency keys, ownership-aware writes, and retry behavior that does not create duplicate business events. The write router should encode ownership and health decisions, not just round-robin traffic. Infrastructure as code should build nodes from the same definition so parameter drift does not creep in. Monitoring and disaster recovery runbooks should sit beside the cluster, not in a separate forgotten wiki. Change management matters too: schema changes, extension upgrades, node additions, and failover drills should have owners and review gates. A multi-master system can be reliable, but only if the people operating it treat replication as an always-on discipline. The technology gives you possibility; process turns it into uptime. The operating model should be owned by a team, not by a document. Someone must review drift reports, maintain runbooks, update dashboards after incidents, and verify that new application features respect ownership rules. Multi-master is a living system. Its reliability depends on routine care, not a one-time implementation project. Additional speaker note: The operating model is the maintenance system for correctness. Dashboards, backup validation, schema governance, conflict reviews, and drills are not paperwork. They are the controls that keep a sophisticated replication topology understandable after the initial implementation team has moved on.

sections.heading: Automatic DDL Replication
paragraphs: [3 minutes] Schema management deserves its own slide because it is one of the easiest places to break logical replication. In core postgres, DDL is not part of the logical replication stream. If you run an alter table on node A, node B and node C do not automatically receive the same schema change. That creates drift, and drift can break apply workers or produce subtle application failures. The slide contrasts that manual reality with automatic DDL replication in pgEdge. The value is not just convenience. It is reducing the chance that one node has a different table definition during active writes. Even with automation, the discipline remains the same: plan schema changes, apply them consistently, validate them everywhere, and treat schema as cluster-wide state rather than a local edit. Automatic DDL replication addresses a painful class of operational errors. In core logical replication, data changes flow, but DDL does not automatically follow. That means a table altered on one node may receive replicated rows on another node whose schema is still old. The apply worker then fails, or worse, the application sees inconsistent capability by region. The left side of the slide shows that drift clearly. The pgEdge path is valuable because DDL can be coordinated cluster-wide, reducing manual synchronization mistakes. But automatic does not mean careless. You still need compatibility planning, migration windows for risky changes, and rollback thinking. Additive changes are easier than destructive ones. Index builds, column defaults, and constraints all have operational cost. The goal is not just to broadcast DDL; it is to keep schema as consistent cluster state. For DDL, remember that automatic propagation still deserves review. Adding a nullable column is usually low risk. Dropping a column, changing a type, or adding a constraint can be disruptive. The safest teams classify DDL changes, test them against replicated staging clusters, and maintain backward-compatible application deployments so database and code can roll forward safely. Production qualifier for this slide: automatic DDL and near-zero data loss depend on replication lag, supported object types, change discipline, and operational guardrails. Present these as achievable operating goals under constraints, not as unconditional behavior in every topology.

sections.heading: ZODAN: Adding Nodes
paragraphs: [3 minutes] Adding a node is a moment where operational discipline shows up. The ZODAN workflow on this slide is designed so traffic continues while the new node is introduced. First, ZODAN creates the required replication slots and subscriptions while the existing nodes keep serving the application. Second, the new node takes an initial copy and then catches up by applying ongoing changes from the cluster. Third, once it reaches the current replication position, it is promoted into the active mesh and begins participating as a full peer. The same pattern helps with replacement, scale-out, and major-version upgrade workflows. The key idea is controlled membership change. You do not want node addition to be a weekend maintenance ritual; you want it to be a repeatable, observable operation. Adding a node tests whether your automation is real. Manually building subscriptions and slots while traffic is live invites mistakes: wrong credentials, wrong publication, missing table, or inconsistent initial copy. ZODAN automates the membership workflow. Existing nodes continue serving traffic while the new node subscribes and catches up. The initial sync brings base data across; ongoing replication closes the gap; promotion enables writes only when the node is ready. The same model is useful for replacement and upgrades because it avoids treating topology changes as rare hero work. The operational promise is zero downtime, but the engineering requirement is observability. You should be able to see catchup position, remaining lag, slot state, and promotion readiness before allowing the new node into the active mesh. Node addition also has security and capacity implications. The new node needs credentials, network access, slot capacity, storage sizing, and monitoring enrollment before it carries traffic. Automating subscriptions is only part of the job. The node must enter the same operational envelope as the existing peers: backups, alerts, runbooks, and ownership policy.

sections.heading: pgEdge Spock
paragraphs: [3 minutes] This is where the pieces come together in pgEdge Spock. Spock is a postgres extension for active-active logical replication. It is not a fork of postgres, and it does not require changes to the postgres core. In the diagram, nodes in the US, EU, and AP regions can all accept reads and writes, while Spock handles origin tracking, loop prevention, replication between peers, and the mechanics needed for convergence. The important point for architects is that Spock builds on standard postgres concepts rather than replacing postgres with a different database. You still need the design discipline we discussed: identity strategy, conflict rules, monitoring, schema control, and split-brain protection. Spock gives you the replication machinery; good architecture tells that machinery what safe behavior looks like. Spock is the technology layer that packages many of these active-active mechanics for standard postgres. The important phrase is standard postgres. This is not a fork that asks you to abandon your ecosystem. It is an extension that adds bidirectional logical replication behavior, origin awareness, and active-active coordination on top of familiar database operations. But no extension eliminates the need for design judgment. Spock can move changes, tag origins, and support the mesh; you still decide identity strategy, conflict rules, ownership, monitoring thresholds, and split-brain policy. That separation is healthy. Database technology should provide reliable mechanisms, while architecture defines safe use. When those two line up, active-active postgres becomes an operational pattern rather than an experiment. This is also where standard postgres expertise remains valuable. You still inspect catalogs, reason about slots, tune workers, manage indexes, and read logs. Spock extends the replication model, but it does not make postgres knowledge obsolete. In fact, active-active deployments reward teams that understand both the extension behavior and the underlying database mechanics. Additional speaker note: pgEdge Spock can reduce the mechanics of active-active logical replication, but it does not remove the need for disciplined design. Clear identity strategy, tested conflict handling, controlled DDL, monitoring, and realistic recovery procedures remain the difference between a powerful architecture and an operational risk. Production qualifier for this slide: pgEdge Spock reduces the mechanics of active-active logical replication, but it still depends on identity strategy, conflict resolution, DDL governance, monitoring, and recovery drills. The tool helps, but it does not replace design discipline.

sections.heading: Thank You
paragraphs: [2 minutes] Let me close by connecting the thread across the whole deck. We began with physical replication and write ahead log streaming: excellent for high availability, but built around one primary writer. Then we moved to logical replication, where row-level changes flow through publications, subscriptions, and slots. From there we built the multi-master model: every node can accept writes, publish local changes, and subscribe to peers. That model creates real benefits, but it also demands real controls: identity that cannot collide, deterministic conflict handling, origin-aware loop prevention, schema discipline, monitoring, testing, and safe node operations through tools like ZODAN and pgEdge Spock. If you are evaluating active-active postgres, the question is not just can we replicate writes. The question is can we operate the rule system around those writes. Thank you, and I am happy to take questions. For the closing, I want to leave you with a checklist you can take back to your own environment. First, identify which workloads truly need multi-writer behavior and which only need read locality or failover. Second, fix identity before you create a mesh. Third, write conflict rules in business language and then implement them consistently. Fourth, monitor lag, slots, conflicts, clocks, and routing health as first-class signals. Fifth, rehearse the failure modes: partitions, node loss, drift, and schema change. If those items are not in place, pause before calling the design production-ready. Multi-master is powerful because it gives users local write availability and teams flexible topology. It is safe only when the rule system around it is explicit, automated, and practiced. Thank you, and I am happy to take questions. My final recommendation is to run a tabletop exercise after this talk. Take one table, one tenant, one conflict, one node failure, and one schema change. Ask the team what happens, who is paged, which query proves state, and what the user sees. If that conversation is crisp, your design is maturing. If it is vague, you have found the next work item.

takeaways: [2 minutes] Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining this advanced technical session at Postgres Conference in San Jose.
[4 minutes] Logical replication changes the unit of replication.
[6 minutes including live demo] Let us walk through the SQL workflow on this slide in order.
[3 minutes] This comparison slide is useful because it separates three patterns that often get mixed together.
[3 minutes] This slide shows the core limitation very clearly.

entries.title: mysql to postgresql migration
titles: mysql to postgresql migration
titleKeys: mysql to postgresql migration
paragraphs: SCENE: Black screen. MySQL and PostgreSQL logos face off. Hero comparison card flies in. Five glowing stats appear across the bottom: 60-80%, 10x, 1000+, #1, $0. NARRATION: MySQL got you here. Simple. Fast. Everywhere. [PAUSE] But you've hit the ceiling. Window functions you can't trust. JSON that's slower than it should be. GROUP BY rules from 1995. No transactional DDL. And Oracle owns the roadmap. [CUT] Five numbers. Sixty to eighty percent of your queries port as-is. Ten times faster JSONB search. Over a thousand extensions. Number one most-admired database four years running. Zero Oracle license fees. [PAUSE] I'm Dr. Ibrar Ahmed. Today - the complete MySQL to PostgreSQL playbook. Forty slides. Every conversion. Every gotcha. Every fix. If you're a developer, DBA, or engineering lead - bookmark this video. You'll come back to it. ★ RETENTION HOOK: Stay for slide 36 - ten MySQL behaviors that silently break in PostgreSQL. Number four costs people entire weekends.

SCENE: Three-column card layout: SQL Standard, Advanced Features, Reliability. Critical orange callout at bottom: 60-80% queries port as-is. NARRATION: Three reasons you migrate. [CUT] One - SQL standard. Real window functions. Recursive CTEs. MERGE. RETURNING. LATERAL joins. GROUPING SETS, CUBE, ROLLUP. MySQL has none of these or partial support. [CUT] Two - power features. JSONB with GIN indexing - ten times faster than MySQL JSON. PostGIS - gold standard for geospatial. Built-in full-text search. Custom types. A thousand-plus extensions. [CUT] Three - reliability. True MVCC. Transactional DDL - yes, you can rollback a CREATE TABLE. Logical replication. Community-governed. No Oracle license surprises. [PAUSE] And the good news. MySQL to PostgreSQL is easier than Oracle to PostgreSQL. Both open-source. Both MVCC. Expect sixty to eighty percent of queries to port with minimal changes. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Run this on your MySQL right now: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.routines WHERE routine_schema = 'your_db'. That number is your conversion effort. CHAPTER 2 · Architecture & Data Types - 1:00-3:30 (slides 3-4)

SCENE: Ten-row comparison table fills the screen. Storage Engine row highlights first. NARRATION: Architecture. The biggest shift first. [CUT] MySQL has pluggable storage engines - InnoDB, MyISAM, Memory. PostgreSQL has one unified engine. Everything is a heap table with MVCC. Simpler. [CUT] Database equals schema in MySQL - no namespaces. PostgreSQL: one database, multiple schemas, search_path resolves. [CUT] Connection model. MySQL uses threads - cheap, lightweight. PostgreSQL uses OS processes - heavier, you must pool. This is the number one operational surprise for MySQL DBAs. We cover PgBouncer on slide twenty-five. [CUT] Character sets. MySQL's utf8 is three bytes. Not real UTF-8. You need utf8mb4. PostgreSQL is always real four-byte UTF-8. No confusion. No mistakes.

SCENE: Twenty-row reference table. UNSIGNED warning callout highlights red at the bottom. NARRATION: Every MySQL type. Every PostgreSQL equivalent. Twenty rows. [CUT] TINYINT becomes smallint. TINYINT-one becomes boolean - pgLoader does this automatically. INT becomes integer. [PAUSE] Here's the trap. INT UNSIGNED has no PostgreSQL equivalent. Unsigned integers do not exist in PG. INT UNSIGNED must become bigint. BIGINT UNSIGNED must become numeric-twenty-zero. [CUT] DOUBLE becomes double precision. DECIMAL maps to numeric - exact match. VARCHAR maps to varchar. TEXT maps to text. MEDIUMTEXT and LONGTEXT - all become text. No size variants needed. [PAUSE] The critical one. DATETIME maps to timestamp. But MySQL TIMESTAMP - which auto-converts to UTC - must map to timestamptz, not timestamp. Get that wrong and your timezone data is silently corrupted. ENUM becomes a separate CREATE TYPE. SET becomes an array. JSON - always use jsonb. ★ RETENTION HOOK: The UNSIGNED trap catches every migration. Search your schema for UNSIGNED right now. Every one needs manual review. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Run: SELECT column_name, column_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE column_type LIKE '%unsigned%' AND table_schema = 'your_db'. Fix those first. CHAPTER 3 · SQL & Code Conversion - 3:30-8:00 (slides 5-10)

SCENE: Side-by-side code blocks. MySQL left in orange. PostgreSQL right in cyan. VS badge in center. NARRATION: The query-level changes you'll make a hundred times. [CUT] Backtick quoting becomes double-quote - or just lowercase everything. LIMIT ten comma twenty - MySQL's offset syntax - becomes LIMIT twenty OFFSET ten. Standard SQL. [CUT] IFNULL becomes COALESCE. IF-condition becomes CASE WHEN. CONCAT works in both, but PostgreSQL also gives you the double-pipe operator - cleaner. [CUT] ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE becomes ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE - and you must name the conflict target. [CUT] GROUP BY with non-aggregated columns - MySQL allows it with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off. PostgreSQL always enforces the standard. Add every selected column to GROUP BY. [CUT] SHOW TABLES becomes backslash-dt in psql. DESCRIBE becomes backslash-d. Muscle memory. Takes a week.

SCENE: Three PostgreSQL options side-by-side: SERIAL, IDENTITY, RETURNING. NARRATION: AUTO_INCREMENT. Three PostgreSQL replacements. [CUT] SERIAL - the legacy way, creates a hidden sequence. GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY - the modern SQL-standard way. Recommended. [PAUSE] And the upgrade. RETURNING. In MySQL you call LAST_INSERT_ID after an INSERT. Race condition risk every time. In PostgreSQL: INSERT INTO orders VALUES something RETURNING id. Atomic. One statement. No race. [CUT] Use RETURNING on every INSERT and UPDATE. One of the best features you gain.

SCENE: MySQL DELIMITER procedure on left. PostgreSQL dollar-quote function on right. NARRATION: Stored procedures. The DELIMITER hack goes away. [CUT] MySQL needs DELIMITER slash-slash because semicolons confuse the parser. PostgreSQL uses dollar-quoting - double-dollar-sign. No DELIMITER. No confusion. [CUT] OUT parameters become function RETURN values - much cleaner. SET-variable becomes colon-equals assignment. Session variables with at-sign do not exist - use return values or temp tables. [PAUSE] The body logic translates almost directly. IF, WHILE, FOR, CASE - all the same. The syntax wrapper is different. The logic inside is ninety percent identical.

SCENE: MySQL inline trigger on left. PostgreSQL two-step function-plus-trigger on right. NARRATION: Triggers split into two parts. [CUT] A trigger function that returns trigger. And a CREATE TRIGGER that attaches it. [CUT] The function MUST return NEW for BEFORE INSERT or UPDATE triggers. Return NULL and the operation silently cancels. That catches everyone. [CUT] One function - reusable across tables. PostgreSQL also gives you TRUNCATE triggers, multiple triggers per event, built-in variables like TG_TABLE_NAME and TG_OP. More powerful. But the two-step pattern is the mental model you must internalize.

SCENE: Ten-row function table with risk badges: green Easy, yellow Review, red Manual. NARRATION: String functions. Most map directly. [CUT] CONCAT, CONCAT_WS, REPLACE, LPAD, RPAD, SUBSTRING - identical. [PAUSE] The one that breaks everything: GROUP_CONCAT. It becomes string_agg with an explicit delimiter. GROUP_CONCAT-column becomes string_agg-column-comma. If you used ORDER BY inside GROUP_CONCAT, move it inside string_agg. [CUT] LOCATE becomes position. REGEXP becomes the tilde operator. HEX and UNHEX become encode and decode with bytea casting. [CUT] Search your codebase for GROUP_CONCAT first. It's in every MySQL application.

SCENE: Side-by-side code blocks. MySQL date functions left. PostgreSQL equivalents right. NARRATION: Dates. The format strings are completely different. [CUT] MySQL DATE_FORMAT uses percent-Y-percent-m-percent-d. PostgreSQL to_char uses YYYY-MM-DD. No percent signs. [CUT] DATEDIFF does not exist - subtract two dates, you get an integer of days. UNIX_TIMESTAMP becomes extract-epoch-from-now. DATE_ADD with INTERVAL becomes just plus-interval. Simpler, actually. [CUT] YEAR-of-column becomes extract-year. NOW and CURDATE work the same. Mechanical. Tedious. Straightforward. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Global find-and-replace: DATE_FORMAT → to_char, IFNULL → COALESCE, GROUP_CONCAT → string_agg. Those three cover fifty percent of function conversions. CHAPTER 4 · Advanced Features - 8:00-11:00 (slides 11-17)

SCENE: Side-by-side JSON code. MySQL generated-column workaround left. PostgreSQL GIN index right. NARRATION: JSON. This is where PostgreSQL dominates. [CUT] MySQL stores JSON as text. PostgreSQL has jsonb - binary storage. The containment operator at-greater-than with a GIN index searches all paths at once. [CUT] MySQL: create a generated column, index it, query the generated column. PostgreSQL: create one GIN index, query with at-greater-than or arrow operators. Orders of magnitude faster. [CUT] Plus jsonpath queries - the SQL-JSON standard. If you use JSON heavily, this alone justifies the migration.

SCENE: Eleven-row table. MySQL types on left. PG types including four PG-only entries highlighted cyan. NARRATION: Indexes. B-tree, UNIQUE, standard - all map directly. [CUT] FULLTEXT becomes GIN on tsvector - we cover that on slide thirty-four. SPATIAL becomes GiST with PostGIS. Prefix indexes - KEY column ten - become expression indexes with the left function. [PAUSE] Here's what you gain. GIN for arrays, JSONB, full-text - MySQL has nothing equivalent. BRIN for huge time-series tables - one thousandth the size of a B-tree. Partial indexes - index only rows WHERE active equals true. Covering indexes with INCLUDE - index-only scans without bloating the key. [CUT] After migration, review your indexes for these. Game-changers.

SCENE: MySQL view on left with no-materialized-view warning. PostgreSQL materialized view plus recursive CTE on right. NARRATION: Views convert directly - same syntax. [CUT] The upgrade: materialized views. MySQL doesn't have them. You'd build cache tables manually. PostgreSQL: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW, then REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY - no locks on readers. Use pg_cron to schedule refreshes. [CUT] Recursive CTEs - WITH RECURSIVE - let you traverse trees and graphs. Parent to child, any depth, one query. MySQL 8 added basic CTEs. PostgreSQL's are more mature and better optimized.

SCENE: MySQL inline PARTITION BY on left. PostgreSQL declarative separate-partition on right. NARRATION: Partitioning syntax differs significantly. [CUT] MySQL defines partitions inline with the CREATE TABLE. PostgreSQL uses declarative syntax - create the parent, then create each partition separately with FOR VALUES. The primary key must include the partition key in both. [CUT] MySQL KEY partitioning has no equivalent - convert to HASH. MySQL PARTITION BY RANGE of YEAR-of-column uses an expression - PostgreSQL only allows column references for range partitioning. Partition directly on the timestamp column. [CUT] PostgreSQL gives you DETACH PARTITION for zero-downtime partition management. DEFAULT partitions catch overflow.

SCENE: MySQL user-at-host on left. PostgreSQL role-based with pg_hba.conf callout on right. NARRATION: The user model is fundamentally different. [CUT] MySQL: users are name-at-host. CREATE USER app at ten-dot-zero-dot-zero-dot-percent. Host-based access is in the SQL. [CUT] PostgreSQL: roles with LOGIN attribute. Host-based access lives in pg_hba.conf - a separate config file. You MUST configure pg_hba.conf for network access. [CUT] MySQL grants on mydb-dot-star become GRANT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA. And add ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES to cover future tables - otherwise new tables won't inherit permissions. This catches every team.

SCENE: MySQL multi-level charset diagram on left with utf8 warning. PG UTF-8 simplicity on right. NARRATION: Character sets. MySQL's biggest gotcha. [CUT] MySQL's utf8 is NOT real UTF-8. It's three bytes maximum. No emoji. No many CJK characters. You need utf8mb4 for real UTF-8. [CUT] And MySQL allows different charsets per column, per table, per database. A nightmare. PostgreSQL: encoding is set once at CREATE DATABASE. UTF-8. Always. No utf8 versus utf8mb4 confusion. [CUT] Before migration: SHOW CREATE TABLE on every MySQL table. If anything uses latin1 or MySQL utf8 - convert to utf8mb4 BEFORE migrating. Otherwise: encoding errors.

SCENE: Eight-row engine mapping table. MyISAM row highlighted with convert-first warning. NARRATION: Storage engines. [CUT] InnoDB - the default - maps directly to PostgreSQL's default. Both MVCC, both row-level locking, both foreign keys. [CUT] MyISAM - convert to InnoDB BEFORE migration. Run ALTER TABLE engine equals InnoDB on every MyISAM table. MyISAM has no transactions, no crash recovery. PostgreSQL has no equivalent. [CUT] MEMORY tables become UNLOGGED tables - fast but lost on crash. CSV engine becomes the file_fdw extension. FEDERATED becomes postgres_fdw - actually more powerful. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Run: SELECT table_name, engine FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'your_db' AND engine != 'InnoDB'. Convert every non-InnoDB table before you start. CHAPTER 5 · Migration Execution - 11:00-13:30 (slides 18-22)

SCENE: Seven horizontal step cards pulse as each phase is named. Persistent roadmap marker shown. NARRATION: Every migration follows seven phases. [CUT] Assess - audit your schema, stored programs, engine types, charsets. Convert - translate DDL, types, procedures, triggers, rewrite MySQL-specific SQL. Migrate - choose your tool, move schema and data. Validate - row counts, checksums, query comparison. Tune - postgresql.conf, PgBouncer, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, index review. Cutover - rehearsed, timed, rollback-ready. Operate - monitoring, backups, replication, autovacuum. [PAUSE] The roadmap marker at the top of every slide tells you which phase you're in. Use it to navigate.

sections.heading: Hero · MySQL → PostgreSQL Migration Guide
paragraphs: SCENE: Black screen. MySQL and PostgreSQL logos face off. Hero comparison card flies in. Five glowing stats appear across the bottom: 60-80%, 10x, 1000+, #1, $0. NARRATION: MySQL got you here. Simple. Fast. Everywhere. [PAUSE] But you've hit the ceiling. Window functions you can't trust. JSON that's slower than it should be. GROUP BY rules from 1995. No transactional DDL. And Oracle owns the roadmap. [CUT] Five numbers. Sixty to eighty percent of your queries port as-is. Ten times faster JSONB search. Over a thousand extensions. Number one most-admired database four years running. Zero Oracle license fees. [PAUSE] I'm Dr. Ibrar Ahmed. Today - the complete MySQL to PostgreSQL playbook. Forty slides. Every conversion. Every gotcha. Every fix. If you're a developer, DBA, or engineering lead - bookmark this video. You'll come back to it. ★ RETENTION HOOK: Stay for slide 36 - ten MySQL behaviors that silently break in PostgreSQL. Number four costs people entire weekends.

sections.heading: Why MySQL → PostgreSQL?
paragraphs: SCENE: Three-column card layout: SQL Standard, Advanced Features, Reliability. Critical orange callout at bottom: 60-80% queries port as-is. NARRATION: Three reasons you migrate. [CUT] One - SQL standard. Real window functions. Recursive CTEs. MERGE. RETURNING. LATERAL joins. GROUPING SETS, CUBE, ROLLUP. MySQL has none of these or partial support. [CUT] Two - power features. JSONB with GIN indexing - ten times faster than MySQL JSON. PostGIS - gold standard for geospatial. Built-in full-text search. Custom types. A thousand-plus extensions. [CUT] Three - reliability. True MVCC. Transactional DDL - yes, you can rollback a CREATE TABLE. Logical replication. Community-governed. No Oracle license surprises. [PAUSE] And the good news. MySQL to PostgreSQL is easier than Oracle to PostgreSQL. Both open-source. Both MVCC. Expect sixty to eighty percent of queries to port with minimal changes. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Run this on your MySQL right now: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.routines WHERE routine_schema = 'your_db'. That number is your conversion effort. CHAPTER 2 · Architecture & Data Types - 1:00-3:30 (slides 3-4)

sections.heading: Architecture: MySQL vs PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: Ten-row comparison table fills the screen. Storage Engine row highlights first. NARRATION: Architecture. The biggest shift first. [CUT] MySQL has pluggable storage engines - InnoDB, MyISAM, Memory. PostgreSQL has one unified engine. Everything is a heap table with MVCC. Simpler. [CUT] Database equals schema in MySQL - no namespaces. PostgreSQL: one database, multiple schemas, search_path resolves. [CUT] Connection model. MySQL uses threads - cheap, lightweight. PostgreSQL uses OS processes - heavier, you must pool. This is the number one operational surprise for MySQL DBAs. We cover PgBouncer on slide twenty-five. [CUT] Character sets. MySQL's utf8 is three bytes. Not real UTF-8. You need utf8mb4. PostgreSQL is always real four-byte UTF-8. No confusion. No mistakes.

sections.heading: Data Type Mapping: MySQL → PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: Twenty-row reference table. UNSIGNED warning callout highlights red at the bottom. NARRATION: Every MySQL type. Every PostgreSQL equivalent. Twenty rows. [CUT] TINYINT becomes smallint. TINYINT-one becomes boolean - pgLoader does this automatically. INT becomes integer. [PAUSE] Here's the trap. INT UNSIGNED has no PostgreSQL equivalent. Unsigned integers do not exist in PG. INT UNSIGNED must become bigint. BIGINT UNSIGNED must become numeric-twenty-zero. [CUT] DOUBLE becomes double precision. DECIMAL maps to numeric - exact match. VARCHAR maps to varchar. TEXT maps to text. MEDIUMTEXT and LONGTEXT - all become text. No size variants needed. [PAUSE] The critical one. DATETIME maps to timestamp. But MySQL TIMESTAMP - which auto-converts to UTC - must map to timestamptz, not timestamp. Get that wrong and your timezone data is silently corrupted. ENUM becomes a separate CREATE TYPE. SET becomes an array. JSON - always use jsonb. ★ RETENTION HOOK: The UNSIGNED trap catches every migration. Search your schema for UNSIGNED right now. Every one needs manual review. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Run: SELECT column_name, column_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE column_type LIKE '%unsigned%' AND table_schema = 'your_db'. Fix those first. CHAPTER 3 · SQL & Code Conversion - 3:30-8:00 (slides 5-10)

sections.heading: SQL Syntax: MySQL → PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: Side-by-side code blocks. MySQL left in orange. PostgreSQL right in cyan. VS badge in center. NARRATION: The query-level changes you'll make a hundred times. [CUT] Backtick quoting becomes double-quote - or just lowercase everything. LIMIT ten comma twenty - MySQL's offset syntax - becomes LIMIT twenty OFFSET ten. Standard SQL. [CUT] IFNULL becomes COALESCE. IF-condition becomes CASE WHEN. CONCAT works in both, but PostgreSQL also gives you the double-pipe operator - cleaner. [CUT] ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE becomes ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE - and you must name the conflict target. [CUT] GROUP BY with non-aggregated columns - MySQL allows it with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off. PostgreSQL always enforces the standard. Add every selected column to GROUP BY. [CUT] SHOW TABLES becomes backslash-dt in psql. DESCRIBE becomes backslash-d. Muscle memory. Takes a week.

sections.heading: AUTO INCREMENT → Sequences & Identity
paragraphs: SCENE: Three PostgreSQL options side-by-side: SERIAL, IDENTITY, RETURNING. NARRATION: AUTO_INCREMENT. Three PostgreSQL replacements. [CUT] SERIAL - the legacy way, creates a hidden sequence. GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY - the modern SQL-standard way. Recommended. [PAUSE] And the upgrade. RETURNING. In MySQL you call LAST_INSERT_ID after an INSERT. Race condition risk every time. In PostgreSQL: INSERT INTO orders VALUES something RETURNING id. Atomic. One statement. No race. [CUT] Use RETURNING on every INSERT and UPDATE. One of the best features you gain.

sections.heading: Stored Procedures & Functions
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL DELIMITER procedure on left. PostgreSQL dollar-quote function on right. NARRATION: Stored procedures. The DELIMITER hack goes away. [CUT] MySQL needs DELIMITER slash-slash because semicolons confuse the parser. PostgreSQL uses dollar-quoting - double-dollar-sign. No DELIMITER. No confusion. [CUT] OUT parameters become function RETURN values - much cleaner. SET-variable becomes colon-equals assignment. Session variables with at-sign do not exist - use return values or temp tables. [PAUSE] The body logic translates almost directly. IF, WHILE, FOR, CASE - all the same. The syntax wrapper is different. The logic inside is ninety percent identical.

sections.heading: Trigger Conversion
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL inline trigger on left. PostgreSQL two-step function-plus-trigger on right. NARRATION: Triggers split into two parts. [CUT] A trigger function that returns trigger. And a CREATE TRIGGER that attaches it. [CUT] The function MUST return NEW for BEFORE INSERT or UPDATE triggers. Return NULL and the operation silently cancels. That catches everyone. [CUT] One function - reusable across tables. PostgreSQL also gives you TRUNCATE triggers, multiple triggers per event, built-in variables like TG_TABLE_NAME and TG_OP. More powerful. But the two-step pattern is the mental model you must internalize.

sections.heading: String Function Mapping
paragraphs: SCENE: Ten-row function table with risk badges: green Easy, yellow Review, red Manual. NARRATION: String functions. Most map directly. [CUT] CONCAT, CONCAT_WS, REPLACE, LPAD, RPAD, SUBSTRING - identical. [PAUSE] The one that breaks everything: GROUP_CONCAT. It becomes string_agg with an explicit delimiter. GROUP_CONCAT-column becomes string_agg-column-comma. If you used ORDER BY inside GROUP_CONCAT, move it inside string_agg. [CUT] LOCATE becomes position. REGEXP becomes the tilde operator. HEX and UNHEX become encode and decode with bytea casting. [CUT] Search your codebase for GROUP_CONCAT first. It's in every MySQL application.

sections.heading: Date & Time Function Mapping
paragraphs: SCENE: Side-by-side code blocks. MySQL date functions left. PostgreSQL equivalents right. NARRATION: Dates. The format strings are completely different. [CUT] MySQL DATE_FORMAT uses percent-Y-percent-m-percent-d. PostgreSQL to_char uses YYYY-MM-DD. No percent signs. [CUT] DATEDIFF does not exist - subtract two dates, you get an integer of days. UNIX_TIMESTAMP becomes extract-epoch-from-now. DATE_ADD with INTERVAL becomes just plus-interval. Simpler, actually. [CUT] YEAR-of-column becomes extract-year. NOW and CURDATE work the same. Mechanical. Tedious. Straightforward. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Global find-and-replace: DATE_FORMAT → to_char, IFNULL → COALESCE, GROUP_CONCAT → string_agg. Those three cover fifty percent of function conversions. CHAPTER 4 · Advanced Features - 8:00-11:00 (slides 11-17)

sections.heading: JSON: MySQL vs PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: Side-by-side JSON code. MySQL generated-column workaround left. PostgreSQL GIN index right. NARRATION: JSON. This is where PostgreSQL dominates. [CUT] MySQL stores JSON as text. PostgreSQL has jsonb - binary storage. The containment operator at-greater-than with a GIN index searches all paths at once. [CUT] MySQL: create a generated column, index it, query the generated column. PostgreSQL: create one GIN index, query with at-greater-than or arrow operators. Orders of magnitude faster. [CUT] Plus jsonpath queries - the SQL-JSON standard. If you use JSON heavily, this alone justifies the migration.

sections.heading: Index Types & Conversion
paragraphs: SCENE: Eleven-row table. MySQL types on left. PG types including four PG-only entries highlighted cyan. NARRATION: Indexes. B-tree, UNIQUE, standard - all map directly. [CUT] FULLTEXT becomes GIN on tsvector - we cover that on slide thirty-four. SPATIAL becomes GiST with PostGIS. Prefix indexes - KEY column ten - become expression indexes with the left function. [PAUSE] Here's what you gain. GIN for arrays, JSONB, full-text - MySQL has nothing equivalent. BRIN for huge time-series tables - one thousandth the size of a B-tree. Partial indexes - index only rows WHERE active equals true. Covering indexes with INCLUDE - index-only scans without bloating the key. [CUT] After migration, review your indexes for these. Game-changers.

sections.heading: Views, Materialized Views & CTEs
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL view on left with no-materialized-view warning. PostgreSQL materialized view plus recursive CTE on right. NARRATION: Views convert directly - same syntax. [CUT] The upgrade: materialized views. MySQL doesn't have them. You'd build cache tables manually. PostgreSQL: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW, then REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY - no locks on readers. Use pg_cron to schedule refreshes. [CUT] Recursive CTEs - WITH RECURSIVE - let you traverse trees and graphs. Parent to child, any depth, one query. MySQL 8 added basic CTEs. PostgreSQL's are more mature and better optimized.

sections.heading: Table Partitioning Conversion
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL inline PARTITION BY on left. PostgreSQL declarative separate-partition on right. NARRATION: Partitioning syntax differs significantly. [CUT] MySQL defines partitions inline with the CREATE TABLE. PostgreSQL uses declarative syntax - create the parent, then create each partition separately with FOR VALUES. The primary key must include the partition key in both. [CUT] MySQL KEY partitioning has no equivalent - convert to HASH. MySQL PARTITION BY RANGE of YEAR-of-column uses an expression - PostgreSQL only allows column references for range partitioning. Partition directly on the timestamp column. [CUT] PostgreSQL gives you DETACH PARTITION for zero-downtime partition management. DEFAULT partitions catch overflow.

sections.heading: Users, Roles & Grants
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL user-at-host on left. PostgreSQL role-based with pg_hba.conf callout on right. NARRATION: The user model is fundamentally different. [CUT] MySQL: users are name-at-host. CREATE USER app at ten-dot-zero-dot-zero-dot-percent. Host-based access is in the SQL. [CUT] PostgreSQL: roles with LOGIN attribute. Host-based access lives in pg_hba.conf - a separate config file. You MUST configure pg_hba.conf for network access. [CUT] MySQL grants on mydb-dot-star become GRANT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA. And add ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES to cover future tables - otherwise new tables won't inherit permissions. This catches every team.

sections.heading: Character Sets & Collation
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL multi-level charset diagram on left with utf8 warning. PG UTF-8 simplicity on right. NARRATION: Character sets. MySQL's biggest gotcha. [CUT] MySQL's utf8 is NOT real UTF-8. It's three bytes maximum. No emoji. No many CJK characters. You need utf8mb4 for real UTF-8. [CUT] And MySQL allows different charsets per column, per table, per database. A nightmare. PostgreSQL: encoding is set once at CREATE DATABASE. UTF-8. Always. No utf8 versus utf8mb4 confusion. [CUT] Before migration: SHOW CREATE TABLE on every MySQL table. If anything uses latin1 or MySQL utf8 - convert to utf8mb4 BEFORE migrating. Otherwise: encoding errors.

sections.heading: MySQL Storage Engines → PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: Eight-row engine mapping table. MyISAM row highlighted with convert-first warning. NARRATION: Storage engines. [CUT] InnoDB - the default - maps directly to PostgreSQL's default. Both MVCC, both row-level locking, both foreign keys. [CUT] MyISAM - convert to InnoDB BEFORE migration. Run ALTER TABLE engine equals InnoDB on every MyISAM table. MyISAM has no transactions, no crash recovery. PostgreSQL has no equivalent. [CUT] MEMORY tables become UNLOGGED tables - fast but lost on crash. CSV engine becomes the file_fdw extension. FEDERATED becomes postgres_fdw - actually more powerful. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Run: SELECT table_name, engine FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'your_db' AND engine != 'InnoDB'. Convert every non-InnoDB table before you start. CHAPTER 5 · Migration Execution - 11:00-13:30 (slides 18-22)

sections.heading: Migration Roadmap: 7 Phases
paragraphs: SCENE: Seven horizontal step cards pulse as each phase is named. Persistent roadmap marker shown. NARRATION: Every migration follows seven phases. [CUT] Assess - audit your schema, stored programs, engine types, charsets. Convert - translate DDL, types, procedures, triggers, rewrite MySQL-specific SQL. Migrate - choose your tool, move schema and data. Validate - row counts, checksums, query comparison. Tune - postgresql.conf, PgBouncer, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, index review. Cutover - rehearsed, timed, rollback-ready. Operate - monitoring, backups, replication, autovacuum. [PAUSE] The roadmap marker at the top of every slide tells you which phase you're in. Use it to navigate.

sections.heading: pgLoader: One Command Migration
paragraphs: SCENE: Terminal showing pgLoader one-liner. Full config file with CAST rules and EXCLUDING below. NARRATION: pgLoader. The fastest MySQL to PostgreSQL tool. [CUT] One command: pgloader mysql-colon-slash-slash-source postgresql-colon-slash-slash-target. Done. Schema and data in one shot. [CUT] For production, write a dot-load config file. CAST rules override type mapping - tinyint to boolean, int with auto_increment to serial. EXCLUDING filters out temp tables. Workers and concurrency control parallelism. [PAUSE] pgLoader handles eighty percent automatically - TINYINT-one to boolean, ENUM creation, index recreation, sequence reset. [CUT] What it does NOT handle: stored procedures, triggers, views logic. Those are manual. Use pgLoader for data. Manual conversion for code.

sections.heading: AWS DMS & Other Migration Tools
paragraphs: SCENE: Three-column tool comparison: AWS DMS, pgLoader, manual mysqldump. Decision matrix at bottom. NARRATION: Three tools. Three use cases. [CUT] pgLoader - best for databases under five hundred gigabytes when you can tolerate brief downtime. One-shot, simple, fast. [CUT] AWS DMS - best for databases over five hundred gigabytes or when you need zero-downtime cutover. Full load plus change data capture. Streams binlog changes in real time. Pair with AWS Schema Conversion Tool for DDL. [CUT] Manual mysqldump plus psql - only for small databases under ten gigabytes. Maximum control. Maximum effort. [PAUSE] Decision matrix. Under ten gigs simple schema - pgLoader one-liner. Ten to five hundred gigs - pgLoader with config file. Over five hundred gigs or zero-downtime - AWS DMS.

sections.heading: DDL Conversion Checklist
paragraphs: SCENE: Fifteen-row DDL pattern table with risk badges. Red rows for ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and SET type. NARRATION: Fifteen DDL patterns to convert. [CUT] ENGINE equals InnoDB - remove. DEFAULT CHARSET - remove, it's database-level. AUTO_INCREMENT - GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY. INT UNSIGNED - bigint. TINYINT-one - boolean. DATETIME - timestamp. TIMESTAMP - timestamptz. [CUT] ENUM - two-step: CREATE TYPE then use it. SET - text array. ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - trigger function, covered next slide. COMMENT on column - separate DDL. ZEROFILL - to_char or lpad at display. [CUT] INSERT IGNORE - ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. REPLACE INTO - ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. [PAUSE] Print this slide.

sections.heading: ON UPDATE CURRENT TIMESTAMP Pattern
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL built-in on left. PostgreSQL three-step trigger pattern on right. NARRATION: The number one MySQL feature people miss. ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. [CUT] MySQL: add it to a column and the timestamp auto-updates on every UPDATE. Built-in. No code. [CUT] PostgreSQL doesn't have it. You need a trigger function. [PAUSE] Create set_updated_at - one function that sets NEW.updated_at to now and returns NEW. Create it once. Then attach it to every table that needs auto-update timestamps with CREATE TRIGGER BEFORE UPDATE EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at. [CUT] Search your MySQL dump for ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Every table that has it needs this trigger. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Create the set_updated_at function right now. You'll attach it to dozens of tables. CHAPTER 6 · Validation & Tuning - 13:30-16:00 (slides 23-27)

sections.heading: Post Migration Validation
paragraphs: SCENE: Row count SQL on left. Ten-point validation checklist on right with checkmarks. NARRATION: Validation is non-negotiable. Ten checks. [CUT] One - row counts match for every table. Not estimated. Exact SELECT COUNT star. Two - NULL counts match. Three - MIN, MAX, SUM on numeric columns match. Four - foreign keys valid, no orphans. Five - sequences reset to max-id-plus-one. Six - indexes exist and are valid. Seven - constraints enabled and enforced. Eight - application queries produce identical results. Nine - edge cases: empty strings versus NULLs, date boundaries. Ten - performance: key queries within SLA using EXPLAIN ANALYZE. [PAUSE] Run ANALYZE first. Without it, the planner has no statistics and plans will be terrible.

sections.heading: Essential postgresql.conf Settings
paragraphs: SCENE: Ten-row MySQL-to-PG parameter mapping table. work_mem warning callout at bottom. NARRATION: Map your MySQL tuning knowledge. [CUT] innodb_buffer_pool_size becomes shared_buffers - set to twenty-five percent of RAM. Not more than forty. innodb_log_file_size becomes max_wal_size - two to four gigabytes. [PAUSE] sort_buffer_size becomes work_mem - but careful. work_mem is per-operation, not per-connection. A query with five sorts uses five times work_mem. With a hundred connections, that adds up fast. Start at sixty-four megabytes. [CUT] query_cache_size - PostgreSQL has no query cache. Use Redis or the application layer. [CUT] The two MySQL doesn't have: effective_cache_size - set to seventy-five percent of RAM, tells the planner what to expect from OS cache. random_page_cost - set to one-point-one for SSD. Default four-point-zero is for spinning disks. Huge impact on query plans.

sections.heading: PgBouncer: Required for Production
paragraphs: SCENE: Connection overhead comparison: MySQL 256KB vs PG 5-10MB. PgBouncer config on right. NARRATION: The operational change that catches every MySQL DBA. [CUT] MySQL - one thread per connection. Two hundred fifty-six kilobytes overhead. PostgreSQL - one OS process per connection. Five to ten megabytes overhead. [PAUSE] One thousand MySQL connections: two hundred fifty megabytes. One thousand PostgreSQL connections: ten gigabytes. [CUT] You will run PgBouncer. Transaction mode. Twenty-five server connections for two thousand app connections. [PAUSE] Install it day one. Not day two. Not after the first out-of-memory error. Day one.

sections.heading: EXPLAIN ANALYZE: MySQL vs PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL tabular EXPLAIN on left. PostgreSQL tree EXPLAIN with buffers on right. NARRATION: Query analysis. [CUT] MySQL EXPLAIN gives you a flat table - type, rows, extra. Limited. [CUT] PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS gives you the actual execution tree. Every node's actual time versus estimated rows. Buffer cache hits versus disk reads. Planning time versus execution time. [PAUSE] Paste the output into explain.dalibo.com for a visual tree. [CUT] Always use ANALYZE and BUFFERS together. EXPLAIN without ANALYZE is estimated only. With BUFFERS, you see if the query is hitting cache or going to disk. That's the difference between finding the problem in two minutes and guessing for two hours.

sections.heading: Autovacuum: PG's Critical Background Worker
paragraphs: SCENE: Dead tuple explanation on left. Autovacuum config with per-table override on right. NARRATION: Autovacuum. No MySQL equivalent. [CUT] MySQL's InnoDB purge thread runs silently. PostgreSQL's autovacuum does the same job - cleans dead tuples left by MVCC - but it must be monitored and tuned. [CUT] Default scale_factor is zero-point-two. Twenty percent dead rows before vacuum kicks in. Too lazy for hot tables. Set it to zero-point-zero-five. Five percent. [CUT] For your busiest tables, use per-table overrides: ALTER TABLE orders SET autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor equals zero-point-zero-one. [CUT] Monitor n_dead_tup in pg_stat_user_tables. If it grows, autovacuum is falling behind. [PAUSE] And never - never - disable autovacuum. Transaction ID wraparound will make your database read-only. ★ RETENTION HOOK: Autovacuum misconfiguration is the number one cause of PostgreSQL performance degradation after migration from MySQL. Set it up correctly on day one. CHAPTER 7 · Cutover & Operations - 16:00-18:00 (slides 28-37)

sections.heading: Cutover Plan: Zero Downtime
paragraphs: SCENE: Six step cards in a timeline: Rehearse → Full Load → Freeze → Verify → Switch → Rollback. NARRATION: Cutover. [CUT] T-minus two weeks: rehearse on staging. Time every step. [CUT] T-minus one day: full pgLoader load. If using DMS, start CDC replication. [CUT] T-zero minute zero: stop application writes to MySQL. Wait for CDC lag to hit zero. [CUT] T-zero minute five: verify checksums on critical tables. Run smoke test queries. [CUT] T-zero minute fifteen: update connection strings. DNS switch. Health check. Monitor error rates. [CUT] T-zero minute thirty: if errors exceed threshold, revert DNS to MySQL. MySQL was frozen - data is consistent. [PAUSE] Keep MySQL alive for forty-eight hours after cutover. The rollback drill is not optional. Practice it.

sections.heading: Backup & Recovery
paragraphs: SCENE: Seven-row tool mapping table. Minimum backup strategy callout at bottom. NARRATION: Backup. [CUT] mysqldump becomes pg_dump. Percona XtraBackup becomes pg_basebackup - built into PostgreSQL core. [CUT] For production, use pgBackRest - incremental, parallel, S3 support, point-in-time recovery. Enable WAL archiving for continuous backup. [PAUSE] Minimum strategy: daily pg_basebackup. Continuous WAL archiving to S3. pgBackRest for automation. Monthly restore drills. [PAUSE] A backup you have not restored is not a backup.

sections.heading: Replication: MySQL vs PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: Eight-row feature comparison table. Logical replication row highlighted as PG advantage. NARRATION: Replication. [CUT] MySQL binlog replication maps to PostgreSQL WAL streaming. Functionally equivalent. Semi-synchronous maps to synchronous_commit. [PAUSE] The upgrade: logical replication. Built-in PUBLICATION and SUBSCRIPTION. Subscribe to specific tables. Filter rows. Replicate across major versions. [CUT] This enables zero-downtime major version upgrades - something MySQL makes much harder. [CUT] For failover: Patroni plus etcd is the industry standard. Automatic leader election. Automatic promotion.

sections.heading: Monitoring: MySQL → PostgreSQL
paragraphs: SCENE: Nine-row monitoring mapping table. pg_stat_statements row highlighted as must-enable. NARRATION: Monitoring. [CUT] SHOW PROCESSLIST becomes pg_stat_activity. More detail. [CUT] Performance Schema becomes pg_stat_statements - the number one tuning extension. Enable it immediately. Add it to shared_preload_libraries and restart. [CUT] slow_query_log becomes log_min_duration_statement - set to two hundred milliseconds. [CUT] SHOW TABLE STATUS becomes pg_stat_user_tables - dead tuples, last autovacuum, sequential scans versus index scans. [CUT] InnoDB buffer pool hit ratio becomes a simple calculation from pg_stat_bgwriter. Target ninety-nine percent cache hit ratio. ▸ DO THIS NEXT: Add pg_stat_statements to shared_preload_libraries right now. Restart. CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements. You cannot tune what you cannot measure.

sections.heading: Common Post Migration Errors & Fixes
paragraphs: SCENE: Twelve-row error table. Each row: red error message, cause, green fix. NARRATION: The exact errors your application throws on day one. [CUT] Column capital-N-Name does not exist - PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase. Use double quotes or rename. [CUT] Operator does not exist int equals varchar - MySQL auto-casts, PostgreSQL doesn't. Add explicit casts. [CUT] Column not in GROUP BY - add every non-aggregated column. [CUT] LIMIT ten comma twenty syntax error - LIMIT twenty OFFSET ten. [CUT] Function IFNULL does not exist - COALESCE. Function GROUP_CONCAT does not exist - string_agg. [CUT] Duplicate key violates unique constraint - sequence out of sync. Fix with setval. [PAUSE] Pin this slide. You'll hit at least eight of these.

sections.heading: Application Code & ORM Changes
paragraphs: SCENE: Connection string before/after. Django, Rails, Laravel config snippets. NARRATION: Connection strings. [CUT] MySQL colon three-three-zero-six becomes PostgreSQL colon five-four-three-two. [CUT] Python: mysqlclient becomes psycopg2. Node: mysql2 becomes pg. Java: jdbc-mysql becomes jdbc-postgresql. [CUT] ORMs. Django - change ENGINE to django.db.backends.postgresql. Rails - adapter postgresql. Laravel - DB_CONNECTION equals pgsql. [PAUSE] Most ORMs abstract the SQL differences. But raw SQL queries need manual review. Test boolean handling - MySQL zero-slash-one becomes PostgreSQL true-slash-false.

sections.heading: Full Text Search Conversion
paragraphs: SCENE: MySQL FULLTEXT on left. PostgreSQL tsvector with weights and ranking on right. NARRATION: Full-text search. [CUT] MySQL FULLTEXT index with MATCH AGAINST becomes PostgreSQL tsvector with the double-at operator. [CUT] Add a tsvector column with setweight for title-versus-body weighting. Create a GIN index. Search with to_tsquery. Rank with ts_rank. Highlight results with ts_headline. Language-aware stemming. [PAUSE] PostgreSQL full-text is production-grade. Many teams remove Elasticsearch after migration. Built-in search is good enough.

sections.heading: Must Install PostgreSQL Extensions
paragraphs: SCENE: Three-column grid: Performance, Security, Data. Four extensions each. NARRATION: Extensions. Install these on every production server. [CUT] Performance: pg_stat_statements - query stats, non-negotiable. auto_explain - automatic EXPLAIN for slow queries. pg_buffercache - inspect shared buffers. pg_prewarm - preload indexes after restart. [CUT] Security: pgAudit - detailed audit logging. pgcrypto - encryption and gen_random_uuid. pg_trgm - trigram similarity, fuzzy matching. [CUT] Data: pg_cron - replaces MySQL EVENT SCHEDULER. sections.heading: MySQL Specific Gotchas to Watch
paragraphs: SCENE: Ten-row gotcha table with risk badges. First three rows highlighted red as highest impact. NARRATION: Ten silent killers. [CUT] One - zero-zero-zero-zero dates. MySQL allows them. PostgreSQL throws an error. Clean before migration. [CUT] Two - empty strings in NOT NULL columns. MySQL uses empty string where NULL was intended. Review your app logic. [CUT] Three - silent truncation. MySQL silently cuts VARCHAR overflow. PostgreSQL throws an error. Check max lengths. [CUT] Four - case sensitivity. MySQL is case-insensitive by default. PostgreSQL is case-sensitive. Use CITEXT extension or LOWER in queries. [CUT] Five - backslash escaping. MySQL interprets backslash-n as newline. PostgreSQL treats backslash as literal. Use E-prefix for escape sequences. [PAUSE] Six through ten - boolean zero-slash-one versus true-slash-false, transactional DDL differences, implicit COMMIT behavior, NO_ZERO_DATE mode. [PAUSE] The first four cause eighty percent of post-migration bugs. ★ RETENTION HOOK: Items one through four - zero dates, empty strings, truncation, case sensitivity - together explain eighty percent of post-migration application failures. Test for each one explicitly.

sections.heading: Performance Comparison & Expectations
paragraphs: SCENE: Two-column layout: PG Faster (green) and Needs Tuning (red). NARRATION: What to expect. [CUT] PostgreSQL is faster at: complex queries - the optimizer is superior. JSONB operations - GIN-indexed containment is ten to a hundred times faster. Full-text search with ranking. Concurrent mixed workloads. Large aggregations with parallel query. Geospatial with PostGIS. [CUT] Where it may need tuning: simple point lookups at extreme scale - InnoDB clustered index can be marginally faster. Connection handling - PgBouncer is mandatory. Bulk inserts - use the COPY command, five to ten times faster than INSERT. Table bloat - configure autovacuum properly. [PAUSE] Bottom line: eighty percent of workloads match or beat MySQL out of the box. The remaining twenty percent needs PgBouncer, COPY, and autovacuum tuning. [CUT] Conversion: remove ENGINE and CHARSET, add IDENTITY columns, convert ENUM and SET types, rewrite procedures in PL/pgSQL, add set_updated_at triggers. entries.title: pg perf e04 connection pooling
titles: pg perf e04 connection pooling
titleKeys: pg perf e04 connection pooling
paragraphs: So, you know how this goes... you look at your database one day, and there are, what, five hundred connections open. And the strange thing is, if you actually go and check, most of them aren't really doing anything at all. They're just sort of... sitting there, idle. And the natural reaction, the one everybody has, is to think, well, we probably just need more connections. But honestly, that's kind of the opposite of what you need. What you're really looking for here is a pool. So, let me walk you through it.

Let's start by just... looking at what's actually happening, before we change anything. So I run a little count on pg_stat_activity, grouped by state, and, yeah, you can pretty much see the whole story right there. About four hundred and seventy of them are idle. Only twenty-eight or so are actually doing any work. Five hundred in total. So almost all of it, really, is just sitting there idle.

Now, this is the part that's really easy to forget. Every single one of those connections, even the idle ones, is a real process running on the machine. It's not a lightweight little socket, it's a whole process. So if I count them up, five hundred, and then sort of... add up the memory they're each holding, it comes to almost five gigabytes. And that's before a single query has even run. And then on top of that, you've got five hundred processes all sharing sixteen cores, so the scheduler ends up just... thrashing, really, trying to keep everyone moving.

And, I mean, this is what it actually feels like when it goes wrong. It's, uh... it's usually the middle of the night, the app's just scaled up, and you're sitting there tailing the log, and you start seeing it. Too many clients already. Out of memory. Maybe some client that opened a transaction and then just... wandered off, still holding a lock. And you check pg_stat_activity, and there's five hundred connections, and again, most of them aren't doing anything. So that... that's the moment the pager goes off.

So the obvious thing to try, and honestly I think we've all done this at least once, is you just raise max_connections. Push it up to a thousand, restart, and for a second it feels like you've fixed it. But what actually happens is... now you've got twice as many processes on the same memory, and it falls over even sooner. You start getting out-of-memory errors. So you haven't really added any capacity, you've just, sort of, given yourself twice as many processes to look after.

The real fix here is a pooler. So something like PgBouncer just sits quietly in front of Postgres. All of your clients, all five hundred of them, connect to the pooler instead, and it keeps a small handful of real connections open to the database, and it just... hands them around as people need them. So you've got five hundred coming in the front, and maybe thirty-two going out the back. Same amount of work, much, much smaller footprint.

And the setting that really controls all of this is default_pool_size. So even when you've got five hundred clients all hitting it at once, Postgres, in this example anyway, only ever sees about thirty-two backends. Which is, what, roughly six percent. The clients just quietly share those connections between them, and if anyone has to wait, it's usually only a millisecond or two, but Postgres itself just stays nice and calm through all of it.

The config, honestly, is smaller than most people expect. You point the databases section at your actual Postgres, and then there are really just a few settings that matter. pool_mode, set to transaction, that's the important one. max_client_conn, set fairly high. And default_pool_size... I'd start somewhere around two to four times your core count, and then actually measure it, rather than just picking a number and hoping it's right.

And then you run it, and, this is the step people always seem to skip, you actually prove it worked. So you restart pgbouncer, you point the app at the pooler's port instead of the database's, and then you just... ask it. SHOW POOLS. And there it is, right in front of you. Five hundred clients connected, only twenty-eight on the server side, and nothing sitting in the queue. So, yeah, that's it quietly doing its job.

Just a quick word on the modes, because this is the bit that tends to catch people out. Session mode holds onto a connection for the client's whole session, so, honestly, it barely pools at all. Transaction mode, that's really the sweet spot for a web app, it borrows a connection just for the length of a transaction and then gives it straight back. And then statement mode is more aggressive again, but it's a bit niche. So for a normal web app, you'll almost always want transaction.

So any time you want to actually see what's going on under the hood, you just ask the pooler directly. SHOW POOLS. And you look at cl_active, which is your connected clients, five hundred of them. But then sv_active, the real backends, that's only twenty-eight. And cl_waiting is zero, which is really the reassuring part, it means nobody's stuck waiting in a queue. So that... that's what a healthy pool actually looks like.

And, really, that's the whole payoff. Same five hundred clients, exactly the same load. Before, we had five hundred backends, around five gigs of memory just sitting there idle, and those too-many-clients errors popping up. And after... thirty-two backends, the memory's back, the errors are gone. Same machine, the whole time. You've just, sort of, stopped wasting it.

There is one catch, though, and it's genuinely worth knowing going in. In transaction mode, each statement can end up on a different backend connection. So any session-level state, a SET, a session-scoped prepared statement, an advisory lock, it's just... not something you can rely on from one statement to the next. So the way around it is either to keep that state inside a single transaction, or, for those particular paths, put them on session mode instead.

So, the usual traps, just briefly. Raising max_connections instead of putting a pooler in, that's the big one to avoid. Using session mode for a web app, when transaction is really what you want. Sizing the pool way too big, sort of 'just to be safe,' instead of sizing it and then measuring. And then forgetting that your application pool, multiplied by the number of instances, can quietly add up to more than the server pool. So it's really worth counting that one end to end.

And when something does feel off, the trick is really just... don't guess, ask the pooler. So, SHOW POOLS, and if cl_waiting is slowly creeping up, that's telling you the pool's too small. SHOW CLIENTS and SHOW SERVERS will show you who's actually stuck. And if you're seeing prepared-statement errors, well, the older versions of PgBouncer just don't hold onto them, though the newer ones can, with a setting. But most of what you need is right there in the admin console.

So if we put the whole thing together, start to finish... you count your idle connections first, just to see the problem for yourself. You put PgBouncer in front, in transaction mode. You size the pool to your cores. You point the application at the pooler. And then, finally, you verify, and cl_waiting should just be sitting there at zero. And that, really, is the whole fix.

So... five hundred clients, thirty-two backends. That, in a nutshell, is connection pooling. No new hardware, nothing dramatic, you've just, sort of, let the database breathe again. If you found this one useful, it would genuinely help if you subscribed, the next one's on autovacuum and bloat, and, honestly, it's a good one. So, I'll see you in that one.

sections.heading: Hook (on camera)
paragraphs: This table takes up ten gigabytes on disk, but the real data inside is onlyabout two gigabytes . // That means roughly eighty percent of it is dead rows. /The answer is not a bigger disk. / The answer is autovacuum that keeps up. //Let me show you how this happens, and how to fix it.

sections.heading: The Scenario
paragraphs: Let's start by looking at the tables. / This query lists each table with itslive rows and its dead rows. // The orders table stands out. / It has about twomillion live rows and about eight million dead ones. // These numbers areestimates, but the pattern is clear. / Most of this table is dead space.

sections.heading: Why It Hurts
paragraphs: This happens because Postgres never changes a row in place . // Every update ordelete keeps the old version and marks it as dead. / So the table grows to tengigabytes, even though only about two gigabytes is live data. // The problem isthat a sequential scan still reads the whole ten gigabytes , including all ofthe dead rows.

sections.heading: Why Bloat Happens (MVCC)
paragraphs: Here is the idea in one picture. // You insert a row, and that is the firstversion. / When you update it, Postgres does not touch the old version. / Itwrites a new one and marks the old one dead. / Update it again, and you get athird version. // So one row, updated twice, now has three versions on disk, andtwo of them are dead. / This is how a table slowly bloats.

sections.heading: Dead vs Live
paragraphs: This is what the file looks like inside. // The red blocks are dead rows , andthe green blocks are the live data . / About eighty percent of it is dead. // Asequential scan reads every block, dead or alive. / If you want the exactfigure, the pgstattuple extension will measure it for you.

sections.heading: Pain Points
paragraphs: In production, this usually shows up as several problems at once. // You may seea transaction ID wraparound warning in the logs. / The disk fills up. / A querythat used to take forty milliseconds now takes nine hundred . / And autovacuumruns for over an hour without catching up. // All of these point to the samecause. / Autovacuum is falling behind, or something is blocking it.

sections.heading: The Wrong Fix
paragraphs: The common mistake is to run VACUUM FULL to shrink the table. // Avoid this on alive table during the day. / VACUUM FULL takes an exclusive lock and rewritesthe entire table. / While it runs, every query has to wait, even a simple read,and the application starts timing out. // It does reclaim the space, but itblocks everyone while it works.

sections.heading: The Real Lever
paragraphs: The better tool is already built in. / It is autovacuum . // It removes deadrows in the background without an exclusive lock , so normal reads and writeskeep working. / It returns that space to the table so new rows can reuse it. //There is no rewrite, and no downtime.

sections.heading: Why It Fell Behind
paragraphs: So why did autovacuum fall behind? // By default, it only starts once abouttwenty percent of the table is dead. / For the orders table, that is fifty rowsplus twenty percent of two million, which is about four hundred thousand deadrows before it even begins. // Newer versions add a cap, but the pattern is thesame. / The larger the table, the longer it waits.

sections.heading: The 20% Trigger
paragraphs: Here are the two cases side by side. // A small table reaches its twenty percentmark quickly, so autovacuum runs early and stays ahead. // A large table likeorders reaches that mark much later, so it tolerates hundreds of thousands ofdead rows first. / On large, busy tables the default is too slow, so we lower itper table .

sections.heading: Tune The Table
paragraphs: You change this on the single table, not the whole server. // With ALTER TABLE,you lower the scale factor to about two percent , so autovacuum starts muchsooner. / You also raise the cost limit, so it can do more work before itpauses. // These are reasonable starting values. / Test them against your ownworkload.

sections.heading: Run & Verify
paragraphs: To clear the backlog you already have, run vacuum once by hand. // VACUUMVERBOSE shows you what it did. / It removes about eight million dead rows, andnormal traffic keeps running the whole time. // When you check the table again,the dead row count is back near zero .

sections.heading: What Autovacuum Does
paragraphs: Here is what autovacuum actually does. // A launcher starts several workerprocesses, three by default . / They mainly do two things. / Vacuum removes deadrows, and analyze keeps the planner statistics up to date. // During a vacuum,it also freezes very old rows, to prevent transaction ID wraparound. / Yourarely run any of this yourself.

sections.heading: Monitor It
paragraphs: You can watch all of this with one query on the same view. // Three columnsmatter most. / The number of dead rows right now, / when autovacuum last ran, /and how many times it has run. // If the dead count is high and the last run wasa while ago, autovacuum is behind, and it is time to tune.

sections.heading: The Win
paragraphs: Let's be clear about the result. // After tuning and vacuuming, the dead rowsdrop to near zero, and the table stops bloating. / That is the main win. // Butthe file usually stays around ten gigabytes . / Vacuum makes that spacereusable, but it does not return it to the disk. // If you need the space back,use pg_repack , which rewrites the table down to about two gigabytes while itstays online. / For most tables, keeping autovacuum ahead is enough.

sections.heading: Reuse, Not Shrink
paragraphs: This is the point people often miss. // A plain vacuum frees space inside thefile so new rows can reuse it, but the file itself does not get smaller . // Toactually shrink it and return space to the operating system, you need pg_repack, which does this while the table is online. // Also remember that a singlelong-running transaction can block cleanup, because vacuum cannot remove rowsnewer than the oldest open transaction.

sections.heading: The Gotcha
paragraphs: Two things to keep in mind. // First, after a vacuum the file usually staysaround ten gigabytes, so track your disk usage separately. // Second, watch fora session that has been idle in a transaction for a long time. / That onetransaction holds back cleanup for the whole database, because vacuum cannotremove anything newer than it. / Check for it before blaming autovacuum.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
paragraphs: Here are four common mistakes. // Turning autovacuum off to save resources,which always makes things worse. / Running VACUUM FULL during business hours. /Leaving the default settings on a very large table, so autovacuum never fires intime. / And ignoring a long idle transaction that blocks cleanup. // Autovacuumis not the problem. / The defaults simply are not tuned for a large, busy table.

sections.heading: Known Issues & Debug
paragraphs: When dead rows will not clear, check two things. // First, sort your sessions bystart time and find the oldest transaction, which is usually the cause. //Second, use pg_stat_progress_vacuum to see what a running vacuum is doing rightnow. / Once you clear the old transaction, vacuum can finish its work.

sections.heading: Checklist
paragraphs: Here is the full process. // Measure your dead rows. / Lower the scale factor onthe busy tables, and raise the cost limit. / Clear any long-runningtransactions. / Run one manual vacuum to catch up. / Then confirm the dead rowcount is near zero. // And only if you need the disk space back, use pg_repack.

sections.heading: Subscribe (on camera)
paragraphs: That is autovacuum and bloat. // Keep the dead rows under control, tune yourbusy tables, and use pg_repack only when you need the disk space back. // Ifthis was helpful, please subscribe . / The next episode is about missing indexes. / Thanks for watching.
