entries.title: Information and Entropy: Why Compressing Language Is Predicting It
titles: Information and Entropy: Why Compressing Language Is Predicting It
titleKeys: information and entropy why compressing language is predicting it
paragraphs: When you turn text into ones and zeros, you usually want that stream as short as it can honestly be. A simple byte-based encoding spends eight bits on each ordinary English character, whether it shows up all the time or almost never. So the natural question is, is there some kind of hard floor on how efficiently text can be compressed?

If you are a little clever, you spend fewer bits on the letters that show up often, and more on the rare ones. E gets a short code. Q gets a longer one. That alone can get you down to roughly four bits per character on average. Not magic. Just matching code length to how often each symbol actually appears.

And once you start looking at patterns across longer stretches of text, not just single characters, you can do better still. Words, phrases, the habit English has of making the next letter almost obvious. That is the whole game modern compressors play. But again, what is the limit? Not a tip for shaving another tenth of a bit. The actual floor.

This question goes back at least to the nineteen forties, to Claude Shannon's paper that kicked off information theory. A Mathematical Theory of Communication. The core result we are walking toward is the noiseless coding theorem, and the definitions of information and entropy hiding inside it. The good definitions usually show up after the insight, not before it.

What is strange is how useful that old math turned out to be for modern machine learning. When large language models are pretrained, the usual description is next-token prediction, scored with something called cross-entropy loss. That name comes straight out of information theory. We are not deriving it yet. Just naming the bridge for now.

Prediction and compression are connected more deeply than they first appear. You predict probabilities, those set code lengths, and a coder shortens the message. Some people say compression is intelligence. Hard to judge, because intelligence is a squishy word. The safer claim is that the math of compression is strangely relevant to artificial intelligence. Next, you and I rediscover information and entropy by asking about the limits of compressing language.

Language is complicated, so we warm up on something smaller with the same essential ideas. Imagine a robot on a faraway moon. From Earth we send it only four moves: up, down, left, or right. They are not equally likely. Half of everything we send is up, a quarter is down, and left and right each get one eighth. And we will pretend every instruction is independent of the last. The bits are slow and costly. So what is the most efficient way to encode that stream?

The straightforward student says, four options, so two bits each. Maybe zero zero for up, zero one for down, one zero for left, one one for right. On the receiving end that is trivial. Chop the bitstream into pairs and translate. Always two bits per instruction, no matter which move you sent. Simple, and a little wasteful.

The clever student points out that ignores how often up shows up. They propose uneven lengths. A single zero for up, one zero for down, one one zero for left, and one one one for right. Half the time you spend one bit, a quarter of the time two bits, and the rest three. Weighted together that is one point seven five bits per instruction, which beats a flat two.

But how does the robot know where one instruction ends? The rule is simple once you see it. Read bits until what you have is a complete codeword, then stop and start fresh. That only works if no codeword is a prefix of another. If you tried to add a fifth move with the code one zero zero, then after reading one zero you would not know whether that was already Down, or the start of the new instruction. That kind of encoding is called a prefix code.

There is a clean way to picture every possible binary string. Each layer is every string of a given length. Everything that starts with zero lives on the left half. Everything that starts with one lives on the right. And that idea repeats as you go down. Critically, every string is a prefix of everything sitting below it. So a codeword claims the whole descendant region beneath it.

Watch what happens with the clever student's code. Giving up the single bit zero to Up eats half of all possible codewords. Down's one zero eats another quarter. Left and right each take an eighth. Nothing is left over. And those fractions are exactly the probabilities of the instructions. That alignment, between data size and probability, is the founding insight of information theory.

It feels like this scheme might be perfect. But how would you know there is not some ultra-clever method that works on long sequences of instructions and pushes the average even lower? That is the third student's job. They are not building a code yet. They are asking what properties a perfect code would have to have.

Their idea is that random noise should be incompressible, so idealized perfect compression should emit a bitstream that behaves like random bits. Each bit a fair coin flip, independent of the others. And interestingly, the clever student's encoding already does that. Half the time the message starts with Up, so the first bit is zero half the time. Otherwise it is a one, and the next bit is another fair flip.

Why is noise incompressible? Zoom out to whole messages. If a compressed string of n bits really looks like noise, then all two to the n strings of that length are equally likely, which means the underlying messages were equally likely at one over two to the n. Try to shorten one of them and it eats a neighbour's space on the diagram. Those neighbours get bumped up a layer. Save one bit here and you pay two bits somewhere else. You are pushing a bump in a rug.

In this clean dyadic case, a message assigned n bits has probability one over two to the n. Take log base two of both sides and flip the sign, and you get that the bits allocated equal negative log base two of p. That negative log expression is the fundamental formula of information theory. Not an arbitrary definition we start with at all. Something you get dragged to by asking about perfect compression.

Shannon defined that value to be the information of an event. Unlikely messages carry a lot of it. Nearly certain ones carry almost none. Picture a probability as a thin slice of pie, and the information as a bar that grows taller as that slice gets squeezed toward zero. You can also write it as the log of one over p. Same quantity. Intuitively it is asking how many times you have to chop the space of possibilities in half to isolate what happened.

Nobody is encoding the letter i with a codeword that is somehow four point one nine bits long. Average these information values, and you get the compression floor. That is a claim about averages over all possible messages, not a fractional codeword on one letter. Fractional bits live at that abstract layer. Real encodings still land on whole numbers of bits.

The robot had clean powers of two. Language does not. The probability of each new letter depends heavily on everything that came before it, and those probabilities are messy fractions. If you plot negative log base two for each one, you get fractional information values. Low for predictable letters, high for surprises. And I should say, the numbers on screen here are illustrative model probabilities, not the true distribution of English.

The probability of a whole phrase is the product of each successive letter's conditional probability. That is the chain rule. And because logs turn multiplication into addition, the information of the full message breaks into a sum of the information of each letter given its context. That is why it still makes sense to talk about fractional bits adding up to a length.

sections.heading: The problem
paragraphs: When you turn text into ones and zeros, you usually want that stream as short as it can honestly be. A simple byte-based encoding spends eight bits on each ordinary English character, whether it shows up all the time or almost never. So the natural question is, is there some kind of hard floor on how efficiently text can be compressed?

If you are a little clever, you spend fewer bits on the letters that show up often, and more on the rare ones. E gets a short code. Q gets a longer one. That alone can get you down to roughly four bits per character on average. Not magic. Just matching code length to how often each symbol actually appears.

And once you start looking at patterns across longer stretches of text, not just single characters, you can do better still. Words, phrases, the habit English has of making the next letter almost obvious. That is the whole game modern compressors play. But again, what is the limit? Not a tip for shaving another tenth of a bit. The actual floor.

This question goes back at least to the nineteen forties, to Claude Shannon's paper that kicked off information theory. A Mathematical Theory of Communication. The core result we are walking toward is the noiseless coding theorem, and the definitions of information and entropy hiding inside it. The good definitions usually show up after the insight, not before it.

What is strange is how useful that old math turned out to be for modern machine learning. When large language models are pretrained, the usual description is next-token prediction, scored with something called cross-entropy loss. That name comes straight out of information theory. We are not deriving it yet. Just naming the bridge for now.

sections.heading: entropy
paragraphs: Some of his early experiments scanned books for short strings, n-grams, and counted what tended to follow. After t h, how often is the next letter e? That works for short contexts. It falls apart for longer ones, especially any string that never appeared in the books you scanned. And those longer contexts are exactly where language is most predictable, which is where you stand to gain the most compression.

So Shannon used a different model of English he had available: a person. The story is he would ask someone to guess each next letter, write the letter when they missed, and put a dash when they got it right. The reduced transcript has fewer letters, but in a precise sense it carries the same information. An identical guesser, given only that reduced text, could reconstruct the original.

In his nineteen fifty one paper, Prediction and Entropy of Printed English, he tightened the design. More people, and counts of how many guesses until the next letter was correct. That is his estimate, from probing human brains as black-box models.

You already have what you need to reinvent entropy. For any distribution over symbols, average the information of each symbol, weighted by its probability. That is H, the sum of p times negative log base two of p. On the diagram, it is the total area of those rectangles. For the robot, because the code was perfect, that area is exactly one point seven five bits per instruction.

Play with the shape. Spread probability evenly across the symbols and H goes up. Squish almost everything into one dominant event and H collapses, because that event carries almost no information. Split probability more evenly across outcomes, and H rises again. Qualitatively, entropy measures uncertainty. Precisely, in units of bits, it is the minimum average number of bits per symbol you need.

entries.title: GPT-6 Astra Explained: From Answering to Doing
titles: GPT-6 Astra Explained: From Answering to Doing
titleKeys: gpt 6 astra explained from answering to doing
paragraphs: Most models stop at an answer. This one doesn't. Goal. Reason. Act. Observe. Adapt. Complete. It'll take a correction mid-job, run tools side by side, work the screen itself, and fix what its own tests break. At two and a half times the token price. The product used to be one turn wide: you asked, you got an answer. Astra is built for work that never fitted one turn. From answering, to doing.

That loop trained all of us. User, model, answer. Clean, predictable, and almost useless for the work that actually fills a week. Think about researching a market, or untangling a repository somebody left behind, or building the deck, or driving a website. None of that is one reply. Every one of them is a path, and a single-turn chat was never built to walk one.

So Astra stops being the whole show and becomes part of a workflow. You set the goal, it works out the next move, and then it reaches for whatever it needs: the web, your files, code, the computer itself. Whatever it calls comes back as an observation, and that changes what it thinks next. To keep this concrete, we'll follow one job for the rest of the film. Fix a broken billing service, and deliver the report. The loop keeps turning until that job is done.

OpenAI isn't shipping five disconnected tricks here. Computer use, coding, research, professional work, artifacts. On their own they're demos. Wired together they're a system. The hard jobs used to mean a person moving between apps, carrying context by hand and losing the thread halfway. More of that now stays inside one continuous task, and the model stays oriented while the requirements move underneath it.

Start with computer use. Astra can work through an interface the way you would: see what's on screen, decide, act, check what changed, and carry on. It isn't sitting there waiting for you to paste text into a box. That doesn't make it magic, and it certainly isn't flawless. The environment still matters, permissions still matter, the harness around the model still matters. But the architecture moved, and the move is the story.

Coding has the same shape. If you're serious, you're not hoping a prompt drops a perfect snippet. You need something that reads the repository, finds the right files, makes the edit, runs the tests, reads the failure, and fixes it. This is where our billing service gets repaired: the tests fail, it reads why, and goes again. Autocomplete was always good at the first answer. Agentic coding is about surviving the second and the third.

Research works the same way. Searching is one shot; researching is a loop. Take the claim sitting in our brief, forty-one percent market share. One source is the vendor's own number, and two independent ones disagree with it. So the vendor figure loses, and the two that agree carry forward. The numbers here are illustrative, but the shape is real. What you want at the end is an answer that survived contact with evidence, not the first page that sounded certain.

And the output finally leaves the chat bubble. One job can hand you a document, a spreadsheet, a presentation. Then the brief changes, the way briefs do. Use our template. Watch what happens: the content holds, while the structure and the style move. That separation is what turns a generated file into something a team can actually work with.

Here's the part you'll feel first. You can steer while the job is still running. It's already out there searching, comparing, analysing, and halfway through you say: wait, enterprise products only. The old habit was to stop everything and start again. Astra keeps what it already earned and bends the path instead. That isn't free, and it doesn't erase work that's already done. It just means adapting no longer costs you a restart.

There's a quieter cost that everybody feels. Waiting. Tool A runs, then nothing. Tool B runs, then nothing again. And if those two never depended on each other, that gap was pure waste. Async tool calling lets other work carry on while a tool is still out. Your application still runs the tool, so this is for the functions you own, not a blank cheque on everything hosted. But when the work is independent, nothing has to sit idle.

Then there's how hard you ask it to think. Low, medium, high, extra high, max. Format some JSON on low; make an architecture call on high. And here's the part that's genuinely new: you can change the effort mid-conversation, and the cached prefix survives, so the easy stretch stays cheap and the hard problem gets the compute. More reasoning still means more waiting and more cost, and the dial guarantees nothing.

Now, context. A million and fifty thousand tokens in, a hundred and twenty-eight out. But that envelope isn't new: Sol carries the same. The story isn't more room; it's how well Astra finds what matters inside it. On OpenAI's long-context retrieval evaluation: ninety-six point three against Sol's seventy-three point eight. The box didn't get bigger; it got easier to search.

The benchmark numbers look aggressive, and the label matters more than the digits: these are OpenAI-reported maxima across effort settings. FrontierMath tier four, ninety-seven point six. ARC-AGI-three, ninety-nine point nine. On BenchCAD, Astra at ninety-five point nine against Sol's eighty-three point three. Vendor numbers, and real workloads always wander away from them. Capability arrives with a bill.

About that bill. Astra runs roughly two and a half times the token price of Sol: ten dollars per million in against four, a dollar cached against forty cents, fifty on output against twenty. And anything above two hundred and seventy-two thousand input tokens bills at higher long-context rates. But two and a half times the token price isn't two and a half times the cost of a finished job, and that's the number that actually matters.

More agency only works with tighter boundaries. The intent comes from you, and policy and permissions sit between the model and the tools. Reading the repository might be allowed. Running the tests might be allowed. Deploying to production might not. If a path isn't allowed, it stops there. OpenAI describes extra monitoring when the model looks like it's drifting off-scope, which isn't perfect prevention.

So which jobs go where? Debug an eighteen-file repository, and that's Astra. Tag a hundred thousand support tickets, and a cheaper model will do it. Research thirty sources and synthesise them: Astra. Pull fields out of an invoice: cheaper. Browse, code, test and deliver the report: Astra. Tidy this paragraph: cheaper. The best model isn't the biggest one, it's the one that fits the job.

So come back to where we started. Prompt, model, answer. That loop still exists and it still has a place. But the unit of work changed underneath it: goal, reason, act, observe, adapt, complete. Astra isn't interesting because it writes a prettier paragraph. It's interesting because the unit is now a job.

entries.title: The KV Cache: Why Generation Is Fast, and What It Costs You
titles: The KV Cache: Why Generation Is Fast, and What It Costs You
titleKeys: the kv cache why generation is fast and what it costs you
paragraphs: Without this one cache, the same answer takes roughly seven hundred and fifty times the arithmetic.

At the end of the last video I left you with a problem. The model had just written a handful of tokens, and for every single one of them it went back and recomputed keys and values for the entire sentence, including all the parts that had not changed at all. That is not a small inefficiency. It is the difference between a model that answers you in a second and one that takes a minute, and the fix has a name.

So let us be precise about what is actually being recomputed. To produce one new token, the model runs attention, and attention needs a query for the token it is working on right now, together with a key and a value for every token that came before it. The query belongs to the present. The keys and the values are the past, and the past is the part that keeps getting rebuilt from nothing.

A quick refresher, because everything from here rests on it. The query is what the current token is looking for. The key is what each earlier token advertises about itself. And the value is the content that actually moves forward once a match has been made. One query for the token being written, and then a key and a value sitting at every position behind it.

Here is the property that makes all of this possible. The key and the value for a given token depend only on that token and the ones before it, and never on anything that comes later, which is exactly what causal masking bought us. So once you have worked out the key and the value for position four, they are correct, and they stay correct no matter how much text gets generated afterwards.

Which means that on every step the model was recalculating numbers that were already right. At step ten it rebuilt nine keys and nine values it had computed a moment earlier, threw them away, and then did the whole thing again at step eleven. Only one column of that work was ever genuinely new, and it was the column belonging to the token that had just arrived.

Put real numbers on it. Say you send a thousand token prompt and ask for a thousand tokens back. With no cache, every step runs the whole forward pass over everything so far, so the total comes to about one and a half million token passes through the network. With a cache it is two thousand. That is roughly seven hundred and fifty times the arithmetic, to produce exactly the same reply.

The fix is almost insultingly simple. Compute each key and each value once, keep them in memory, and when the next step comes around do not recompute anything, just append. One new token means one new key and one new value, added to the end of something you already have. That store is the key value cache, and every serious inference engine is built around it.

So what is actually in there? Two tensors for every layer in the model, one holding keys and one holding values, and both of them grow by a single row for every token. It is not really a cache in the web sense, with hits and misses and eviction policies, because nothing is ever looked up by content. It is closer to an accumulator, a running record of the past that only ever gets appended to.

Now watch what a single step looks like once that store exists. The new token arrives and gets projected into one query, one key and one value. The key and the value go straight onto the end of the cache. The query then attends over every key already sitting there, and that is the entire step, one row of fresh work against a wall of old work it never had to touch.

The shapes say the same thing more precisely. During prefill the query is a matrix with one row per prompt token, so multiplying it by the keys gives you a full square of scores. During decode the query is a single row, so that same multiplication produces one row of scores instead of a square. A matrix multiply has quietly become a matrix vector product.

And that changes the shape of the attention cost. Without the cache, attention for a single step grows with the square of the context, so accumulated attention work over a long generated reply can grow cubically. With the cache, each new attention step is linear in the existing context, so the accumulated attention work grows quadratically. On a long answer, that difference is enormous.

This splits the whole process in two, and the two halves behave completely differently. Prefill takes your entire prompt at once and pushes it through the model in a single pass, filling the cache in one go. Decode then produces one token at a time, reading that cache and appending to it. Same weights and the same mathematics, but the machine is doing something quite different in each.

That is why the first token takes so much longer than the rest. Prefill has to chew through thousands of prompt tokens before anything comes back at all, and it is limited by raw arithmetic, so a longer prompt means a longer wait. Decode is one token at a time and is limited instead by how fast memory can be read. When you see time to first token quoted separately from tokens per second, this is why.

You might reasonably wonder why we only keep the keys and the values, and never the queries. It is because a query gets used exactly once. Token five asks its question, receives its answer, and that question is never asked again, because attention is causal and nothing later ever looks back at it. Keys and values are consulted by every token that follows. Queries are consumed on the spot.

The causal mask has a rather nice fate here as well. During prefill you still need it, because the whole prompt is being processed at once and the earlier positions must not be allowed to see the later ones. During decode it simply disappears, because the only query in flight belongs to the newest token, and everything in the cache is already behind it.

So that is the mechanism, and it really is that small. Compute the keys and values once, keep them, append one row per token, and let each new query read the entire store. Everything from here is about what that store costs you, because keeping it is not free, and on a busy server it turns out to be the thing that runs out first.

Here is how big it gets. Two, because you are storing keys and values. Times the number of layers, since every layer keeps its own. Times the number of key value heads, times the width of each head, times how many tokens you are holding, times the bytes you spend on each number. Six factors, and every trick in the second half of this video attacks one of them.

Put a real model through it. Llama three at eight billion parameters has thirty two layers, eight key value heads, and a head width of one hundred and twenty eight, stored at two bytes a number. Multiply that out and a single token costs you one hundred and twenty eight kilobytes of cache. Which sounds like nothing at all, until you fill an eight thousand token context and one conversation is holding a full gigabyte.

And that is one user. A server is not serving one user. Put sixteen of those conversations on the same accelerator and the cache is sitting at sixteen gigabytes, which is more than the fifteen the weights themselves take at two bytes per parameter. At that point the thing you cached has outgrown the thing doing the computing, and it is still growing with every token.

sections.heading: The problem
paragraphs: Without this one cache, the same answer takes roughly seven hundred and fifty times the arithmetic.

sections.heading: waste
paragraphs: At the end of the last video I left you with a problem. The model had just written a handful of tokens, and for every single one of them it went back and recomputed keys and values for the entire sentence, including all the parts that had not changed at all. That is not a small inefficiency. It is the difference between a model that answers you in a second and one that takes a minute, and the fix has a name.

So let us be precise about what is actually being recomputed. To produce one new token, the model runs attention, and attention needs a query for the token it is working on right now, together with a key and a value for every token that came before it. The query belongs to the present. The keys and the values are the past, and the past is the part that keeps getting rebuilt from nothing.

A quick refresher, because everything from here rests on it. The query is what the current token is looking for. The key is what each earlier token advertises about itself. And the value is the content that actually moves forward once a match has been made. One query for the token being written, and then a key and a value sitting at every position behind it.

Here is the property that makes all of this possible. The key and the value for a given token depend only on that token and the ones before it, and never on anything that comes later, which is exactly what causal masking bought us. So once you have worked out the key and the value for position four, they are correct, and they stay correct no matter how much text gets generated afterwards.

Which means that on every step the model was recalculating numbers that were already right. At step ten it rebuilt nine keys and nine values it had computed a moment earlier, threw them away, and then did the whole thing again at step eleven. Only one column of that work was ever genuinely new, and it was the column belonging to the token that had just arrived.

sections.heading: mechanism
paragraphs: The fix is almost insultingly simple. Compute each key and each value once, keep them in memory, and when the next step comes around do not recompute anything, just append. One new token means one new key and one new value, added to the end of something you already have. That store is the key value cache, and every serious inference engine is built around it.

So what is actually in there? Two tensors for every layer in the model, one holding keys and one holding values, and both of them grow by a single row for every token. It is not really a cache in the web sense, with hits and misses and eviction policies, because nothing is ever looked up by content. It is closer to an accumulator, a running record of the past that only ever gets appended to.

Now watch what a single step looks like once that store exists. The new token arrives and gets projected into one query, one key and one value. The key and the value go straight onto the end of the cache. The query then attends over every key already sitting there, and that is the entire step, one row of fresh work against a wall of old work it never had to touch.

The shapes say the same thing more precisely. During prefill the query is a matrix with one row per prompt token, so multiplying it by the keys gives you a full square of scores. During decode the query is a single row, so that same multiplication produces one row of scores instead of a square. A matrix multiply has quietly become a matrix vector product.

And that changes the shape of the attention cost. Without the cache, attention for a single step grows with the square of the context, so accumulated attention work over a long generated reply can grow cubically. With the cache, each new attention step is linear in the existing context, so the accumulated attention work grows quadratically. On a long answer, that difference is enormous.

sections.heading: cost
paragraphs: Here is how big it gets. Two, because you are storing keys and values. Times the number of layers, since every layer keeps its own. Times the number of key value heads, times the width of each head, times how many tokens you are holding, times the bytes you spend on each number. Six factors, and every trick in the second half of this video attacks one of them.

Put a real model through it. Llama three at eight billion parameters has thirty two layers, eight key value heads, and a head width of one hundred and twenty eight, stored at two bytes a number. Multiply that out and a single token costs you one hundred and twenty eight kilobytes of cache. Which sounds like nothing at all, until you fill an eight thousand token context and one conversation is holding a full gigabyte.

And that is one user. A server is not serving one user. Put sixteen of those conversations on the same accelerator and the cache is sitting at sixteen gigabytes, which is more than the fifteen the weights themselves take at two bytes per parameter. At that point the thing you cached has outgrown the thing doing the computing, and it is still growing with every token.

There is a second cost, and it is the one people tend to miss. At small batch sizes, generating one token requires reading the model weights and the active key value cache for relatively little arithmetic. That often makes decode limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw compute. As batching increases, arithmetic intensity rises and the balance can shift back toward compute.

sections.heading: fixes
paragraphs: So, the fixes, and each one shrinks a different factor. The first goes after the head count. Multi query attention gives every query head one single shared key and value head, which is an enormous saving and costs you a little quality. Grouped query attention splits the difference, letting a small group of query heads share one key value pair, and it is widely used in modern language models.

The next factor is bytes per number. The cache does not have to be stored at the same precision as the weights, and in practice it survives being squeezed rather well. Going from sixteen bits down to eight halves it outright, and there are engines that push parts of it lower still. Reducing key value precision is one of the most direct ways to cut cache memory, when the inference runtime supports it.

Now a subtler problem. If you reserve one contiguous block of memory for the longest reply a request might produce, most of it sits empty, and the gaps left behind are too small for the next request to use. That is fragmentation, and it is an old problem with an old solution. Paged attention keeps the cache in fixed size blocks with a table pointing at them, which is virtual memory, applied to attention.

The token count is the next factor, and the blunt fix is to stop keeping all of them. A sliding window holds only the most recent few thousand and lets the rest fall off the front, which caps the cache no matter how long the conversation runs. There is a catch, though. Models lean very heavily on the first few tokens of a sequence, an effect known as an attention sink, so those have to be kept alongside the window or the output falls apart.

The last one does not shrink the cache at all. It reuses it. If many requests begin with the same prefix, the keys and values for that prefix can be reused rather than recomputed independently. Some hosted APIs expose this kind of prefix caching, and may charge less for cached input.

sections.heading: close
paragraphs: So the whole picture fits on one screen. Fewer key value heads, fewer bytes for each number, fewer tokens kept, better packing, and shared prefixes. Every one of them is a line item in the same small formula, and every one of them trades something away. There is no version of this where the memory comes back for free.

Which brings us back to where the very first video ended. The model predicts one token, appends it, and reads the whole thing again to choose the one after that. That is still exactly what happens. The only difference is that reading the whole thing again no longer means computing the whole thing again, because the past is sitting in memory, already done.

There is still something unsatisfying here, though. Every step reads the entire model and the entire cache just to produce one token, which is an enormous amount of memory traffic for a single word. So what if you could guess several tokens ahead using something small and cheap, and then check them all in one pass with the real model? That is speculative decoding, and that is the next one.

The fix is almost insultingly simple.
So, the fixes, and each one shrinks a different factor.
So the whole picture fits on one screen.

paragraphs: Look at this chat window. The user asked a simple question. The assistant started to type a reply, and then the line just stops mid thought. There is no magic finish button. Something has to decide what comes next, one piece at a time.

Now watch what happens. A single word appears. Then another. Then another. Nothing mystical is happening here. The system is guessing the next word over and over, the same way your phone predicts the next word in a text message, except the vocabulary is enormous.

And every one of those words came from a ranked list. The model did not invent a whole paragraph at once. It kept picking the next token from a probability board, one slot at a time, until the reply looked complete enough to stop.

So when you talk to a chatbot, this is the whole machine in practice. Your prompt goes in. The model ranks every possible next word. It picks one. It appends it to the reply. Then it repeats until the answer feels done. That loop is the product.

We will walk four stops on this tour. First, how the next word gets ranked. Second, how those ranks get learned from text. Third, how preference training steers the tone toward helpfulness. And fourth, why transformers made this scale possible. One running sentence carries us the whole way. Let's go.

Start with a half written conversation on screen. A short system line tells the model to be helpful. Then the user writes: Meet me by the bank. The assistant slot below is empty. That empty slot is exactly what the model has to fill, word by word, from the context above it.

Feed that text into the model and it does not return one sure answer. Instead it returns a score for every word in its vocabulary, tens of thousands of candidates. We will sketch only the top of that board. Which sits at forty one percent. The at eighteen. Sure at twelve. River and Cash are way down the list at this early step, because the model has barely started the reply and has not yet committed to a meaning for bank.

If you always take the top word on the board, you get the same reply every single time. Which. Then one. Then the. The result is clean and predictable. It also sounds a little stiff, like reading from a script rather than answering a person. Production systems sometimes use greedy decoding for tests, but rarely for chat.

If you allow a random draw from the board instead, the highlight box can jump to a lower rung. Same scores underneath. Different pick on top. Maybe Sure lands instead of Which. The model weights did not change. The draw did. That single random choice can send the whole sentence down a different path.

That is why the same prompt can produce different answers on different tries. The ranking function is fixed for a given input. The sampler is allowed to roll the dice among the high probability words. Both pieces matter. Think of the model as the odds and the sampler as the coin flip.

Once a word is chosen, it joins the chat history. The board rebuilds from the longer text. Which made one climb higher. One made the climb to the. Three cycles of append and re rank and you already have the start of a real sentence. Each new word changes the odds for the next one.

Always taking the top word sounds safe, and it often sounds flat or repetitive. Letting the model take a slightly less likely word now and then is what makes the reply feel less like a fixed template and more like a person thinking out loud. Variety comes from the draw, not from rewriting the model.

You can also reshape the board before you draw. Sharpen it and the top word dominates every time. Flatten it and the lower rungs get a real chance to win. Same model underneath. Different dial on how bold the sampler is allowed to be. Apps expose this as temperature or top p settings.

Prompt. Distribution. Pick. Append. That is the chatbot in one line. Everything else in this video is about how that ranking gets good enough to be genuinely useful. Keep that loop in your head while we zoom out to training.

The ranking is not a pile of handwritten rules sitting in a file. It is controlled by a huge set of continuous numbers, usually called parameters or weights. Change those numbers and the whole board changes shape. There is no separate dictionary of answers baked in.

At the start those numbers are random. Feed in Meet me by the bank and the board looks like noise. Zzqt at nineteen percent. The at fourteen. Banana at eleven. Nothing useful yet, because the model has not learned language. It is just a giant grid of untuned dials.

Training is simple in spirit. Take a scrap of real text from books, forums, or code. Hide the last word. Pass everything before it into the model. Compare what it ranked highest with the true last word that was hidden. Every training step is a guessing game with a known answer, repeated at industrial scale.

Then an algorithm called backpropagation tweaks all of those dials a tiny bit at once. The true word gets a little more probability. The wrong words get a little less. One example. One small nudge toward sanity. No human writes the fix by hand.

Do that for many trillions of examples and two things happen. Predictions improve on the training text itself. And the model starts ranking words sensibly on sentences it has never seen written that exact way before. That second part is what people mean when they say generalization. Meet me near the bank can rank bank high even if that exact line never appeared in training.

GPT three trained on about three hundred billion tokens. If a person read nonstop at a normal pace, call it two hundred fifty words a minute, that pile would take roughly two thousand three hundred years to finish. The model also has about one hundred seventy five billion parameters holding what it learned. Later models train on much more than that, but the scale was already staggering in twenty twenty.

sections.heading: 19 Trillions Of Nudges
paragraphs: Do that for many trillions of examples and two things happen. Predictions improve on the training text itself. And the model starts ranking words sensibly on sentences it has never seen written that exact way before. That second part is what people mean when they say generalization. Meet me near the bank can rank bank high even if that exact line never appeared in training.

The arithmetic behind it is worse. Published figures put GPT three training around three point one four times ten to the twenty third floating point operations. Imagine you could do one billion additions and multiplications every second. Finishing that job would still take about ten million years. The numbers are almost impossible to picture.

Nobody waits ten million years in a lab. Special chips called GPUs run huge batches of those multiplies in parallel across thousands of cores. That is what makes training a large language model possible in weeks or months instead of geological time. Parallel hardware matched the parallel math.

All of that so far is called pretraining. The goal was autocomplete on internet text, not careful assistance. A model that finishes Reddit threads well is not automatically a safe helper in a product. That gap is why chatbots need a second stage after pretraining.

A pretrained model can finish a sentence that sounds fluent and still be useless, rude, or flat wrong. It learned to predict text, not to serve a user. Ask for directions and you might get a plausible paragraph that invents a street. Chatbots get another training pass so the ranks lean toward what people actually want from an assistant in practice.

sections.heading: 25 Humans Mark The Board
paragraphs: Workers compare pairs of replies side by side. They flag the bad ones and prefer the good ones. Those human choices become more nudges on the same parameter dials. The board still predicts the next word. The preferred style just becomes more likely over time. Same machinery, different target.

Tone, refusals, formatting, and caution all shift after alignment. The core loop does not change at all. It is still prompt, distribution, pick, append. Preference training steers the dials. It does not replace next word prediction. You are tuning probabilities, not swapping the engine.

The common name for this stage is reinforcement learning from human feedback. Remember the idea more than the acronym. People score outputs. The parameters move a little. The assistant gets easier and safer to use. After RLHF, Meet me by the bank is more likely to get a clarifying question than a random completion.

Before twenty seventeen, most language models read a sentence one word at a time in strict order. Recurrent networks were the default. That made them hard to train at huge scale, because each next step had to wait on the last one to finish. Long contexts became slow bottlenecks on hardware.

Then a Google paper introduced the transformer architecture. The key shift for scale is that the model can take the whole window of tokens in parallel. That parallel structure is a much better fit for GPUs, which are built to do the same operation on many pieces of data at once.

Inside the transformer, the first move is to turn each word into a long list of numbers. Training only works on continuous values, so language has to be encoded that way first. Those lists are called embeddings. Think of them as a starting address for each word before context rewrites it.

sections.heading: 31 Bank Has Two Meanings
paragraphs: Here is why context matters for our running example. Bank can mean the edge of a river. Bank can also mean the place that holds cash. Same spelling on the page. Different job inside the sentence. The model has to use surrounding words to pick the right sense.

Attention is the operation that lets every token look at the others and refine its numbers. Surrounding words pull bank toward river or toward cash depending on context. The list of numbers for bank is no longer generic. It is contextual and specific. Once bank leans river, the next word board favors water, shore, and Which. That is how Which one, the river becomes a natural next step.

Transformers also run a second kind of step, a feed forward network, on each token position. That gives the model extra capacity to store patterns about language learned during training. Attention mixes information across the window. Feed forward digests what each token should mean on its own.

Those two operations stack many times in depth. GPT three uses dozens of layers. By the end, the last vector in the sequence has been shaped by the whole context window and by everything learned in training. One final projection turns it into the same kind of next word board you saw at the start. Depth is what makes the ranks sharp enough to feel intelligent.

Researchers design the skeleton and the training recipe. The specific behavior is an emergent result of how hundreds of billions of parameters settle during training. GPT three has about one hundred seventy five billion of them. That is why fluent answers are easy to get and exact reasons are hard to pin down.

You can see that the words are useful in practice. You usually cannot see a clean human story for why this exact ranking appeared on this step. Treat the board as a powerful predictor, not a transparent mind you can open up. Honesty about that limit keeps expectations grounded.

sections.heading: 37 Four Lines To Keep
paragraphs: Rank the next word from context. Train the dials on massive text until the board stops looking like noise. Align with human preference so the tone fits an assistant. Attend across the window so context can rewrite meaning, like bank becoming river or cash. That is a large language model, from the outside in. The loop you saw in the first minute is still running underneath every reply.

If you want the inside of attention, query, key, value, masking, and multi head attention, I already made that episode. This one was the map of the territory. That one is the street level tour through the math. Watch this first if the loop was new. Watch that one when you want the gears.
If this helped you see how chatbots actually work under the hood, subscribe for more. Next up is attention, end to end. See you there.

entries.title: What Is an LLM? How ChatGPT Generates Answers
titles: What Is an LLM? How ChatGPT Generates Answers
titleKeys: what is an llm how chatgpt generates answers
paragraphs: You type a question into ChatGPT, and a few seconds later a fluent answer appears. It can feel like the machine already had that answer ready to send. It did not. The reply is being built while you watch it, one small piece at a time. And the real puzzle is how it picks each piece.

LLM stands for large language model. Large means a very large number of learned settings inside it. Language means we're focusing on its text behaviour here. Model means a system that learns patterns from examples instead of following rules someone wrote by hand. Put those three words together and you get a machine that can continue almost any sentence. At its core, its job is surprisingly simple.

It reads everything written so far, and it predicts what small piece of text should come next. Here is an unfinished line. The kitchen smelled like fresh, blank. You already feel the answer. The model works the same way, except it does it with numbers. It scores every possible next piece. Bread might land near seventy percent, coffee near eighteen, with a little left over for rain and soup. Those numbers are illustrative, but the move is real. It predicts the next token.

Then it does something almost boringly simple. It takes the winner, sticks it on the end of the line, and runs the whole prediction again on the longer line. The, kitchen, smelled, like, fresh, bread. Same loop every time. Predict, append, predict again. So a long answer is not one giant leap out of a stored essay. It is one token at a time, until the reply looks finished.

That small piece has a name. A token. A token is a chunk of text the model works with, and it is not always a word. Sometimes a whole word fits in one token, like hello. Sometimes a longer word splits, and extraordinary becomes extra and ordinary. Depending on the tokenizer, even a familiar name like YouTube breaks into You and Tube. These splits come from one example tokenizer, not a universal law.

So where do those probabilities come from? From billions of learned numbers called weights. Picture them as tiny dials packed inside the model. Nobody set those dials by hand, and no one wrote a rule for the kitchen sentence. Training set them, across an enormous amount of text. Each dial changes how strongly one pattern pushes the next prediction toward one token instead of another. They are not a filing cabinet of stored answers. They are the settings that steer every guess the model makes.

So how does a dial get set? Show the model a line with the ending hidden. Birds fly south for the, blank. Early on it might say winter at forty one percent, and summer at twenty two. Now check the real text. The real text says winter. Measure how far off the guess was, then nudge the dials slightly in the direction that would have made winter more likely. Ask again, and winter edges up, maybe to forty three. Predict. Check. Adjust. Repeat. Nobody wrote a rule about birds. The pattern came out of the correction.

Now imagine that same correction happening again, and again, and again. Lots of text. Lots of examples. Lots of tiny adjustments, far more than any person could read in a lifetime. Do that at enormous scale, and the dials slowly settle into something very good at predicting language. That is the plain story of training, with none of the math.

Here is why the result can feel intelligent. Ask it to explain how a fridge keeps food cold, and the answer arrives one piece at a time. Each single step is only a next token prediction, the same move you saw with bread. But repeat a simple step often enough, with enough learned pattern behind it, and you get behaviour that looks planned. Simple step. Complex result. Whatever we call that behaviour, the process underneath is still token by token.

There is one more idea you need, and it explains a lot of odd behaviour. Watch a short conversation. My cat is called Luna. Got it. What is my cat's name? The name came back because it was sitting in the context, the text the model can see on this turn. Now push that private fact out of the window. From this conversation alone, the name is gone. Context is what the model can see right now, not a lifelong memory of you.

Which brings us to the failure everyone runs into. Ask a factual question. Who wrote Romeo and Juliet? A bare model, with no tools attached, writes a fluent and confident sentence. William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet. Now look beside it, at the fact check panel. It is empty. Source lookup, none. Nothing was checked against the world. This particular answer happens to be right, and that is exactly the trap. Generating text and verifying text are two different operations. Likely is not verified. If it matters, check it.

One last piece of vocabulary, because people mix these two up all the time. The LLM is only the text generating engine sitting in the middle. An app like ChatGPT wraps that engine in software you never see: system instructions, the conversation context, tools and search, safety controls, and the interface you type into. So an LLM is not the whole chatbot. The chatbot is a product built around one, and the wrapper decides what the engine gets to see.

So here is the whole mental model, on one screen. Text becomes tokens. Tokens become next token probabilities. The model chooses one, appends it, and repeats until the reply is done. Training set the weights beforehand, across a huge amount of text. Context is what it can see right now, on this turn. Keep those two ideas apart in your head, and most of the confusion about these systems goes away.

Now you know the simple version, and you have the core mental model. Inside that stack there is still more waiting for you: weights, attention, embeddings, training, context windows, even models you can run on your own machine. If you want to go a level deeper and watch that machinery in detail, that is the next video. Watch next. How LLMs actually work.

entries.title: mcp
titles: mcp
titleKeys: mcp
paragraphs: If you are building anything with AI in 2026, MCP is the most important protocol you need to understand. It is what turns a language model from a very smart chatbot into an agent that can actually do things in the world. It is open. It is adopted by every major AI company. And most tutorials about it are still surface level.

Over the next twenty two slides, I am going to explain MCP from the ground up. We start with the problem it solves. We go through the full architecture. We cover all six primitives, not just tools, all six. We cover security, authentication, how to build your first server, what is coming in 2026, and the six mistakes everyone makes. By the end of this video you will understand MCP better than most developers who are already using it. Let us start with the problem.

Before MCP, connecting an AI to real-world data was an N times M integration nightmare. If you had four AI models and ten data sources, you had forty custom connectors. Each connector was built for one model, one data source. Change the model, rewrite the connector. Change the data source API, update every connector that touches it. One team described it as a brittle mess of custom wrappers. Another spent three days every time they needed a new tool integration.

OpenAI tried to solve this with function calling in 2023. It worked, but only inside OpenAI's ecosystem. Anthropic had its own tool use format. Google had its own. Incompatible. Proprietary. If you wanted to build a system that worked across models, you were back to writing custom glue code for each combination.

Let me give you the facts. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, was launched by Anthropic in November 2024. It was open sourced immediately under the MIT license. In December 2025, Anthropic donated the protocol to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, co-founded by Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI. MCP is now a community-governed open standard, not an Anthropic product.

The protocol was adopted by OpenAI in March 2025, by Google and Microsoft shortly after. As of May 2026, it has over eighty one thousand GitHub stars and ninety seven million monthly SDK downloads. The April 2026 MCP Developer Summit in New York City drew twelve hundred attendees. This is not a niche protocol anymore. This is infrastructure.
The official SDKs cover Python, TypeScript, C sharp, and Java. Community SDKs exist for Rust, Go, and others. The ecosystem is moving fast.

The host is the user-facing application. Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, Cursor, or your own custom app. The host starts and manages one MCP client per server. It owns user consent. It decides which tools the LLM can call. It sees everything that happens in the session. The host is the authority.

The client is instantiated by the host. There is one client per server, each in its own isolated session. The client maintains a stateful JSON-RPC 2.0 channel to the server. It forwards tool calls from the LLM to the server and brings responses back. Think of the client as a typed, isolated communication channel.

The server exposes capabilities. Tools, resources, prompts. It receives requests from the client and executes them. It can also send reverse requests back to the client, which is where the really interesting capabilities come from. Sampling and elicitation, which we will cover in detail later. Servers should be lightweight. Ideally stateless. An interface layer over your actual systems, not a stateful application tier.

One host, many clients, many servers. That is the topology. Your Claude Desktop might have five MCP clients simultaneously. One talking to a GitHub server, one to a Postgres server, one to your Stripe billing server. The LLM sees a unified tool surface. It does not know or care which server any tool came from.

Every message in MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0. If you have not used JSON-RPC before, it is simple. Every request has a jsonrpc version, an id, a method name, and a params object. Responses have the same id plus a result or an error. Notifications are one-way messages with no response expected.

For example, the host asks the server to list its tools by sending a tools/list request. The server responds with an array of tool definitions. When a tool definition changes, the server sends a notifications/tools/list_changed notification to the client. No response needed. The client handles it.

The second transport is Streamable HTTP. The server runs as a remote HTTP service. Communication uses HTTPS with Server-Sent Events for streaming. This was introduced in the November 2025 spec. It is what you use for cloud-deployed servers, multi-user platforms, and anything that needs to serve more than one client at a time. The active work item on the 2026 roadmap is making Streamable HTTP stateless, which will unlock true horizontal scaling behind load balancers.

Every MCP connection follows the same initialization handshake. This is not optional ceremony. This is where security boundaries are established and capabilities are negotiated. Understand the handshake and you understand what is actually safe in any MCP system.

Step one. The client sends an initialize request. It includes its protocol version, its capabilities, and its client info. Capabilities are things like whether the client supports sampling, elicitation, and roots. This tells the server what it is allowed to request back.

Step two. The server responds with an InitializeResult. It declares its own capabilities. What tools, resources, and prompts it has. Whether it supports dynamic list changes. This response is the server's contract with the client.

Step three. The client sends an initialized notification to confirm the handshake is complete. The session is now live. Step four is the operation phase. Tools list, tools call, resources read, prompts get. All the actual work happens here.

Step five is shutdown. The transport connection is closed gracefully. No special protocol message is required. The entire lifecycle from initialization through shutdown is what makes MCP sessions predictable and auditable. Neither side can call features the other did not declare. This is by design.

This is the slide most MCP tutorials skip. MCP defines exactly six first-class primitives. Three are server-side. Three are client-side. Most tutorials only cover one of the six. The rest are where the real power lives.

sections.heading: What Is Mcp
paragraphs: ⏱ 01:15-02:15 MCP = The USB-C Port for AI NARRATION So what is MCP exactly? The simplest explanation: MCP is the USB-C port for AI. Before USB-C, every device had its own charger. sections.heading: The Problem
paragraphs: ⏱ 02:15-03:15 Claude Knows Everything Except Your Stuff NARRATION Here is the fundamental problem. Claude can answer questions from its training data. It can write and edit code. It can read files on your filesystem and run bash commands. With web tools it can search the internet. But it cannot query your database, check your analytics dashboard, read your Slack messages, fetch your YouTube channel data, or hit your internal APIs. Claude is brilliant at reasoning. It just has no hands. MCP gives it hands. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Build the frustration with the 'cannot' list. Then the payoff: MCP gives it hands.

sections.heading: Architecture
paragraphs: ⏱ 03:15-04:15 How MCP Works - Client, Server, Primitives NARRATION Let me show you the architecture. The client is Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible tool. Your server is the Python file you are about to write. Between them runs the MCP protocol - JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP. Your server exposes three primitives. Tools are functions Claude can call. Resources are read-only data Claude can pull anytime. Prompts are reusable templates that chain tools into multi-step workflows. Three decorators. Three primitives. That is the whole API. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Walk through the pipeline diagram left to right. Pause between each primitive.

sections.heading: What We Build
paragraphs: ⏱ 04:15-05:00 Demo: A YouTube Analytics MCP Server NARRATION For this tutorial, we are building a YouTube Analytics MCP server. Two tools: get_channel_stats - returns subscriber count, views, and video count. And get_trending_topics - returns what is trending in a given category. One resource: channel_config - read-only access to your channel settings like upload schedule and default category. One prompt: content_ideas - a template that chains both tools together to generate video ideas tailored to your channel. This is not a calculator demo. This is a real server that I actually use for this channel. Your channel data. Your analytics. Accessible directly from Claude. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Quick slide. Set scope clearly. 2 tools + 1 resource + 1 prompt. Move on.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
paragraphs: ⏱ 05:00-05:45 Prerequisites - Three Things NARRATION Before we start coding, you need three things. One: Python 3.10 or later. Check with python dash dash version. Two: pip install fastmcp and requests. One command. FastMCP includes the MCP SDK, the Inspector tool, and all protocol handling. Three: A YouTube Data API key. This is optional for now - you can get one free from Google Cloud Console. We will start without it and add it later. No Docker. No build tools. No config files. Just Python and one pip install. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Fast. Show the terminal commands. This is a 30-second slide.

sections.heading: Project Setup
paragraphs: ⏱ 05:45-06:15 Project Structure NARRATION Here is the entire project structure. server.py is your MCP server - the only file that matters at first. Your API key lives in .env. Never hardcode secrets. Never commit that file. README is optional usage notes. One Python file. One env file. No build step. As your server grows you can split into modules, but start with one file. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Quick. File tree is on screen. Narrate and move.

sections.heading: First Tool
paragraphs: ⏱ 06:15-07:00 Your First Tool - 10 Lines of Python NARRATION Let us write our first MCP tool. Line one: import FastMCP from the fastmcp package. Line two: create a server instance. The string 'youtube-analytics' is the name clients will see. Then, the magic decorator: @mcp.tool. This registers your function as a tool Claude can call. The function itself is just Python. Type hints tell Claude what parameters to send. The docstring becomes the tool description - Claude reads it to decide when to call this tool. Finally, mcp.run with transport equals stdio. This starts the server. Three lines of setup. One decorator. One function. That is a working MCP server. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Walk through the code line by line. Emphasize the decorator pattern - that is the insight.

sections.heading: Real Tool
paragraphs: ⏱ 07:00-08:00 A Real Tool - YouTube Channel Stats NARRATION Now let us replace that toy with something real. Same pattern. @mcp.tool decorator. But now the function calls the YouTube Data API v3. The API key comes from the environment - os.getenv. Never hardcode it. The docstring says: get subscriber count, views, and video count for a YouTube channel. That is what Claude reads when deciding whether to call this tool. The function makes an HTTP request, parses the JSON, and returns a clean dictionary with name, subscribers, views, and video count. Claude now has live access to YouTube analytics. Not cached. Not guessed. Real data, fetched on demand. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Medium. Walk through the code but do not read every line. Focus on the pattern: decorator, type hints, docstring, return structured data.

sections.heading: Resources
paragraphs: ⏱ 08:00-08:45 Resources - Data Claude Can Pull Anytime NARRATION The second MCP primitive is resources. Resources are read-only data Claude can pull at any time. Think of them like REST endpoints for AI - but they do not execute actions, they just return data. Here is a static resource: config colon slash slash channel. It returns your channel settings - your ID, your default category, your upload schedule. And here is a dynamic resource template: stats colon slash slash then a channel ID in curly braces. Claude fills in the parameter. Like a URL route. The key difference: tools are actions. Resources are data. Tools execute on demand. Resources are always available for Claude to read. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Emphasize the tools vs resources distinction. This is where most beginners get confused.

sections.heading: Prompts
paragraphs: ⏱ 08:45-09:30 Prompts - Pre-Built Workflows for Claude NARRATION The third and final primitive is prompts. Prompts are workflow templates. They tell Claude how to use your tools in sequence. This content_ideas prompt says: use get_channel_stats to check the channel performance. Then use get_trending_topics for the category. Then generate video ideas that match both. One prompt. Multiple tool calls. A complete workflow. Clients can surface prompts as slash commands. In Claude Desktop, this might appear as /content_ideas - one click to trigger the full workflow. Prompts accept parameters just like tools. Category defaults to Science and Tech. Count defaults to 5. But the user can override both. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: This is the third primitive - close the loop. Prompts chain tools into workflows.

sections.heading: Test Inspector
paragraphs: ⏱ 09:30-10:15 Test With the MCP Inspector NARRATION Before connecting to Claude, always test your server with the Inspector. Run fastmcp dev server.py. That opens a browser tool at localhost 5173. The Inspector lists every tool, resource, and prompt your server exposes, and lets you call them manually. You see the JSON request and response in real time. If a tool fails here, it will fail in Claude. Fix bugs here first. The most common mistake is forgetting the API key - the Inspector shows that error before Claude ever sees it. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: The terminal shows tools, resources, and prompts being discovered with green checkmarks. Walk through each.

sections.heading: Connect Cli
paragraphs: ⏱ 10:15-11:00 Connect to Claude Code - One Command NARRATION Now the moment of truth. Let us connect to Claude Code. One command: claude mcp add youtube-analytics python path to server.py. That is it. Claude Code remembers the server across sessions. Run claude mcp list to verify it is registered. Then start a new Claude session. You will see 'MCP servers: youtube-analytics' with a green checkmark in the welcome banner. Ask Claude: how many subscribers does my channel have? Watch it call get_channel_stats and come back with the real number. If you need to pass environment variables, use the dash e flag: claude mcp add youtube-analytics dash e YOUTUBE_API_KEY equals your key, then python server.py. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: This is the payoff. Build excitement. CRITICAL: Run claude mcp add live on screen. Show claude mcp list. Show the welcome banner with the green checkmark. Then show the tool call. All real, all recorded. No mockups on connection slides.

sections.heading: Connect Desktop
paragraphs: ⏱ 11:00-11:45 Connect to Claude Desktop - JSON Config NARRATION If you prefer Claude Desktop over the terminal, the setup is a JSON config file. On macOS, it lives in Library, Application Support, Claude, claude_desktop_config.json. On Windows, AppData, Claude. The structure is simple. Under mcpServers, add your server name. Set the command to python, the args to the path to your server file, and add your API key under env. Save the file. Restart Claude Desktop. A hammer icon appears in the chat input - that confirms your MCP server is connected. Same server. Same tools. Works in both Claude Code and Claude Desktop. And the same config pattern applies to Cursor and VS Code Copilot - check each client's docs for its specific config file location. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Walk through the JSON structure. CRITICAL: Screenshot the real Claude Desktop hammer icon appearing after restart. Show the config file, show the restart, show the hammer. Real proof.

sections.heading: Live Demo
paragraphs: ⏱ 11:45-12:45 Live Demo - Claude Uses Your Server NARRATION Let us see the whole system in action. I ask Claude for three video ideas based on what is trending in AI right now. Claude calls get_channel_stats with my channel ID and gets back my subscriber count, video count, and total views. Then it calls get_trending_topics for Science and Tech. Then it combines both results - my channel style plus what is trending - and returns tailored ideas with titles, thumbnail text, and hooks. Two tool calls. Real data. Tailored ideas. Claude is not guessing. It is reading my analytics. This is what about sixty lines of Python gets you. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: THIS IS THE MONEY MOMENT. The entire video exists to reach this slide. Slow everything down. When the first tool call appears on screen, PAUSE for 2 full seconds - let the viewer read it. When the result comes back, pause again. When the second tool call fires, pause. When Claude combines both results into video ideas, let it breathe for 3 seconds before narrating. The viewer needs to SEE the proof, not just hear you describe it. CRITICAL: Before recording, run the server live, ask Claude the question, and screen-record the real output. Replace the mock terminal with your real session. This is non-negotiable - the video's credibility depends on this one slide.

sections.heading: Second Tool
paragraphs: ⏱ 12:45-13:30 Add a Second Tool - Trending Topics NARRATION Adding more tools is trivial. Same pattern every time. @mcp.tool decorator. Function name becomes the tool name. Docstring becomes the description. Type hints become the parameter schema. This get_trending_topics tool calls the YouTube Data API for the most popular videos in a category. It maps human-readable category names to YouTube's numeric IDs. FastMCP registers it automatically. The next time Claude connects, it sees both tools and can use them together. Your server grows one function at a time. No configuration. No registration step. Just add another decorated function. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Fast. The pattern is already established. Just show that it is additive.

sections.heading: Error Handling
paragraphs: ⏱ 13:30-14:15 Error Handling - ToolError + Validation NARRATION Real servers need error handling. FastMCP provides a ToolError exception. When you raise it, Claude gets a structured error message it can explain to the user - or use to retry with different parameters. Three checks prevent ninety percent of runtime errors. First: is the API key set? If not, raise a ToolError with a clear message. Second: is the input valid? Channel IDs should start with UC. Validate before calling the API. Third: did the request succeed? Wrap HTTP calls in try-except. Add a timeout. Without error handling, an exception crashes the server. Claude sees 'tool call failed' with no context. With ToolError, Claude sees exactly what went wrong. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Three checks. Make each one clear. Emphasize ToolError vs unhandled exception.

sections.heading: Security
paragraphs: ⏱ 14:15-15:00 Security - MCP Servers Have Real Power NARRATION This slide is important. MCP servers run your code with your credentials. They have real power. Treat them like production services. On the Do side: store API keys in environment variables. Validate all inputs. Limit tools to read-only where possible. Add timeouts. Pin your dependencies to specific versions. Audit third-party MCP servers before using them. On the Do Not side: never expose tools that delete production data. Never hardcode secrets. Never let tools fetch arbitrary user-supplied URLs. Never auto-update MCP server packages without reviewing changes first. Third-party MCP servers run code on your machine with your credentials. Audit them before you install them. Pin your dependency versions. Do not blindly trust community packages just because they are popular. Pin your versions. Audit your dependencies. MCP servers have real power. Secure them like it. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Serious tone. Do/Don't checklist is on screen. The safety mantra at the bottom drives the point home. Keep it practical, not fearmongering.

sections.heading: Deploy
paragraphs: ⏱ 15:00-15:45 Deploy - Docker + Production Patterns NARRATION When you are ready to go beyond local development, Docker is the easiest path. Five lines in a Dockerfile. Python 3.12 slim. Copy server.py. Install fastmcp and requests. Run. Connect via Docker with claude mcp add, docker run, dash i, dash dash rm, and pass your API key with dash e. For remote access, switch the transport from stdio to streamable-http. Set a host and port. Your server becomes a remote service that any MCP client can connect to over the network. Production tips: add logging. Add health checks. Rate-limit your API calls. Monitor token usage. These are real services now - treat them accordingly. DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Medium. Show the Dockerfile. Mention both local Docker and remote HTTP transport.

sections.heading: What To Build
paragraphs: ⏱ 15:45-16:30 What To Build Next - 5 MCP Server Ideas NARRATION You have the pattern now. Let me give you five ideas for MCP servers worth building. One: a database explorer. Claude queries your Postgres or SQLite. Schema discovery plus safe SELECT queries. Read-only. Two: an email summariser. IMAP connection. Claude reads your inbox, summarises threads, drafts replies. Three: an analytics dashboard. Google Analytics or Plausible. Claude checks page views, traffic sources, user flow. Four: an internal knowledge base. Your Notion pages, your Confluence docs, your markdown files. Claude searches and answers from YOUR documentation. Five: a deploy pipeline. Check CI status. Trigger deploys. Read logs. Claude becomes your DevOps assistant. The pattern is always the same. Import FastMCP. Add @mcp.tool. Write a Python function. Connect. The API you wrap changes. The pattern does not. And before you build from scratch - check the MCP registry. Over 2,000 community servers already exist for GitHub, Slack, Jira, Notion, Postgres, and hundreds more. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Move through the five ideas briskly. Each one gets 5-8 seconds.

sections.heading: Full Recap
paragraphs: ⏱ 16:30-17:00 The Complete MCP Server - Recap NARRATION Let us recap everything you built. Step one: pip install fastmcp. Step two: add the @mcp.tool decorator to your Python functions. Step three: test with the Inspector. Step four: claude mcp add to connect. Done. Claude calls your code. Thirty minutes. About sixty lines to start. Three primitives: tools, resources, and prompts. Claude goes from 'I can't access that' - to 'let me check for you.' DELIVERY NOTES PACING: Fast recap. The pipeline diagram animates step by step. Clean and punchy.

paragraphs: ⏱ 17:00-17:30 Subscribe - CTA: MCP NARRATION If this helped you, subscribe for weekly AI deep dives. Comment MCP and I will link the full server.py source and Claude config templates in the pinned comment. Allah Hafiz. DELIVERY NOTES DELIVERY: Warm close. Subscribe button pulses. Bell shakes.
